Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, February 28, 2017, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. Senior Scholar Athletes 2016-2017 (presenter: Mike Jolly), B. All-State Athletes Fall & Winter 2016-2017 (presenter: Mike Jolly), C. TSD Mission Moment: Katarina Tasich, Troy Union Elementary Writing Assignment, D. National Blue Ribbon Award – Schroeder Elementary School, E. Principal Appreciation Month; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the January 10, 2017 Board of Education Workshop, B. Minutes of the January 17, 2017 Special Board of Education Meeting, C. Minutes of the January 17, 2017 Closed Session Meeting, D. Minutes of the January 17, 2017 Organizational and Regular Meeting, E. Treasurer's Report – December 2016; 6. Personnel — A. Consideration: Board Bargaining Teams; 7. Curriculum — A. Report: Enrollment Projections, B. Consideration: Schools Closed to Open Enrollment, C. Report: Schools of Choice 105 & 105C, D. Consideration: Schools of Choice – Elementary, E. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105C – Elementary, F. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105 – Grades 6-8, G. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105C – Grades 6-8; 8. Business — A. Consideration: Bus Purchase; and the remaining public communication, other and adjournment items. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition 2.A and 2.B.** The Board recognizes the 2016-2017 Senior Scholar Athletes and the fall and winter 2016-2017 All-State Athletes, both presented by Mike Jolly.

**Recognition 2.C: Katarina Tasich and "Blacking out Bullying."** The Mission Moment recognizes a third grader at Troy Union Elementary for her efforts to make the world a better place and to take a stand against bullying. During the month of December, Troy Union students wrote opinion pieces on a variety of topics; the students were excited about the project and wanted their voices to be heard, and many of them reached out to the principal. One topic that caught Mr. Cottone's interest was Katarina's essay — she took a risk and shared that the community should do more to stop bullying. A few days later she formally presented her writing piece to him and outlined the steps that could be taken. The ideas were good, but one really stood out: she suggested that the entire school wear black around a unified message of "Blacking out Bullying." The message caught on at Troy Union and throughout the entire school district, with many community members wearing black to support her message. The item closes: "Katrina is proof that we can all make a difference." Principal Michael Cottone and teacher Jess Bronsteen are invited to describe her efforts, and Katarina receives a certificate and congratulations from the Board.

**Recognition 2.D: Schroeder Elementary, National Blue Ribbon School.** The Board recognizes Schroeder Elementary for its designation as a National Blue Ribbon School, an award that honors Schroeder as one of the very best schools in the United States. U.S. Secretary of Education John B. King, Jr. recognized the school in a ceremony in Washington, D.C. the previous November, and just 329 schools from around the country were chosen for the honor in 2016. The item states that the award affirms the hard work of students, staff, parents and the Schroeder community, and quotes Secretary King: "National Blue Ribbon Schools are proof that we can prepare every child for college and meaningful careers. Your schools are on the cutting edge, pioneering innovative educational practices — professional learning communities, project-based learning, social and emotional learning, positive behavior systems — making you shining examples for your communities, your state and the nation." Principal Brian Canfield and Schroeder staff in attendance come up to receive congratulations and a certificate.

The recognition sits oddly beside item 7.B in the same packet, which recommends closing Schroeder to open enrollment on space constraints — the school is being honored nationally and declared full in the same evening.

**Recognition 2.E: Principal Appreciation Month.** Throughout Michigan, February has traditionally been celebrated as Principal Appreciation Month in recognition of the outstanding work of building-level educational leaders. The resolution recites that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools and districts are to ensure that all Troy students are college and career ready, and commends the district's elementary and secondary principals for their exceptional commitment to excellence.

**Consent minutes: the January 10, 2017 workshop.** President Philippart called the workshop to order at 6:00 p.m. with all seven members present — Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Miletti, Philippart and Schmidt — administrators Deputy Superintendent Dziatczak, Harris, Griffor, Gottlieb and West, and approximately 10 other members of the audience. The business services update covered the Section 23 proposal presentation and consideration, with two bidders named in the minutes — Mondrian Properties and JP Acquisitions — followed by the January 17, 2017 agenda items: appointment of treasurer, establishing fund depositories and the investment resolution for 16/17 and 17/18, portable testing tables and chairs, and bus purchases. The teaching and learning update covered special education and an update on the timeliness of IEPs, plus a professional learning update and scorecard. The workshop adjourned at 9:56 p.m., nearly four hours.

Mondrian Properties is the same firm that would go on to buy the district's Section 16 land in March 2018 and the Section 1 front parcel that September; its first appearance in these packets is here, bidding on Section 23.

**Consent minutes: the January 17, 2017 special board meeting and closed session.** President Philippart called the meeting to order at 6:30 p.m. with all seven members present. Superintendent Machesky was in attendance along with Bill Bowman from Great Northern and Dana Abrahams from Clark Hill — the consultant and the law firm named in the Section 23 item — and there were no other members in the audience. There was no public communication. Resolution 17-001 provided that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), the Board shall go into closed session to discuss the sale of Section 23 property, on a roll call in which all seven members voted yes. The Board moved to closed session at 6:31 p.m. and reconvened at 6:33 p.m., adjourning at 6:56 p.m.

**Consent minutes: the January 17, 2017 organizational and regular meeting.** The organizational business ran 7-0 throughout. Resolution 17-002 had Dr. Philippart serve as acting chairperson to officiate until a president was elected. Resolution 17-003: Dr. Philippart was nominated and elected president of the Troy Board of Education. Mr. Schmidt was nominated and elected vice president. Resolution 17-004: Mrs. Fleming was nominated and elected secretary. Resolutions 17-005 and 17-006 appointed Rick L. West treasurer, and 17-007 adopted the fund depositories and investments resolution. Resolutions through 17-011 continued the designations of legal counsel, the superintendent as deputy secretary, the person for posting notices, and adopted the meeting schedule, each 7-0.

The recognition portion presented the Board members with the ONE Troy ensembles, the minutes echoing the script's language about members who dedicate an incredible amount of time and energy.

Resolution 17-013 established the Employment Dispute Resolution Plan applicable to all applicants for employment, all substitute employees, all nonunion employees and all nonunion administrators and supervisors, 7-0. Resolution 17-015 authorized the Section 23 sale — reproduced in the minutes in the same form it appears in the January packet, authorizing the superintendent to negotiate the terms and conditions of a final Offer To Purchase with the Purchaser on terms acceptable to him after consultation with legal counsel, and to execute it and any documents necessary and incidental to the sale — 7-0. Resolution 17-016 awarded the bid for portable testing tables and chairs to Global Equipment Co., Inc. in the amount of $101,162.00 as an expenditure of the general fund, 7-0. A further resolution adopted the Board Committee Memberships for the remainder of the 2016-2017 school year, 7-0.

In board comments, Mr. Hauff described how successful the MLK Day event was, crediting Kerry Birmingham, Dr. Machesky and the City of Troy with putting on a spectacular event; Mrs. Hammond seconded his comments and thanked everyone for the warm welcome — her first meeting as a trustee.

**Treasurer's Report, December 2016.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $9,396,917.30, with Total General Fund of $9,813,108.65 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $10,842,523.49 — the figure the check register confirms at TOTAL REPORT 10,842,523.49. Adding ACH debits of $32,412.94, outgoing wire transfers of $1,971,606.70 and P-Card purchases of $157,549.67, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $16,877.52, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $12,987,215.28. The middle sections of the packet are the December check register run by fund.

**Personnel 6.A: appointment of Board negotiating teams for TEA contract negotiations.** The collective bargaining agreement between the Troy School District and the TEA/MEA/NEA expires on June 30, 2017; this union represents the teaching staff in the district. The resolution appoints Jordan Harris as the Board's chief spokesperson, with Rick West, Mark Dziatczak, Kris Griffor, Stephanie Trotter and Dave Pass as team members to represent the Board in the upcoming negotiations, and resolves further that the Board desires to reach a fair and equitable agreement with the Association.

The team's composition is notable: the assistant superintendent for employee services leads, with the business services head, the deputy superintendent for teaching and learning, the assistant superintendent for elementary instruction and two others alongside — the district's entire senior administration at the table.

**Curriculum 7.A: enrollment projections.** Dr. Machesky presents on enrollment projections for the 2017-2018 school year and beyond, with the analysis provided by Frederick R. Ignatovich, Ph.D. of STANFRED Consultants, the presentation dated February 7, 2017.

The enrollment history, by headcount, runs 12,165 (2008/09), 12,069 (2009/10), 12,056 (2010/11), 12,328 (2011/12), 12,391 (2012/13), 12,573 (2013/14), 12,556 (2014/15), 12,710 (2015/16) and 12,868 (2016/17) — eight straight years of growth after the 2010/11 trough, apart from a single dip in 2014/15.

The birth-to-kindergarten ratio table runs from 4.58 in 99-00 through 4.46, 4.42, 4.58, 4.67, 4.61 (04-05), 4.65 (05-06), 4.94 (06-07), 5.45 (07-08), 5.29 (08-09), 5.22 (09-10), 5.63 (10-11), 5.67 (11-12), 5.94 (12-13), 6.18 (13-14), 5.82 (14-15), 6.39 (15-16), 6.59 (16-17) and a projected 6.18 for 17-18 — a ratio that has risen by better than a third and a half over the series, meaning a steadily larger share of children born in the district's catchment area enroll in its kindergartens.

The methodology notes are explicit about what the headline figures do and do not count. The K-12 head count excludes 276 students: the Early Childhood Program (77), self-contained special education (137) and GROW, post-secondary special education (62). The projections assume 60 Schools of Choice kindergarten and 10 Schools of Choice first grade students, sibling only. Future enrollments would be expected to fall between the MOST LIKELY and LOW projections, calculated by adding MOST LIKELY plus the LOW divided by two.

The Schools of Choice enrollment series is the report's most dramatic single trend: SOC students attending the Troy School District number 416 in fall 2010/11, 590 in 2011/12, 700 in 2012/13, 821 in 2013/14, 907 in 2014/15, 990 in 2015/16 and 1,120 in fall 2016/17 — an increase of roughly seven hundred students in six years. Read against an overall enrollment that grew by about eight hundred over the same period, nearly all of the district's growth in that window is Schools of Choice students.

Projected future enrollment by grade band and year, excluding SCSE, ECP and GROW, then with them included: 2017/18, K-5 5,458, 6-8 2,987, 9-12 4,307, total K-12 12,752 or 12,992 including; 2018/19, K-5 5,370, 6-8 3,074, 9-12 4,307, total 12,751 or 12,991; 2019/20, K-5 5,320, 6-8 3,074, 9-12 4,387, total 12,781 or 13,021; 2020/21, K-5 5,369, 6-8 2,984, 9-12 4,446, total 12,799 or 13,039; and 2021/22, K-5 5,364, 6-8 2,916, 9-12 4,485, total 12,765 or 13,005. The projection is essentially flat across five years, with the elementary band shrinking slightly and the high school band growing — the shape of a district whose enrollment bulge is aging upward. The current enrollment comparison for grades K-12, including SCSE, ECP and GROW, runs 12,494, 12,573, 12,653, 12,556, 12,612, 12,710, 12,710 and 12,868.

**Curriculum 7.B: schools closed to open enrollment for 2017-2018.** Administration has reviewed enrollment for the elementary, middle and high school attendance areas. Because of the elementary and middle school buildings' total student enrollment and physical space constraints, it recommends that Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park Schools be closed to open enrollment. The district's goal for Athens and Troy High has been to maximize each building's enrollment, which has resulted in both being closed to open enrollment for the past several years; based on current projections for 2017-2018 it is recommended that both be closed again, with the exception of not more than twenty-five incoming ninth grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School, with applications for those twenty-five spots accepted during a two-week window at the end of March and early April.

The resolution closes Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park as well as Athens and Troy High to open enrollment for 2017-2018 with that exception, and provides that students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High currently enrolled in grades 9 through 11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain. The following year's list would add Barnard and Martell to the closed elementary schools.

**Curriculum 7.C: the Schools of Choice report.** Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, and Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent, Teaching and Learning, present recommendations for the 2017-2018 school year.

The elementary enrollment projections from Fred Ignatovich give kindergarten and first grade HIGH / AVERAGE / LOW bands by year: 2014/2015 kindergarten HIGH 827, AVERAGE 807, LOW 787 and first grade HIGH 915, AVERAGE 817, LOW 899; 2015/2016 kindergarten HIGH 791, AVERAGE 763, LOW 733 and first grade HIGH 842, AVERAGE 748, LOW 802; 2016/2017 kindergarten HIGH 839, AVERAGE 811, LOW 784 and first grade HIGH 896, AVERAGE 798, LOW 876; and 2017/2018 kindergarten HIGH 863, AVERAGE 823, LOW 782 and first grade HIGH 941, AVERAGE 822, LOW 919.

The elementary SOC application history records openings advertised, applications received and students enrolled for kindergarten and first grade in each year: 2006-2007, 25 and 25 openings, 72 and 42 applications, 32 and 23 enrolled; 2007-2008, 40 and 10, 92 and 35, 49 and 11; 2008-2009, 30 and 5, 95 and 29, 46 and 7; 2009-2010, 55 and 20, 84 and 47, 62 and 17; 2010-2011, 100 and 50, 132 and 40, 106 and 30; 2011-2012, 160 and 30, 142 and 53, 110 and 36; 2012-2013, 100 and 30, 188 and 39, 117 and 32; 2013-2014, 100 and 30, 183 and 61, 98 and 27; 2014-2015, 50 and 25, 133 and 55, 74 and 35; 2015-2016, 100 and 50, 156 and 40, 98 and 15; and 2016-2017, 100 and 30, 165 and 34, 95 and 27 — totalling 860 and 305 openings advertised, 1,442 and 475 applications received, and 887 and 260 students enrolled across the eleven years.

The data summary for 2016-2017 gives, by building, SOC students against non-SOC with the SOC percentage and its change: Barnard 84 / 411, 16.9% (+0.3); Bemis 23 / 499, 4.4% (-0.3); Costello 53 / 307, 14.7% (+2.3); Hamilton 63 / 452, 12.2% (+1.3); Hill 67 / 255, 20.8% (+2.0); Leonard 45 / 394, 10.2% (+0.7); Martell 69 / 440, 13.5% (-1.2); Morse 22 / 457, 4.5% (-2.0); Schroeder 8 / 512, 1.5% (-0.2); Troy Union 24 / 443, 5.1% (-0.6); Wass 72 / 356, 16.8% (+1.0); Wattles 22 / 477, 4.4% (+0.3); TOTAL 552 SOC and 5,003 non-SOC, 9.9%, up 0.2 points. By grade: kindergarten 100 / 798, 11.1%; first 113 / 769, 12.8% (+1.8); second 83 / 758, 9.8% (-1.1); third 90 / 864, 9.4% (+0.3); fourth 86 / 920, 8.5% (-0.3); fifth 80 / 894, 8.2% (+0.6).

By subgroup, SOC students are 19.5% ELL (108) against 29.8% (1,493) among non-SOC; 14.9% free or reduced lunch (82) against 10.5% (527); and 3.6% special education (20) against 9.7% (484). By ethnicity the SOC population is 56.5% White (312), 24.1% Asian (133), 10.9% Black (60), 6.3% multi-ethnic (35), 1.3% Hispanic (7), 0.9% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (5) and no American Indian students, against a non-SOC population that is 52.9% White (2,645), 38.4% Asian (1,922), 3.6% Black (181), 2.6% multi-ethnic (132), 2.1% Hispanic (105), 0.2% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander (12) and 0.1% American Indian (6).

Kindergarten and first grade enrollment history runs 784 and 811 (2006-2007), 804 and 793, 775 and 830, 739 and 817, 752 and 785, 727 and 832, 768 and 795, 766 and 814, 700 and 787, 755 and 728, and 798 and 769 (2016-2017). Non-Schools of Choice students by grade for 2016-2017 run 798, 769, 758, 864, 920, 894, 927, 903, 985, 875, 887, 914 and 947 for kindergarten through twelfth, totalling 11,441, an increase of 222.

A survey emailed to current Schools of Choice families asked about siblings eligible for kindergarten, first grade and grades 6 through 8 for 2017-2018: 51 kindergarten students plan to attend, 4 first grade students, and 26 middle school students — 15 in sixth grade, 7 in seventh and 4 in eighth.

The Griffor and Dziatczak memorandum to Dr. Machesky, dated February 28, 2017, lists the factors considered: current enrollment; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of SOC students currently in the district; the projected number of SOC siblings age-eligible to enter under a limited program; and available elementary classrooms. Their recommendations are to use Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection numbers with his recommended formula (most likely plus low, divided by two) as the foundation; to accept SOC applications for 100 kindergarten and 30 first grade students, anticipating more than 100 kindergarten applicants and allowing the district to admit 100 initially with the option of admitting more in the third week of August if space allows — noting that while this is quite close to the opening of school, some families still welcome the opportunity to enroll; to limit Schools of Choice kindergarten applicants to the full-day kindergarten program; and to accept sibling preference applications only for siblings of current SOC students, to attend Baker Middle School only, where current estimates for next year's enrollment approximate 728 and accepting 15 applications during the initial process would bring the district extremely close to an ideal total student population at Baker while leaving room to admit more in August. The memo text also notes that the actual February Count enrollment for both kindergarten and first grade was above both Ignatovich's Most Likely and Low projections.

The memo's own numbers — 100 kindergarten and 30 first grade — do not match the resolutions the Board is asked to adopt, which set 55 and 5. Portions of the memo also carry "2016-2017" where the subject line and the resolutions read 2017-2018, indicating text carried over from the prior year's document; the operative figures are those in the resolutions.

**Curriculum 7.D through 7.G: the four Schools of Choice resolutions.** Michigan law requires a resolution each school year to implement a Schools of Choice program, and Troy adopts four — the same seat counts stated once under Section 105 and again under Section 105c, distinguishing where the applicant's home district sits rather than adding seats.

7.D adopts, under Section 105 of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, acceptance of applications for a limited Schools of Choice program for 2017-2018 for 55 nonresident kindergarten and 5 nonresident first grade students who attend a school district within Oakland County, with total students including non-Oakland County residents under Section 105c. 7.E adopts the same 55 and 5 under Section 105c for students attending a district outside Oakland County where that intermediate school district is contiguous with Oakland ISD's boundaries.

7.F anticipates seats available for 2017-2018 in grades 6 through 8 at Baker, Larson and Smith Middle Schools and adopts, under Section 105, acceptance of applications for 20 nonresident 6th-8th grade students at Baker, 6 at Larson and 1 at Smith, for students attending a district within Oakland County. 7.G adopts the identical building-by-building allocation under Section 105c for students outside the county. The middle school seats are allotted per building rather than as a pooled total — the practice the district would abandon by 2018, when the resolutions read simply "14 fourteen total" across the three schools with placement based on building availability.

**Business 8.A: bus purchase.** Ten of the district's school buses have reached end-of-life. The Michigan School Business Officials School Bus Purchasing Program was used to obtain competitive pricing, which was compared and reviewed by Mr. Dominick Asaro, Transportation Liaison.

Todd Hensley's January 5, 2017 memorandum to Rick West, headed School Bus Replacement Program – 2014 Bond Series 2 – 2016-17 School Year, records that ten of the district's bus fleet have reached their end-of-life cycle; that MSBO offers a cooperative bus purchasing service to obtain competitive pricing from bidding dealers; that this service was used to obtain pricing for several different models matching the district's needs; and that after analyzing three proposals and reviewing them with Dominick Asaro, they collaboratively recommend the low bidder, Hoekstra Transportation, in the amount of $885,322.00 as detailed in the attached bid tabulation. The resolution awards the bid for school buses to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $885,322.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. (The memo attributes the funding to 2014 Bond Series 2 while the resolution names the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.)

Read as a whole, the February 2017 packet is the district's annual enrollment-policy meeting, and its central fact is the Schools of Choice line: 1,120 nonresident students in fall 2016/17 against 416 six years earlier. Nearly all the district's growth over that period came from outside its boundaries, which is why the same meeting closes three elementary and middle schools and both high schools to open enrollment while carefully allotting 55 kindergarten, 5 first grade and 27 middle school seats building by building. The Board also opens its teacher contract negotiation with a June 30 deadline, replaces a tenth of its bus fleet, and honors a school it is simultaneously declaring full and a third grader who talked an entire district into wearing black.

The organizational half elects officers and re-designates the treasurer, depositories, counsel and meeting schedule. The regular half honors Troy High students who raised over $31,500 for a classmate with Non-Hodgkins Lymphoma, appoints David Pass Director of Employee Services from a field of more than fifty applicants, receives the district's first M-STEP results showing Troy ranked #1 in Oakland County on combined ELA and mathematics, and approves a memorandum of understanding with Beijing Weiming Education Group bringing ten Chinese students to Troy for their senior year.

**Meeting**
Organizational and regular meeting, January 19, 2016, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**The organizational half**
The familiar sequence: elect an acting chairperson to officiate until a president is elected, appoint a temporary secretary, then elect president, vice president and secretary; appoint the treasurer; establish fund depositories and the investment resolution; designate board and district legal counsel; designate the superintendent deputy secretary; designate a person for posting notices; and adopt the meeting schedule for the 2016 calendar year.

**Recognition — "Caring for Karen"**
The Board recognizes Troy High students and staff "who came together to raise money for a fellow student battling a life-threatening disease." The school-wide effort was spearheaded by **Harriet Clark's Personal Communication classes and Troy High's Student Government**, and raised **over $31,500 for the Karen Barrientos Cancer fund** — Karen being an 11th grade student at Troy High with Non-Hodgkins Lymphoma. Principal Remo Roncone describes the effort; participants shake hands with the Board and a folder of certificates goes to the teacher for distribution. Dozens of students are named, among them Noor Al-Sharabi, Julia Alaimo, Katie Armstrong, Demiana Attalla, Victoria Bennett, Frenscheska Brikho, Savannah Cavendar-Le Mieux and Eric Cheng.

The first recognition item is Board Recognition Month.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the December 1, 2015 special meeting and workshop, the December 15, 2015 meeting, and the November 2015 Treasurer's Report.

**Treasurer's Report — November 2015**
Total check disbursements are $5,375,669.60, the General Fund group $3,477,732.82 and the General Fund (101) itself $3,172,152.99. Adding $1,962,353.96 of wire transfers, $157,790.88 of P-Card purchases and $17,422.93 of ACH debits, less $1,983.19 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $7,511,254.18.

**Personnel — Director of Employee Services**
**David Pass** is appointed. He has served as principal of Troy Union Elementary for the past four years and was asked to serve as Interim Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction during Kris Griffor's absence. Before Troy he was assistant principal at Avondale Middle School and elementary principal at R. Grant Graham Elementary in Avondale. He holds a degree in elementary education and a graduate degree in curriculum, instruction and leadership from Oakland University, and was then enrolled in the Education Specialist program at the University of Michigan with an anticipated April 2016 graduation.

Unlike the 2017 appointments, the packet publishes the **full applicant list rather than a funnel** — more than fifty names including Gregory Hampton, Brenda Guinan, Sonya Byrd, Virginia Krolczyk, Melissa Daugherty, Renee Klimkowski, Claude Tiller Jr, Reid Perry, Keichea Shauntee-Wilson, Donald Neibert, Joan Newberry, Walter Stevenson Jr., Jay Arnold, Shannon Carrico, Thomas Harrell, Sherry Morton, James Mallett, Carlita Earl, Shawn Shivnen, Rachel Turner, Lisa Kakos, Michael Grant, Brian Bedard and Kellie Cunningham. (Pass would appear a year later on the Board's TEA negotiating team.)

**Curriculum — the first M-STEP results**
Mark Dziatczak reports the district's spring 2015 M-STEP results with an Oakland County comparison. M-STEP tested ELA in grades 3-8 and 11, mathematics in grades 3-8 and 11, science in grades 4, 7 and 11, and social studies in grades 5, 8 and 11.

Troy's county rankings, combined and then grade by grade:

| Subject | Combined | By grade |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ELA (3-8, 11) | **#1** | #1 #1 #1 #1 #1 #2 #1 |
| Mathematics (3-8, 11) | **#1** | #3 #1 #2 #1 #1 #4 #1 |
| Science (4, 7, 11) | #7 | #11 #11 #2 |
| Social Studies (5, 8, 11) | #2 | #1 #5 #4 |

By subgroup, Troy ranks **#2 in ELA and #1 in mathematics for special education students**, and #2 in ELA for economically disadvantaged students. The report's conclusions note that **test standards — the cut scores for proficiency levels — increased for 2015**, the first year of the new assessment.

The science result is the outlier: #11 in the county at both grade 4 and grade 7 against #1 or #2 nearly everywhere else. It is the same relative weakness the 2018 gap analysis would still be tracking.

**Curriculum — the Weiming pilot**
Mark Dziatczak has negotiated a Memorandum of Understanding with **Beijing Weiming Education Group** for a Chinese and American student exchange. Eligible Chinese students would take part in a **three-plus-one year program** — three years at Weiming schools in China, then transferring to Troy for one year. Troy students would have the opportunity to study at a Weiming high school for summer or winter camps or as exchange students.

The stated goal is to encourage international education for Chinese and American students, teachers and administrators "in order to create a greater understanding between the two cultures, thus preparing students for a global economy," and the item notes the program aligns with **recent Oakland County initiatives designed to establish economic partnerships in China**. The resolution approves the MOU and provides that in the first year of the pilot, **a limited number of ten Chinese foreign students will spend their senior year enrolled in the Troy School District**.

**Other**
Board Vice-President Mr. Schmidt is approved to attend the NSBA Advocacy Institute, under Board Policy B-2001, Workshops and Conferences — the earlier policy numbering, before the district renumbered it 1000.01.

The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Election of Acting Chairperson; 3. Appointment of Temporary Secretary; 4. Annual Organizational Meeting of the Board of Education — A. Nomination and Election of Officers (President, Vice President, Secretary), B. Appointment of Treasurer, C. Establish Fund Depositories and Investment Resolution for 2015/16 and 2016/17, D. (The two curriculum items carry the section header "10. BUSINESS" on their item pages while the agenda index lists section 10 as Curriculum.)

**The agenda memo and organizational items.** Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D. writes to the Board setting out the organizational sequence, beginning with the election of an acting chairperson who will conduct the meeting until a president has been elected. The organizational items follow the pattern used in the 2017 packet: nomination and election of president, vice president and secretary in turn; appointment of the school board treasurer; establishment of fund depositories and the investment resolution for 2015/16 and 2016/17; designation of board and district legal counsel; designation of the superintendent to be deputy secretary; designation of a person for posting notices of meetings; and adoption of the meeting schedule for the 2016 calendar year.

**Recognition 5.A: Board Recognition Month.** The annual January item recognizing the work of the Board of Education.

**Recognition 5.B: "Caring for Karen."** The Board recognizes a special group of Troy High students and staff who came together to raise money for a fellow student battling a life-threatening disease. The item records pride in "the all-out school wide effort spearheaded by Harriet Clark's Personal Communication classes and Troy High's Student Government," which raised over $31,500 for the Karen Barrientos Cancer fund. Karen is an 11th grade student at Troy High with Non-Hodgkins Lymphoma.

Mr. Remo Roncone, Troy High's principal, is invited to describe the efforts, after which the staff and students who organized the projects come up to receive recognition. The staging is specified: participants shake hands with the Board, and a folder containing all the certificates is presented to the teacher or administrator for distribution to individuals — a practical accommodation for a group too large to hand certificates to one by one. The students named include Noor Al-Sharabi, Julia Alaimo, Katie Armstrong, Demiana Attalla, Victoria Bennett, Frenscheska Brikho, Savannah Cavendar-Le Mieux and Eric Cheng, among many others.

Harriet Clark, who taught the Personal Communication classes that led the effort, appears again in the April 2017 packet among the 35 Outstanding Teacher nominees, listed as teaching communications, debate and English at Troy High.

**Consent agenda.** Minutes of the December 1, 2015 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the December 1, 2015 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the December 15, 2015 Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for November 2015.

**Treasurer's Report, November 2015.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $3,172,152.99, with Total General Fund of $3,477,732.82 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $5,375,669.60. Adding ACH debits of $17,422.93, outgoing wire transfers of $1,962,353.96 and P-Card purchases of $157,790.88, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $1,983.19, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $7,511,254.18. The middle sections of the packet are the November check register run by fund. The totals here run materially below the equivalent months in the 2017 and 2018 packets, which is what one would expect a year before the 2016 bond program began spending.

**Personnel 9.A: elementary and secondary.** The routine personnel recommendations item.

**Personnel 9.B: Director of Employee Services.** The recommendation is Mr. David Pass. He has served as principal of Troy Union Elementary School for the past four years, and was additionally asked to serve as Interim Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction during Kris Griffor's absence. Prior to coming to Troy he held several positions including assistant principal at Avondale Middle School and elementary principal at R. Grant Graham Elementary in Avondale. He holds a degree in elementary education from Oakland University and a graduate degree in curriculum, instruction and leadership from Oakland University, and is currently enrolled in the Education Specialist program at the University of Michigan with an anticipated graduation date of April 2016. The resolution approves his employment as Director of Employee Services without tenure in the administrative position.

The packet's treatment of the search differs from the practice the district would adopt a year later. Rather than the staged funnel published for the 2017 and 2018 appointments — applications received, first-round interviews, finalists, final selection — this packet simply prints a list headed "Troy School District Applicants for Employee Services" naming more than fifty people: Gregory Hampton, Brenda Guinan, Sonya Byrd, Virginia Krolczyk, Melissa Daugherty, Renee Klimkowski, Claude Tiller Jr, Reid Perry, Keichea Shauntee-Wilson, Donald Neibert, Joan Newberry, Walter Stevenson Jr., Jay Arnold, Shannon Carrico, Thomas Harrell, Sherry Morton, James Mallett, Carlita Earl, Shawn Shivnen, Rachel Turner, Lisa Kakos, Michael Grant, Brian Bedard, Kellie Cunningham and others. Every applicant is named in a public document, with no indication of who was interviewed — a more exposing disclosure than the later funnels, which name only those who reached an interview.

David Pass appears again in the February 2017 packet as a member of the Board's negotiating team for the TEA contract talks, alongside Jordan Harris as chief spokesperson.

**Curriculum 10.A: 2015 M-STEP results and county comparison.** Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent of Teaching and Learning, provides the district results of the spring 2015 M-STEP testing along with a comparison of scores with other Oakland County school districts. The presentation is dated January 12, 2016.

M-STEP in spring 2015 tested English language arts in grades 3-8 and 11; mathematics in grades 3-8 and 11; science in grades 4, 7 and 11; and social studies in grades 5, 8 and 11.

The presentation reports Troy's rank among Oakland County districts for each subject, first combined across grades and then grade by grade. In ELA across grades 3-8 and 11 combined, Troy ranks #1; by grade the ranks run #1, #1, #1, #1, #1, #2 and #1. In mathematics combined, Troy ranks #1; by grade the ranks run #3, #1, #2, #1, #1, #4 and #1. In science across grades 4, 7 and 11 combined, Troy ranks #7; by grade, #11, #11 and #2. In social studies across grades 5, 8 and 11 combined, Troy ranks #2; by grade, #1, #5 and #4.

Two subgroup breakdowns follow. For special education students, Troy ranks #2 in ELA across grades 3-8 and 11 combined and #1 in mathematics. For economically disadvantaged students, Troy ranks #2 in ELA combined.

The conclusions note that test standards — the cut scores that define proficiency levels — increased for 2015. This was M-STEP's first administration, replacing the MEAP, and the higher cut scores meant proficiency rates statewide fell sharply from the prior assessment; the county-rank framing the presentation uses sidesteps that discontinuity by comparing Troy against its peers on the same new test rather than against its own prior-year numbers.

The science result is the one clear weakness in an otherwise dominant showing: #11 in the county at grade 4 and again at grade 7, against #1 or #2 almost everywhere else, recovering to #2 by grade 11. The same relative pattern persists into the 2018 gap analysis, where science remains the subject on which Troy's margin over the county and state is narrowest.

**Curriculum 10.B: Weiming international student pilot.** Mark Dziatczak has negotiated a Memorandum of Understanding between the Troy School District and Weiming Education Group, outlining a Chinese and American student exchange program between Beijing Weiming Education Group and the district.

The MOU outlines the opportunity for eligible Chinese students from Weiming Education Group — referred to as Chinese Foreign Students — to participate in a three-plus-one year program, in which they study for three years at Weiming schools in China and subsequently transfer to the Troy School District for one year. Students from the Troy School District would also have the opportunity to study at one of Weiming's high schools for summer and winter camps and/or as exchange students.

The stated goal is to encourage international education for Chinese and American students, teachers and administrators in order to create a greater understanding between the two cultures, thus preparing students for a global economy. The item further notes that the program is aligned to recent Oakland County initiatives designed to establish economic partnerships in China and to promote opportunities for Oakland County businesses and ventures in China — an unusual justification for a curriculum item, tying a student exchange to county economic development policy.

The resolution approves the Memorandum of Understanding under the terms of the agreement and provides that in the first year of this pilot program, a limited number of ten Chinese foreign students will spend their senior year enrolled as students in the Troy School District.

The structure is worth noting for what it is and is not. It is not a Schools of Choice arrangement — those resolutions, adopted every February under Sections 105 and 105c, govern nonresident Michigan students and turn on which intermediate school district the applicant's home district sits in. This is a separate instrument entirely, admitting foreign nationals for a single senior year under a negotiated MOU, capped at ten students in the pilot year.

**Other 13.A: 2016 NSBA Advocacy Institute Conference attendance.** As required by Board Policy B-2001, Workshops and Conferences, expenditure of district funds for members for out-of-state meetings must have prior approval by resolution. Board Vice-President Mr. Schmidt has indicated his desire to attend the National School Boards Association Advocacy Institute Conference.

The policy citation is itself a small marker of time: by May 2017 the same requirement is cited as Board Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board; Reimbursement of Expenses, following the policy renumbering the Board adopted in December 2016 when it approved the revised Board of Education Bylaws and Policies.

Read as a whole, the January 2016 packet is the district at a quieter moment than the years that follow — no bond program yet spending, monthly disbursements running at half what they would reach by 2018, and an organizational meeting with no change in the Board's composition. What it does contain is a district looking outward in two directions at once: a first set of M-STEP results establishing Troy at or near the top of all Oakland County districts in ELA and mathematics, and a memorandum of understanding with a Beijing education group that would bring ten Chinese seniors into Troy High classrooms, justified partly by Oakland County's own economic ambitions in China. Between them sits a fundraiser in which one high school's communication classes and student government raised over $31,500 for a classmate with cancer.

Michigan High School Athletic Association membership resolution for 2015/2016, enrolling the six (6) secondary schools under the direction of the Troy Board of Education, City of Troy, County of Oakland, as members of the MHSAA, a voluntary nonprofit corporation, and enrolling them to participate in approved interschool athletic activities; the authorization is effective from August 1, 2015 until July 31, 2016 and may not be revoked during that period. The Board delegates supervision and control to the Superintendent or designee and adopts the MHSAA Constitution, By-Laws and current HANDBOOK rules as minimum standards. B. High School Cooperative Team Agreement: the District seeks MHSAA approval to operate a cooperative team in Boys' Ice Hockey with Athens and Troy High Schools, Troy High as the primary school and Athens as the secondary, for the 2015-16 and 2016-17 school years. C. Athletic Code of Conduct, reviewed at the annual "Vision" meeting, with the revised Code of Conduct for Student Athletes attached (Revised December 2004; Revised July 2015) and to be posted on the District website once approved. The Code contains twelve sections. Section I eligibility requires enrollment by the Monday of the fourth week of the semester; high school participants must be under nineteen (19) years of age, seventh and eighth graders under fourteen (14) and fifteen (15) respectively; a physical examination by an M.D., D.O., physician's assistant or nurse practitioner taken after April 15 of the previous school year; a maximum of four (4) seasons of a sport and four (4) first semesters and four (4) second semesters in grades nine through twelve; and academic eligibility requiring passing grades in a minimum of five (5) classes (Niles 4 classes, Intersect 5 classes, IA 6 of 8 classes), with transfer students new to the district meeting the MHSAA minimum of four (4) classes. Section II limits awards to symbolic or merchandise items not exceeding twenty-five dollars ($25.00) in fair market value and bars cash or negotiable documents. Section III on amateur status applies to baseball, basketball, cross country, football, golf, gymnastics, soccer, softball, skiing, tennis, track, volleyball, wrestling, ice hockey, competitive cheer, swimming and diving. Section IV on outside competition imposes ineligibility for a minimum of the next two (2) days of competition for middle school and three (3) days for high school, reflecting Section 13(A) Limited Team Membership of the MHSAA handbook. Sections V through VIII address school attendance, practice attendance, travel to and from away contests, and responsibility for uniforms and equipment. Section IX on tobacco, alcohol and other drugs sets penalties: a first tobacco violation costs a minimum of the next interscholastic event or one week of a season, capped at 10% of regular season contests; a first alcohol or drug violation or second tobacco violation costs two (2) consecutive events or two (2) weeks, capped at 20% of regular season contests, with a mandatory drug workshop consortium at family expense; a second alcohol or drug violation or third tobacco violation brings dismissal from the team, and if less than 50% of the season remains the student is ineligible for the first half (50%) of the next sport, with professional assessment for chemical dependency at a Michigan State Department of Substance Abuse Services approved agency required; a third alcohol or drug violation or fourth tobacco violation brings exclusion from all interscholastic participation for three hundred and sixty-five (365) days; a fourth alcohol or drug violation or fifth tobacco violation forfeits any remaining eligibility in the Troy School District. Seventh and eighth grade athletes are removed from the team on any violation. Sections X and XI cover voluntary summer and off-season programs and supplemental team rules approved by the building principal. Section XII permits appeal within two (2) school days to the building principal, who must convene a meeting within two (2) school days and respond in writing within two (2) school days, with further appeal to the Deputy Superintendent, whose decision is final.

Item 6.A recommends Mr. William Turner as Director, College & Career Programming, beginning July 1, 2019. His 19-year career began as a teacher at Utica High School; he then served as a counselor at Jeannette Junior High School and Stevenson High School, both in Sterling Heights, before joining Troy as a counselor at Troy High School. He has also been Night Supervisor for the district's Adult Education Department and Principal for Troy School District Summer School, and has spent the last seven years as Assistant Principal at Athens High School. He served as a district team member for the New Pedagogies for Deep Learning Cohort, headed the District Vision Team for Career and Technical Education, and mentored five teacher leaders aspiring to administration. He holds a Bachelor of Science in English from Michigan State University, a Master of Arts in School Counseling from Sienna Heights College and an Education Specialist Degree in Education Leadership from Saginaw Valley University.

Item 6.B recommends Ms. Kristin Martin as Assistant Principal, Athens High School. She began as a Social Studies Teacher at Brandon High School in Ortonville and is presently a Social Studies Teacher at Clarkston Junior High and Clarkston High School, having also served as a Behavioral Interventionist at Clarkston High School and Restorative Practice Coordinator at Clarkston Junior High School. She has been part of a Trauma-Informed Champions Learning Group, a Teaching and Learning Council member, and has held various coaching positions. She holds a Bachelor of Liberal Arts and Education from the University of Detroit-Mercy, a Master in the Art of Teaching from Marygrove College, and an Educational Specialist Degree in Leadership from Oakland University.

Item 6.C recommends Mr. Michael Munaco as Assistant Principal, Athens High School. He began as a Computer Technology Teacher at Fitzgerald High School in Warren, moved to Chatterton Middle School in Warren as a History and World Languages Teacher, then became a Business Teacher at Seaholm High School in Birmingham, where he is currently Career Focused Education Department Chair. He has been involved with School Improvement and 5D+ Staff Evaluation. He holds a Bachelor of Arts in Marketing and Management from Northwood University, a Master in the Art of Teaching from Wayne State University, and an Educational Specialist Degree in Leadership with Administrator Certificate from Oakland University.

Item 6.D recommends Ms. Christine DiPilato as Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, on a distinguished 17-year career in education.

The resolution authorizes Administration to proceed with finalizing an agreement with Chartwells to provide food services for the 2019/20 school year, with options to renew for 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 and 2023/24, contingent upon final approval by the Michigan Department of Education, the contract to be consistent with the terms and conditions of the original Request For Proposal dated March 18, 2019 and subsequent addendums.

Item 8.B awards playground loose fill surfacing material — sought by RFP for all 12 elementary schools and the preschool playground at Athens High School, with bids reviewed by the TSD Operations Department — to Rolar Property Services, Inc. in the amount of $145,603.00 as an expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund.

Item 8.C awards preschool technology for the Troy School District Preschool, an RFP for projectors, paging and classroom audio systems reviewed by Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, with Convergent Technology Partners, in the amount of $117,601.85 as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund.

Item 8.D awards flooring replacement bid alternates to Conventional Carpet in the amount of $94,883.00. **Other.** Item 10.A is a resolution commemorating the ratification of the 19th Amendment. The Oakland County Board of Commissioners asked school boards to help commemorate the passage of the amendment guaranteeing and protecting women's constitutional right to vote; districts submitting resolutions receive a 19th Amendment Suffragette Victory Flag to be flown June 10-14, 2019 in honor of the 100th anniversary of Michigan's ratification, with the flags flown again countywide from August 24-28, 2020 in honor of the 100th anniversary of federal ratification. The resolution recites that women of every race, class and ethnic background across America have made historic contributions to the growth and strength of the United States in countless recorded and unrecorded ways, and that the women of this nation initiated the most significant women's movement in history. Item 10.B is a resolution in support of proper funding of education in Michigan.

The attached Superintendent Evaluation System, prepared by Collins & Blaha, P.C., notes that the Michigan Revised School Code requires boards to evaluate superintendents annually and evaluates performance across six components — Visionary Leadership, Policy and Governance, Instructional Leadership, Communication and Community Relations, Organizational Management, and Professionalism and Ethics — with an optional seventh component for statutory factors including proficiency with the teacher evaluation tool under section 1249, progress on school improvement plans, pupil attendance, stakeholder feedback and goal achievement. Board members rate each component highly effective, effective, minimally effective or ineffective and submit individual forms to the Board President; those forms are not retained and are exempt from disclosure under MCL 15.243(1)(m), though the Board's final evaluation is subject to FOIA, and the decision to adopt an overall rating must be made in open session under MCL 15.263. Under MCL 380.1249b(1)(b), 25% of the annual evaluation must be based on student growth and assessment data, the aggregate data used in teacher year-end evaluations district-wide. Ratings convert to numerical scores of 4, 3, 2 and 1; the overall rating is 75% of the performance evaluation tool rating and 25% of the student growth and assessment rating, computed by multiplying the tool score by 7.5 and the assessment score by 2.5, with sums of 40-35 highly effective, 34-25 effective, 24-15 minimally effective and 14-10 ineffective.

**Notice and format.** The Troy Board of Education issued a Board Meeting Agenda for a special meeting on February 2, 2016 at 5:00 PM in the Administration Building, 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, telephone 248.823.4000. The notice states that items do not have to be taken in the order shown and that items identified within the consent agenda will be acted on at one time unless removed. Readers are directed to www.troy.k12.mi.us; when school is in session, meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m., and can also be viewed at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Agenda.** Four items: (1) Pledge of Allegiance; (2) Public Communication; (3) Closed Session - Consideration: Mid-Year Superintendent Evaluation & Negotiations; (4) Adjournment.

**Item 3.A, Closed Session (dated 02.02.16).** The backup states the Board must pass a resolution to go into closed session to discuss mid-year superintendent evaluation and negotiations, and that following passage of the resolution the Board of Education will go into closed session, with no additional business taking place after that time other than to officially adjourn the meeting. The recommended action is to adopt the resolution: "Be it therefore resolved that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8 (c), the Troy Board of Education shall go into closed session to discuss mid-year superintendent evaluation and negotiations." Blank lines are provided for "Moved by" and "Supported by," and a roll call vote is called for with trustees listed as Fleming, Hauff, Miletti, Philippart, Schmidt, Underwood and Edmunds.

**Superintendent's Goals 2015-2016, February 2016 Update.** The attached presentation organizes the Superintendent's goals into five focus areas: Operational, Business Services, Communications & Strategic Planning, Employee Services, and Teaching and Learning.

*Operational.* The Superintendent will provide leadership so that each central office executive leader maintains purposeful visibility, responsiveness and promotes collaborative decision making. Measures listed are weekly building visits measured via the Central Office scorecard, monthly updates on collaborative decision making identified and measured via the Central Office scorecard, and an annual survey measuring visibility, responsiveness and collaborative decision making. The update refers to the attached WIG Scorecard for building visits and collaborative decision making for Central Office team members.

*Business Services.* The Superintendent will provide leadership to develop a world-class Business Services Department, establishing a formal process integrating day-to-day front end and back end central office tasks involving budgeting, administration of collective bargaining agreements, and payroll/fringe benefits, and establishing best practices and workflow within Central Office to maximize efficiency and accuracy of employee services and business operations. The update reports that training on the eFinance system is scheduled for both Employee Services and Business Services staff, with the goal of learning how best to utilize the software to gain efficiencies in all functions of both departments; additional modules within the software were initiated in the last year, cited as cash receipting and ACA compliance, and diligent implementation of additional modules is expected to assist in improving data integrity.

A second Business Services goal is to create a transparent and efficient process in the development of the 16/17 FY budget, including a structured budget development timeline with stakeholder meetings to educate and gather input, and a process to inform and gather input for the Board to monitor the impact of current and future decision making. The updates report that a schedule of budget events was developed and implemented for presentation to the Board of Education in June and December, with budget events also communicated to administration and union leadership; and that implementation of providing a Cash Position Report, a General Fund Budget to Actual Report, and a Treasurer's Report on a monthly basis to the Board of Education was established. A Board Retreat has been scheduled for March 17th to discuss current and future budget issues.

*Communications & Strategic Planning.* The Superintendent will provide leadership to continue implementation of world-class communications media and community support for strategic District initiatives, with goals of successful passage of the November millage renewal in order to maintain full funding, and identifying and supporting the Facility Review Committee. The update states the District's millage renewal was very successful and passed with 73% of the vote, and that the Facilities Study Team continues to meet every Tuesday evening with a formal report to the Board at the February 16th Board meeting.

*Employee Services.* The Superintendent will provide leadership to develop a world-class Employee Services Department, with the same formal-process goal covering budgeting, administration of collective bargaining agreements, and payroll/fringe benefits. The update lists collaborative integration with Employee Services; monthly meetings currently conducted between the Employee Services and Business Services departments; and successful collaboration during the months of October, November and December on the design and implementation of the ACA reporting module within eFinance to generate novel data and reporting forms within the eFinance database.

A second Employee Services goal covers developing policies, procedures and protocol for basic operational duties, including standardization of handbook and policy manuals for employee payroll and fringe benefit administration, an advanced calendar of payroll activities, and employee directory information. Updates: an alternate data source/master spreadsheet of all District teaching positions independent of eFinance is currently being developed; the Activity Calendar for payroll activities is completed through February 2016 with the complete calendar expected by the end of 2016, developed over the course of the school year using a 60-day advance window; and standardization of employee benefits tasks and employee leaves is ongoing, with new systems and procedures to be in place for the start of the 2016-17 school year.

A third Employee Services goal is a comprehensive all-employee audit of payroll and fringe benefit accounts within the Sungard eFinance database to ensure accurate administration and reporting of employee information and wage/benefit data. Updates: a healthcare audit was completed for all employees, over 1,200, in November and December 2015, with employees audited for healthcare and fringe benefit elections/enrollment; employee directory information was validated in the eFinance database; periphery data such as teacher certification areas and expiration dates is currently being refined in eFinance; and a longevity audit of all TEA members was to be conducted February 1st for accuracy.

*Teaching & Learning.* The Superintendent will provide leadership to improve student performance and further the status of TSD as World Class, with goals to identify ambitious learning outcomes for all students with corresponding performance assessments to measure growth; develop a sustainable teaching and learning network through creation of Content Area Teams (CAT) in K-2 writing, K-12 math, 6-12 ELA, Science and Social Studies; and further implement Cultures of Thinking K-12. Each update directs the reader to the PowerPoint.

**OneTroy Collective Commitments to Ensuring Learning for All 2015.** Commitment 1, Deep Learning as Our Fundamental Purpose: schools will build collective knowledge regarding state standards to clarify what all students must know and be able to do as a result of each unit of instruction (evidence: Essentials by Unit for Mathematics PreK-5), and will provide a system of interventions based on examined evidence guaranteeing each student additional time and support until agreed-upon standards are met, monitored and adjusted using a regular cycle of data analysis (evidence: Multi-Tier System of support design for each building). Commitment 2, Building a Collaborative Culture through High-Performing Teams: schools will work in collaborative teams interdependently to clarify what students must learn, gather and analyze evidence of student learning, identify the most powerful teaching strategies/best practices, and transfer these strategies across team members (evidence: List of Collaborative Teams). Commitment 3, A Focus on Results: schools will analyze data from common assessments to identify students needing additional time and support, discover strengths and weaknesses in individual and collective teaching, and measure team progress (evidence: Common Assessments aligned to Essentials; TSD Balanced Assessment Calendar). The document notes latitude at the school site in how teams are organized - by course, grade level, department, interdisciplinary, vertically, partnered with other schools, or electronically - while stating schools do not have the discretion to allow teachers to work in isolation.

**Secondary Principals Collective Commitments 2015-2016.** States the mission - the purpose of the Troy School District is to ensure learning for all members of the school community; the vision - the Troy School District will be a world-class learning institution; and the values - Deepening Learning, Focusing Direction, and Cultivating a Collaborative Culture. Secondary principal collective commitments are to work with the Building Leadership Team to deeply implement CI Plan Cultures of Thinking objectives and to actively support the Teaching & Learning CAT Process to establish Ambitious Outcomes in 4 core areas and a Sustainable Teacher Leadership Network. Timeline: by November 30, 2015 principals will submit a report of their plan for the year for deep COT implementation and a report of actions to be taken to actively support CAT work at their building and by their assigned subject area, if applicable; by June 1, 2016 principals will submit an evaluation of the COT plan for the year and a report of actions actively supporting CAT work. Possible plan items listed include membership and size of the COT Leader Team, percentage of teachers attempting and regularly utilizing COT routines, summaries of professional development opportunities and building resources supporting the initiative, the Building Leadership Team implementation plan, meetings dedicated to CAT building level collaboration, administrative team participation in CAT meetings, promotion of T&L Department work at staff meetings, and additional supports for building level CAT leaders.

**Department of Teaching & Learning.** Goals are to ensure ambitious outcomes for all students and to create a sustainable leadership network. Slide titles cover CAT Facilitators for Elementary ELA and Elementary Math, Middle School ELA and Math, Middle School Science and Social Studies, High School ELA and Math, and High School Science and Social Studies; CAT Meetings at elementary, middle and high school; Sustainable Leadership Network at each level; and Guaranteed and Viable Curriculum slides for elementary, middle and high school.

**Business 8.F: district-owned property.** This is the meeting's substantive act. The district has been conducting pre-sale investigations of district-owned vacant property and offers the resolution for consideration.

The recitals: the Board's mission is to ensure learning for all members of the school community; the Board appreciates and values the real property owned by the district; the district desires to develop an Early Childhood Center to service its preschool programs; the Board desires to explore and consider the sale of certain surplus, vacant real property in order to offset long term debt for the development of an Early Childhood Center; and the Board desires to authorize the district's administration, its legal counsel Clark Hill PLC, and its real estate consultant Great Northern Consulting Group to explore, market and analyze the sale of certain surplus vacant real property as outlined below, with the understanding that any offers or agreements will be brought before the Board for approval.

The six resolved clauses:

1. The district authorizes administration to further investigate the preservation of the Section 1 property, with the exception of the frontage on Square Lake, which will be split into its own parcel and marketed for sale. The remainder of the land may be preserved in perpetuity either by the district or through a conservation easement or other similar form of agreement.
2. The district authorizes the marketing of Section 11 property for purposes of sale.
3. The district desires to develop an Early Childhood Center on approximately 8 acres of Section 16 and preserve the balance of the subject property.
4. The district appoints TMP Architecture as the architect of record and authorizes TMP Architecture to commence the design process for an Early Childhood Center in accordance with their submitted proposal for services dated March 10, 2017. The cost of services is not to exceed $933,716 to complete phases 1 through 4 of the proposal and is approved as an expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund.
5. The cost associated with the selling of property is an approved expenditure of the Capital Maintenance Fund Professional Services Budget.
6. Revenue generated from these property sales shall be restricted in the Capital Maintenance Fund for the purposes of using toward the development of the Early Childhood Center.

John Waldrop, AIA, principal and project manager at TMP Architecture, Inc. of Bloomfield Hills, writes to Rick West on March 10, 2017 with the proposal. He thanks West for the opportunity and notes it has been a pleasure to work with him to develop the project scope and initial concepts, and includes a breakdown of proposed fees by phase based on their previous agreement for the 2013 TSD Bond projects. The fee for architectural and engineering services is $1,167,144.00, based on 6% of an estimated construction cost of $19,452,406, and includes architectural, furniture, mechanical, electrical, civil and landscaping design services but not technology consulting services or design.

The fee by phase is: 1, schematic design, 15%, $175,072; 2, design development, 20%, $233,429; 3, construction documents, 40%, $466,858; 4, bidding, 5%, $58,357; 5, construction, 18%, $210,066; and 6, close out, 2%, $23,343 — totalling $1,167,144. The Board's authorization covers phases 1 through 4 only, at not to exceed $933,716, holding back the construction and close-out phases until the project is actually built.

This resolution is the origin point for most of what the district would do with land and buildings over the next two years, and it is worth reading against what actually followed. The Section 1 disposition described here in a single sentence — frontage split off and marketed, remainder preserved in perpetuity or by conservation easement — is exactly the structure the Board would adopt in three separate resolutions in March 2018, over two dissenting votes and after months of public comment. The Section 16 land is here designated as the Early Childhood Center site on approximately 8 acres, with the balance preserved; in the event, the entire 19.43-acre Section 16 parcel was sold to Mondrian Properties in March 2018 and the preschool was built at 205 Square Lake Road instead. And the financing premise stated here — selling surplus land to offset long term debt, with proceeds restricted toward the center — is the plan that the December 2017 construction resolution and the 2018 bond issue would ultimately supersede.

The estimated construction cost TMP works from, $19,452,406, is also close to what the project ultimately cost when bid 9855 was awarded in March 2018.

Read as a whole, the March 2017 packet is a district converting real estate into a building. Item 8.F sets the whole chain in motion — the consultants, the architect, the parcels, and the rule that the money must stay restricted to the preschool — while the four construction items around it, totalling roughly a million and a half dollars of site work, doors, painting and lockers, are the ordinary maintenance of the buildings it already has.

**Business 8.A — selling Section 16**
The district issued an RFP to purchase 19.43 +/- acres of surplus vacant land south of Long Lake, east of I-75 and west of Livernois (Sidwell 20-16-401-002) and received six proposals, examined with Clark Hill and consultant Great Northern. **Business 8.G — borrowing without a vote**
Having resolved in December 2017 to build an early childhood center, the Board authorizes **2018 School Building and Site Bonds (Limited Tax General Obligation) of not more than $11,000,000**. The authority is Section 1351(2) of Act 451, which lets a board issue bonds without a vote of the school electors so long as total outstanding bonded indebtedness is under 5% of the district's state equalized valuation. Final maturity is capped at 22 years; the bonds sell at public sale between 99% and 110% of par; PFM Financial Advisors LLC is financial advisor. PFM's presale runs a **3.57% NIC** on a 20-year structure at a 3.500% coupon, $11,000,000 of principal against $2,625,963 of interest on each side of the year for $16,251,925 of total principal and interest, with the required millage peaking at 0.20 mills.

**Business 8.H — building it**
Bid 9855 covers complete construction of a **72,000 square foot preschool building** in 19 separate bid categories, of which 3 — joint sealants, roller shades and casework — drew no acceptable bids and will be re-bid in fall 2018. Rob Carson recommends the low qualified bidder in each remaining category: total awards **$17,107,803.00** plus a 5% contingency of **$855,390.15**, for **$17,963,193.15** from the Early Childhood Center Fund. The largest packages are Titan Retail Industries general trades/exterior carpentry $3,204,000.00, Site Development sitework $2,535,000.00, Contrast Mechanical mechanical $1,658,000.00, City Contracting interior carpentry $1,348,800.00, Goyette electrical $1,324,287.00, Men of Steel $1,267,000.00 and Amalio Corporation concrete $1,017,600.00.

**Recognition 2.A: outreach to Parkland students.** The Mission Moment honors students and staff at Troy High School, Athens High School, Boulan Park Middle School and Larson Middle School who took it upon themselves to reach out in a show of support to students at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, the scene of a deadly school shooting the previous month. At Troy High and Boulan Park, students, staff and teachers wrote hundreds of letters and cards to their counterparts in Florida, sending messages of love, prayers and positive thoughts. At Athens, students and art teachers sent student artwork and uplifting messages. At Larson, the Craft Club made a banner that could be hung at the school to let Stoneman Douglas students know that people as far away as Troy were thinking of them. The item observes that though there is no way to take away the pain students in Florida are feeling, the district is proud that its students and staff took the initiative to be part of the healing process. Certificates go to Boulan Park teachers Ann O'Neill and April Reem and student Britta Pingree; Larson teachers Amanda Fisher, Laura Garver and Katy Stanley; Athens teachers Jennifer McLellan and Melissa Velk; and Troy High teacher Jen Opalewski and students Emma Bossenberger, Quinn Kelly and Josiah Willis.

**Recognition 2.B: Larson Middle School, State School of Character.** A select few schools across the country are chosen each year as a State School of Character through the implementation of 11 core principles, which include promoting good character, culture and ethics; fostering student self-motivation; giving students the opportunity for moral action; and engaging families and community members as partners in character-building efforts. Larson was praised for the high quality of its work in all 11 principle areas, and its application has been forwarded for consideration as a National School of Character, to be announced later that spring. The item also commends Wass Elementary School, named a 2018 Honorable Mention School of Character and strongly encouraged to re-apply for the state designation the following fall. Larson Principal Joe Duda and teacher Charlie Tull receive the certificate.

**Consent agenda.** A. Minutes of the February 6, 2018 Board of Education Workshop; B. Minutes of the February 27, 2018 Special Board of Education Workshop; C. Minutes of the February 27, 2018 Board of Education Meeting; D. Treasurer's Report – January 2018.

The February 6 workshop, called to order by President Schmidt at 6:04 p.m. with Mrs. Hammond and Mr. Hauff absent, covered board professional learning — Diversity & Inclusion Part III with Dr. Jay Marks, Diversity Consultant from Oakland Schools, and a Technology Integration 4-Year Plan — a business services update on WAN fiber maintenance and the general trades package, a teaching and learning update on Schools of Choice 105 and 105c, the superintendent's update on enrollment projections, board committee assignments, and other items including the NSBA conference, the MASB Region 8 election, Five Dysfunctions of a Team next steps and a code of conduct update. It adjourned at 10:02 p.m.

The February 27 special workshop began at 6:34 p.m. with all seven members present, along with cub scouts from Wass Elementary, Troop 1708, and approximately 20 other members of the audience. In public communication, Britta Pingree, an eighth grade Boulan Park Middle School student, addressed the Board to share that she was organizing the March 14 student-led walkout at 10:00 a.m. related to the recent Parkland shooting. She indicated the walkout would be held indoors, encouraged students and the community to write letters to the families of the victims in Florida, and asked the Board to continue to promote keeping guns out of schools. The workshop adjourned at 6:58 p.m.

**The February 27, 2018 regular meeting minutes.** President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. with all seven members present — Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Miletti, Philippart and Schmidt — administrators Birmingham, Canfield, Cottone, Dziatczak, Jolly, Griffor, Harris and West, and approximately 150 members of the audience. Every resolution that evening carried 7-0.

The Board recognized the 2017-2018 senior scholar athletes, who maintained a 3.5 cumulative grade point average while participating in an athletic program, and the fall and winter All-State athletes. For the Mission Moment the Board honored Mr. David Easterbrook, benefactor of the new Auto Lab at Troy High. Troy High Principal Remo Roncone described Easterbrook's involvement: the owner of a Troy-based company providing facility design services and equipment to auto dealers across the country, he led the effort to engage outside help to develop a world-class instructional center. The new auto lab is the first phase in updating the high school's facilities to further enhance its STEM curriculum, with future plans for additional classes in automotive technology, engineering, robotics and the skilled trades. Resolution 18-016 adopted the Principal Appreciation Month resolution.

Resolution 18-017 approved the consent agenda. Dr. Machesky reported on enrollment projections, reviewing the district's history and the projections provided by Dr. Fred Ignatovich of Stanfred Consultants, explaining the data collected and analyzed for projecting enrollment for public school districts, the impact of Schools of Choice on current enrollment, the three projection scenarios — low, most likely and high — and how the projections are calculated, and comparing the projected 2017/2018 figures to the actual enrollment. Resolution 18-018 closed Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park as well as Athens and Troy High to open enrollment for 2018-2019, with the exception of not more than 25 incoming ninth grade students residing in the Troy High attendance area who wish to attend Athens, and allowing students with siblings in grades 9 through 11 at Athens and Troy High to open enroll to remain.

Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent for Teaching & Learning, reported on the Schools of Choice recommendations, noting the factors weighed — current enrollment; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; the projected number of SOC siblings age-eligible to enter in 2018-2019; and available classroom space — and that the information had been reviewed in detail at the February 6 workshop. Resolution 18-023 awarded fiber maintenance to Fiber Link, Inc. in the amount of $55,865.00 as an expenditure of the General Fund. Resolution 18-024 awarded bid pack 21A to R & E Development in the amount of $188,971.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. Resolution 18-025 adopted the 2018 Board Committee Memberships. Resolution 18-026 approved Mr. Gottlieb's attendance at the NSBA Annual Conference & Exposition in San Antonio, April 7-9, 2018. In Board comments, Dr. Philippart congratulated the athletes and thanked Mr. Easterbrook, but noted there were no females in the video and asked how the district could help girls see this as a possible career; Mr. Gottlieb echoed her, recalling that he had only 7 female students in his class during his teaching career and wondering what should be done to open the program to more students; Dr. Machesky agreed more work is needed to make the program more viable in the future.
