**Business 8.A: Section 16 purchase agreement.** The School District issued a Request For Proposals To Purchase Real Property to obtain proposals to purchase certain surplus vacant real property located in Section 16, and received six proposals, which the district examined in conjunction with its legal counsel, Clark Hill, and its consultant, Great Northern.

The resolution recites that the RFP covered 19.43 +/- acres of vacant land located south of Long Lake, east of I-75 and west of Livernois in Troy, Michigan, Sidwell Number 20-16-401-002; that the School District received an Offer To Purchase Real Estate from Mondrian Properties, an assumed name for Mondrian Properties, L.L.C., on behalf of an entity to be formed, to purchase the premises for a purchase price of Three Million Three Hundred Eighty Three Thousand and 00/100 ($3,383,000.00) Dollars with an earnest money deposit of Twenty Five Thousand and 00/100 ($25,000.00) Dollars; and that the district has reviewed the Offer and is desirous of accepting it. The resolution authorizes the sale on terms substantially similar to those in the attached Offer and authorizes the Superintendent, or his designee, to execute the Offer and any and all documents necessary and incidental to the sale.

Rick West's March 15, 2018 memorandum to the Board sets out the best and final offers received for the Section 16 property along with the projected number of homes from the six developers: Mondrian Properties at $3,333,000 or $50,000 above the highest offer, proposing 42 single family lots; GFA Development at $3,333,000 for 33 single family lots; JP Acquisitions, LLC at $3,240,000 for 33 single family lots; Clearview Homes at $3,171,000 for 35 single family lots; Pinnacle Homes at $2,975,000 for 35 single family lots; and Robertson Homes at $2,310,000 to $2,520,000 for 33 to 39 single family lots. Mondrian alone bid an escalator rather than a fixed figure, matching GFA's $3,333,000 and adding $50,000 over the highest competing offer; the purchase price carried into the resolution is $3,383,000.00. Copies of each proposal had been provided at the March 6 Board Workshop, and West recommends entering into a purchase agreement with Mondrian Properties as the high bidder. Mondrian also proposed the densest development of the six, 42 lots against 33 to 39 for the others.

**Business 8.B: Section 1 property, division of parcel.** The School District owns 80 +/- acres of vacant land commonly referred to as the Section 1 property, Sidwell Numbers 20-01-300-016 and 20-01-451-001. The resolution recites that the district desires to divide the premises into a parcel of 7.69 +/- acres containing frontage on Square Lake Road, with the balance to be known as the remainder of the Parent Parcel, and authorizes the Superintendent, or his designee, to apply for and obtain lot split approval from the City of Troy's Assessor and to obtain new sidwell numbers for the two individual parcels, together with any documents or surveys necessary and incidental to effectuate the split.

**Business 8.C: Section 1 property, preservation of the Parent Parcel.** Having authorized the split, the Board addresses what becomes of the land it keeps. Once lot split approval is obtained from the City of Troy, the Board authorizes the Superintendent or his designee to: maintain the remainder Parent Parcel in perpetuity in its natural and undeveloped condition, except that the School District shall have the authority to sell its wetlands mitigation credits to a third-party developer for reasonable consideration; negotiate the terms of and enter into a Conservation Easement with the Michigan Department of Environmental Quality or a land conservancy or other similar entity relative to the remainder Parent Parcel, on terms negotiated by the Superintendent or his designee and subject to review and approval by the district's legal counsel; and, simultaneously with the closing of the Conservation Easement, convey the remainder Parent Parcel to a land conservancy or other similar entity, including providing seed money for the maintenance of the conserved Parent Parcel estimated to be $150,000, again subject to counsel's review and approval. The operative resolution authorizes the Superintendent to negotiate and execute those agreements and any other documents necessary and incidental to conservation of the remainder Parent Parcel.

**Business 8.D: Section 1 property, RFP for the vacant front parcel only.** With the split authorized under 8.B and the remainder committed to conservation under 8.C, this resolution provides that once the district obtains lot split approval from the City of Troy, the Board authorizes the Superintendent or his designee to proceed toward the sale of the 7.69 +/- acre parcel fronting Square Lake Road through issuance of a Request for Proposal, returning to the Board with a recommendation for approval of a purchase agreement. Read as a set, items 8.A through 8.D dispose of two separate holdings on two different theories in one evening: Section 16 sold outright to a residential developer for $3,383,000.00, and Section 1 split so that only the 7.69 +/- acre road-frontage strip goes to market while the remainder Parent Parcel is placed permanently beyond development.

**Business 8.E: wireless networks and switches.** An RFP was issued to obtain competitive bids for upgrading the district's network equipment, reviewed by Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, and John Foster of Convergent Technology Partners. Foster's February 26, 2018 recommendation letter on Network Equipment Bid #9852 records that bids and proposals were received, opened and publicly read at 2:30 p.m. on January 23, 2018. Four proposals came in: CDW at $2,215,578.22, Delta at $1,835,891.19, Presidio at $1,805,226.40 and Sentinel at $2,946,971.40, with several voluntary alternates from Delta and Presidio. All bidders provided compliant proposals.

Foster recommends award to Presidio together with Voluntary Alternates #1, #3 and #5: base bid $1,805,226.40, Voluntary Alternate #1 at $14,976.00 for Cisco ISE Endpoint Plus licensing, Voluntary Alternate #3 at $23,602.00 for outdoor access points at Athens High, Troy High, Baker Middle, Boulan Park Middle, Larson Middle and Smith Middle, and Voluntary Alternate #5 at $3,824.00 for additional fiber ports at the Troy High MDF, for a total award of $1,847,628.40. Unlike the fiber maintenance award the month before, here the recommended vendor is also the low bidder: Presidio "has presented a solution that is both the lowest bid and meets the stringent requirements defined in the request for proposal," providing a highly reliable network with enough bandwidth to meet the district's needs for years to come. Listed features include dual-5GHz capability on access points offering nearly double the performance and capacity, automatic interference detection, classification and mitigation, a Cisco and Apple partnership offering access to Apple engineering, advanced RF tuning and optimization, automatic localization of wireless services such as AirPlay, AirPrint and Chromecast, and single-pane-of-glass management. The resolution awards the network equipment to Presidio in the amount of $1,847,628.40 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

**Business 8.F: musical instruments, vocal music and art supplies.** Invitations to bid were sent to seventeen potential bidders to provide closed sealed pricing for the required musical instruments, vocal music and art supplies. Twelve responses were received; two of those were not received prior to the due date and were not opened. Todd Hensley, Purchasing Supervisor, reviewed the proposals with Joe Havrilla, Instrumental Music Coordinator; Rosanne Thomas, Vocal Music Coordinator; and Katherine Hosbach, Visual Arts Coordinator, and they recommend the low bidders to specification.

The awards are: Dick Blick Company $29,979.00; Evola Music $18,220.00; K & S Music $960.00; Lone Star Percussion $2,839.63; Music & Arts $15,423.20; Marshall Music $92,349.50; Sam Ash Music $13,311.00; Washington Music Center $186,732.40; Wenger Corporation $27,819.00; and Woodwind & Brasswind, Inc. $6,002.00 — a total of $393,635.73, approved as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund. The packet carries the underlying line-item worksheets by building, itemizing instruments and equipment down to individual pieces such as a Wenger chair move and store cart for the Smith Middle School orchestra at $361.00.

**Business 8.G: Early Childhood financing.** In December 2017 the Board passed a resolution to proceed with the construction of an Early Childhood Center, and the district now proceeds with issuing general obligation school building and site bonds. The authority matters as much as the amount: Section 1351(2) of Act 451, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, as amended, authorizes the board of education of a school district to borrow money and issue bonds or notes **without the vote of the school electors** if the total outstanding bonded indebtedness of the district is less than 5% of the state equalized valuation of the taxable property within the district. The Board deems it necessary to undertake the construction of an early childhood center facility, and deems it advisable to authorize bonds in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed Eleven Million Dollars ($11,000,000), or such lesser amount as determined by the Superintendent or Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, to pay a portion of the costs of the project and the costs of issuance. The district has posted notice under Section 308 of Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, that the bonds will be secured by a pledge of the district's full faith and credit, subject to constitutional and statutory tax rate limitations, and must either be granted qualified status within the meaning of Act 34 or receive prior approval of the bonds from the Michigan Department of Treasury.

The attached authorizing resolution is captioned Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, Resolution Authorizing 2018 School Building and Site Bonds (Limited Tax General Obligation), for a regular meeting held March 20, 2018 at 7:00 p.m. prevailing Eastern Time. It authorizes bonds designated the 2018 School Building and Site Bonds to be issued in one or more series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $11,000,000. Bond details: registered as to principal and interest in denominations of $5,000 or integral multiples, dated as of the date of delivery or such other date as the Authorized Officer determines at sale, maturing May 1 or November 1 in principal amounts determined at sale, with **final maturity no later than twenty-two years from the date of issue**. The bonds shall be sold at public sale at a price not less than 99% and no more than 110% of principal amount, may be issued as serial or term bonds or both, and are subject to redemption prior to maturity at times and prices determined by the Authorized Officer; term bonds designated by the original purchaser are subject to mandatory redemption per the maturity schedule in the notice of sale. Interest is paid by check drawn on the Transfer Agent and mailed to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month prior to each payment date; principal is payable at a bank or trust company selected as registrar and transfer agent; the bonds may be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company. The resolution appoints PFM Financial Advisors LLC as financial advisor and directs filings with the Municipal Advisory Council of Michigan at 535 Griswold, Suite 1850, with the Official Statement supplied under Rule 15c2-12.

PFM's presale schedule of estimated payments needed to retire the bonded debt models a 20-year, $11,000,000 issue at a **presale NIC of 3.57%**. The structure carries a 3.500% interest rate on all principal maturities, with no principal due in the first two years — interest only at $192,500 each side of the year — and principal beginning at $390,000 in tax year 2020 and rising to $750,000 in tax year 2039. Annual principal and interest sits close to $775,000 across the life of the issue, from $385,000 in the interest-only years up to a peak of $776,375. The totals are $2,625,963 of November 1 interest, $2,625,963 of May 1 interest, $11,000,000 of principal and $16,251,925 of total principal and interest. Projected taxable value grows from $3,747,756,940 in tax year 2017 at rates of 3.15%, then 1.00%, 1.50% and 2.00% thereafter, reaching $5,939,674,035 by tax year 2041, and the mills needed for all debt stay between 0.10 and 0.20 across the schedule.

**Business 8.H: Early Childhood Center construction.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on the construction of a new early childhood center, with responses reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations, and the bond team of TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow. Carson's March 14, 2018 memorandum to Rick West on RFP 9855 records that the scope of work included complete construction of a 72,000 square foot preschool building; that the RFP consists of 19 separate bid categories, 3 of which — joint sealants, roller shades and casework — will be re-bid in the fall of 2018 due to a lack of acceptable bids; and that all proposals were reviewed for bid thoroughness, accuracy and project alternates by the project team of Barton Malow, TMP and Lecole Planners. He recommends the low qualified bidder in each remaining category.

The awards are: 03000 Concrete, Amalio Corporation, $1,017,600.00; 04000 Masonry, Baker Construction, $830,300.00; 05000 Steel, Men of Steel, $1,267,000.00; 06000 General Trades/Exterior Carpentry, Titan Retail Industries, $3,204,000.00; 07000 Roofing/Shingles, Streng Roofing, $742,000.00; 08000 Exterior Doors/Aluminum Windows, Hewett Company, $490,000.00; 09200 Interior Carpentry, City Contracting, $1,348,800.00; 09300 Tile, Empire Tile, $178,550.00; 09650 Flooring, Conventional Carpet, $389,000.00; 09900 Painting, Continental Contracting, $53,500.00; 10110 Visual Display, Cig-Jan Products, $44,377.00; 11400 Food Service Equipment, Stafford-Smith Co., $119,919.00; 21100 Fire Suppression, Professional Sprinkler, $199,780.00; 22000 Plumbing, Contrast Mechanical, $940,000.00; 23000 Mechanical, Contrast Mechanical, $1,658,000.00; 23093 Temperature Controls, MCMI, Inc., $433,000.00; 26000 Electrical, Goyette Company, $1,324,287.00; 32000 Sitework, Site Development, $2,535,000.00; and 32120 Paving, Nagle Paving, $332,690.00. Total awards are $17,107,803.00, the 5% contingency is $855,390.15, and the total recommended amount is $17,963,193.15. A separate purchase order will be issued for each bid category, funded from the ECC Fund. The resolution awards bid 9855 in the amount of $17,963,193.15 as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund.

The attached bid tabulation records the allowances included in the base bids and removed during post-bid reviews — $20,000 general trades, $50,000 interior carpentry, $100,000 mechanical (Barnard, Bemis, Wass Addendum #1) and $30,000 electrical — with the $120,000 sitework allowance kept. It also shows how close the concrete category was: Amalio at $1,010,800.00 with a bid clarification adding exterior column enclosures at $6,800.00, against McCarthy Construction at $1,025,200.00, Gemelli Concrete at $1,169,000.00 and Fessler Bowman at $1,260,000.00, with each bidder's familial-disclosure and Iran-certification boxes checked.

Taken as a whole, this is the meeting at which the Early Childhood Center stopped being a decision and became a project: an $11,000,000 borrowing authorized without going to the voters under the Act 451 debt-capacity test, and $17,963,193.15 of construction awarded the same evening — the gap between the two covered from the district's own Early Childhood Center Fund and, in part, by the proceeds of the land it was selling in the four business items immediately preceding.

**Meeting**
Board of Education, Troy, Michigan — regular board meeting, September 15, 2020, held remotely via Zoom Webinar with public notice posted so community members could participate remotely. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:05 p.m. Present via Zoom videoconference with Mr. Schmidt were board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Pagel and West; and approximately 275 additional members of the audience.

**Recognitions**
- ASBO International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting Program honored the district for its Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2019; Finance Director Kandice Moynihan and her staff were recognized.
- Student representatives for 2020-2021 were introduced: Carlton Thomas (Troy College & Career High School, second year, not in attendance, works as a student technology support technician, plans a journeyman's electrician license); Pranay Gupta (International Academy-East, second year, robotics, Forensics club, symphony and full orchestras); Nathania Nartey (Athens High School, Summa Cum Laude, varsity track and cheer); and Sejal Patil (Troy High School, HOSA, Student Government, founder of Connect4Cancer, plans to become a surgical oncologist).
- Wass and Wattles Elementary Schools received the 2020 National School of Character Award from Character.org, two of 84 schools nationwide, under Principals Matt Jansen and Dr. Joyce Brasington; Wass teacher Mark Cavataio spoke on behalf of Wass.

**Public communication (agenda items)**
Troy residents Troy Otto (in-person learning), Matthew Sims (safe and effective return to in-person education), Rebecca Anders (in-person instruction for students with IEPs) and Stacey Olsen (support for virtual schooling) addressed the Board.

**Actions**

| No. | Action | Mover / support | Vote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20-072 | Consent agenda items A-D: minutes of the August 5, 2020 Special Workshop, August 12, 2020 Special Meeting, August 18, 2020 Special Meeting, and Treasurer's Report - July 2020 | Hauff / Anne | 7-0 |
| 20-073 | Personnel recommendations (18 new hires) | Hammond / Philippart | 7-0 |
| 20-074 | Purchase of acrylic shields from IMBranded for $445,387.90, approved as a General Fund expenditure | Wilson / Philippart | 7-0 |
| — | Closed session for negotiations under the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c) | Anne / Philippart | 7-0 |

New hires approved under 20-073: Jordan Moses, Jaynie Sorenson, Rachel Cervi, Katelyn Bowman, Megan Feeley, Eric Kravako, Kasey Garvelink, Erica Peplinski, M. **Reports**
- Staffing: John Pagel, Director of Employee Services, reviewed teacher staffing for 2020/2021, citing retirements and resignations, full-year leaves of absence, FTE status and student enrollment.
- Equity: Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent for Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent for Secondary Instruction, presented on equity and inclusion work and professional learning, including the expanded partnership with the National Equity Project and community conversations.

Official minutes of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, for the board meeting of September 15, 2020, conducted as a Zoom Webinar. A public notice was posted in order to allow community members to participate remotely.

CALL TO ORDER AND ATTENDANCE. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:05 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present via Zoom videoconference were board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson — a full seven-member board. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Pagel and West; and approximately 275 additional members of the audience.

RECOGNITION — ASBO CERTIFICATE OF EXCELLENCE. The Association of School Business Officials International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting Program honored the Troy School District for excellence in the preparation and issuance of a high quality Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2019. The minutes note that the Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting was created by ASBO International to enable business officials to achieve a high standard of financial reporting, and recognize Kandice Moynihan, Finance Director, and her staff for their effort and continued dedication to excellence.

STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES FOR BOARD MEETINGS. President Schmidt introduced and welcomed four high school student representatives to the Board for the 2020-2021 school year. Carlton Thomas of Troy College & Career High School, beginning his second year as a student representative, was not in attendance; the minutes describe him as a senior and one of TCCHS's strongest leaders academically and socially, devoted to his family, currently employed by the Troy School District as a student technology support technician, with post-secondary goals of obtaining a journeyman's license as an electrician and eventually owning his own electrical company. Pranay Gupta of International Academy-East, also in his second year as a representative, is a senior involved in the school's robotics team, Forensics club, and the school's symphony and full orchestras, and plans to pursue engineering and business in college. Nathania Nartey is a senior and a Redhawk at Athens High School, an all-A honors and Summa Cum Laude student who competes on the varsity track and cheer teams and values the sense of community sports provide and Athens' community-outreach opportunities. Sejal Patil is a senior at Troy High School active in Troy High's HOSA chapter and Student Government and founder of a club called Connect4Cancer; she plans to become a surgical oncologist and lists photography, piano, biking and helping her community among her hobbies.

REPORTS FROM STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES. Pranay Gupta shared a brief update on how the school year had started, noting the International Academy-East had been in school for 19 days. Nathania Nartey shared a brief update on how the virtual learning platform was going at Athens High School, and Sejal Patil did the same for Troy High School. Carlton Thomas was not present.

NATIONAL SCHOOL OF CHARACTER AWARD. The Board honored Wass and Wattles Elementary Schools for receiving the 2020 National School of Character Award. Wass and Wattles were two of 84 schools across the country to receive the distinction from Character.org, a national advocate and leader for character in education. The program recognized the schools for using character development to drive a positive impact on academics, student behavior and cultural climate. Under the leadership of Principals Matt Jansen and Dr. Joyce Brasington, the committee praised the schools for promoting good character, culture and ethics; fostering student self-motivation; giving students the opportunity for moral action; and engaging families and community members as partners in character-building efforts. Mr. Jansen invited Wass teacher Mark Cavataio to speak on behalf of Wass Elementary, and Dr. Brasington shared remarks about the Wattles staff.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS. None.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS). Troy resident Troy Otto addressed the Board regarding in-person learning for students. Troy resident Matthew Sims addressed the Board regarding a safe and effective return to in-person education. Troy resident Rebecca Anders addressed the Board regarding in-person instruction for students with IEPs. Troy resident Stacey Olsen addressed the Board in support of virtual schooling for Troy students.

GENERAL — CONSENT AGENDA (RESOLUTION 20-072). It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C and D on the consent agenda: minutes of the August 5, 2020 Special Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the August 12, 2020 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the August 18, 2020 Special Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for July 2020. On a roll call vote, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Schmidt all voted yes: 7 yes, 0 no.

PERSONNEL — ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY (RESOLUTION 20-073). It was moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Board approve the personnel recommendations. The new hires listed are Jordan Moses, Jaynie Sorenson, Rachel Cervi, Katelyn Bowman, Megan Feeley, Eric Kravako, Kasey Garvelink, Erica Peplinski, M. Katherine Allen, Morgan Clark, Alexander Welsh, Shelby Allard, Kristina Forbes, Lauren Church, Katelyn Atkinson, Rachel Scott, Madison Hileman and Andre Gilford. On a roll call vote, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt and Wilson voted yes: 7 yes, 0 no.

STAFFING UPDATE. John Pagel, Director of Employee Services, provided a brief update on teacher staffing for the 2020/2021 school year and described the factors influencing the number of teachers hired, including retirements and resignations, full-year leaves of absence, FTE status, and student enrollment.

CURRICULUM — EQUITY UPDATE. Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent for Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent for Secondary Instruction, shared a PowerPoint presentation on the equity and inclusion work happening in the District and the professional learning staff are participating in. They discussed the district's continued and expanded partnership with the National Equity Project and the hosting of community conversations with students, staff and families. Board discussion followed the presentation.

ENROLLMENT UPDATE. Kris Griffor provided an update on the District's enrollment status, thanked the Central Enrollment team for their work enrolling the many new families who had joined the District, and reported enrollment numbers as of that day while noting the numbers were still changing daily.

BUSINESS — PURCHASE OF PPE (RESOLUTION 20-074). It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart that the district purchase acrylic shields from IMBranded in the amount of $445,387.90 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the General Fund. On a roll call vote, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson and Anne voted yes: 7 yes, 0 no.

BOND, BUILDING AND SITE SINKING FUND UPDATE. Mr. West, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, and Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, provided an update on building improvement projects, the Niles relocation project, and the renovation of the Troy School District Learning Center, sharing a PowerPoint with slides of site improvement projects at various schools throughout the District. Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, provided an update on technology bond projects completed over the summer, including upgrades to AV systems, additional security cameras and iPads.

OTHER — SUPERINTENDENT'S UPDATE. Dr. Machesky, Superintendent, shared a PowerPoint presentation providing an update on the District's Return to Learn Plan.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). None. Mr. Schmidt announced that the next Board Workshop would be held Tuesday, October 6 at 6:00 p.m. and the next regular Board Meeting on October 20 at 7:00 p.m.

CLOSED SESSION — NEGOTIATIONS. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), the Troy Board of Education go into closed session to discuss negotiations. On a roll call vote, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne and Gottlieb voted yes: 7 yes, 0 no. The Board moved into closed session at 10:08 p.m. and the meeting reconvened at 10:09 p.m.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 10:53 p.m. The minutes are respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Board presentation titled "What is a Board Member?" prepared for the October 20, 2020 Troy Board of Education meeting, laying out the legal and ethical framework governing individual school board members and then applying it to a specific case. After reviewing the Michigan School Code, the National School Boards Association Code of Ethics, Michigan Association of School Boards governance standards and the district's own Code of Ethics in Policy Manual Section 1000.01, the deck presents the case for disclaiming and censuring Trustee Elizabeth Hammond over Facebook posts to a Troy Parent Group on September 23 and 24, 2020. It closes with a motion by Nancy Philippart declaring that Trustee Hammond's opinions and actions are those of an individual community member and do not represent the Troy Board of Education.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Purpose**
A governance presentation to the Troy Board of Education on the role and limits of an individual school board member, followed by the case for disclaiming and censuring Trustee Elizabeth Hammond.

**Governance framework**
School board members are elected officials who must uphold the Michigan Constitution's mandate to provide free public elementary and secondary education. Under the School Code, board powers include actions incidental or appropriate to operating the district and in the interests of public elementary and secondary education; educating pupils K-12, preschool and adult education; providing for the safety and welfare of students; acquiring and disposing of school property; matters involving the receipt and expenditure of school funds; and joint agreements and cooperative arrangements — but actions cannot conflict with or circumvent state prohibitions.

**Ethical standards cited**
- National School Boards Association Code of Ethics: "As a member of my local Board of Education I will strive to improve public education, and to that end I will take no private action that will compromise the board or administration."
- Michigan Association of School Boards Board of Education Governance Standards, endorsed by the Michigan State Board of Education, standards 3.a (no independent legal authority for individual members), 3.c (follows established policies and procedures), 3.d (supports decisions of the Board after a vote regardless of individual position), and 3.g (understanding of and respect for district structure and protocols).
- TSD Policy Manual Section 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board: each member has signed a Code of Ethics acknowledging no individual legal authority, decisions only by majority vote at a public meeting, no private action compromising the Board or administration, respect for confidentiality of privileged information, abiding by majority decisions, and a positive working relationship with the Superintendent.

**Remedies for violations**
Censure is defined via Oxford Languages as the expressing of "formal disapproval"; by majority vote the Board may censure a member for violating federal or Michigan law, the Bylaws or Board policy. Separately, Michigan law requires a board to act only as a board; under Section 1201 of the Revised School Code trustees may exercise power only collectively at a regular or properly called special meeting. A disclaiming motion passed by a board majority alerts the community that an individual trustee's actions do not represent the will of the board.

**Prior counsel to Trustee Hammond**
The deck states she was informally advised on at least three occasions: the President's letter of October 2, 2019; the Board self evaluation of January 2020; and the special board meeting of September 29, 2020.

**Posts at issue**
Four Facebook exchanges in the Troy Parent Group are quoted: a September 23, 2020 post asserting the current plan "DOES NOT" adhere to safety protocols and "PUTS THE ENTIRE COMMUNITY AT RISK"; a September 24, 2020 exchange about the 4 p.m. timing of the September 29 special board meeting ("unfortunately I couldn't control the time"); a September 24 reply about face shields ("We are so screwed. Thank you for being so vocal."); and a September 24 post describing pulled special education small groups as "a potential SUPER SPREADER."

**District responses**
The Return to Learn plan was approved by the county and state and developed with epidemiologists, nurses and public health leaders at the Oakland County Health Division, and meets all state-mandated safety measures while exceeding many recommended protocols — masks Pre K-12, elementary cohorting and reduced secondary class changes, seating charts, staggered passing times, plexiglass barriers, additional PPE, limits on guests, mandatory health screening, attendance policy changes, enhanced cleaning, OCHD nurse walkthroughs and dedicated building nurses. Special education protocols include mandatory handwashing, assigned seats and distancing, open classroom doors, no more than three students in a room at once, and wipe-down of work areas. Special meetings are scheduled around board member availability via a timing poll to which Trustee Hammond responded without requesting additional times, and meetings are streamed on Zoom or, when more than 1,000 people attend, to Facebook and YouTube.

**Labor exposure**
A September 24, 2020 letter from the Troy Education Association asserts that a board member discussing plan specifics with individual members outside collective bargaining is an unfair labor practice under PERA; the deck notes Trustee Hammond is the only board member active on social media and warns a PERA complaint could lead to a lawsuit and financial damages.

**Motion**
Nancy Philippart moves that the actions of Trustee Hammond are not the actions of the Troy Board of Education and that the community be alerted that, unless specifically authorized by motion of the board, Trustee Hammond's opinions and actions are as an individual community member.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presentation titled "WHAT IS A BOARD MEMBER?" delivered to the Troy Board of Education on October 20, 2020. It begins as a primer on school board governance and ethics and concludes as the formal case for disclaiming and censuring Trustee Elizabeth Hammond.

GOVERNANCE. The deck establishes that school board members are elected officials who must uphold the Michigan Constitution's mandate to provide free public elementary and secondary education. Under the School Code, the general powers a Board of Education may execute include actions incidental or appropriate to the performance of a function related to the operation of the district; actions in the interests of public elementary and secondary education; educating pupils in K-12, preschool and adult education; providing for the safety and welfare of students; acquiring and disposing of school property; matters involving the receipt and expenditure of school funds; and joint agreements and cooperative arrangements. The slide adds the qualification that actions cannot conflict with or circumvent state prohibitions.

HOW SCHOOL BOARDS WORK. Two external standards are quoted. The National School Boards Association Code of Ethics for School Board Members provides: "As a member of my local Board of Education I will strive to improve public education, and to that end I will take no private action that will compromise the board or administration." The Michigan Association of School Boards Board of Education Governance Standards, endorsed by the Michigan State Board of Education, state that the individual school board member understands and respects both the authority and responsibilities of the Board of Education, and the deck cites four sub-standards: 3.a, the board member acts in accordance with Michigan law, which does not vest individual board members with any type of independent legal authority; 3.c, the board member follows established policies and procedures; 3.d, the board member supports decisions of the Board of Education after a vote is taken regardless of his or her individual position prior to the vote; and 3.g, the board member demonstrates understanding of and respect for school district structure and protocols.

HOW WE DO THIS IN THE TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT. The district's own Code of Ethics is set out in TSD Policy Manual Section 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board. Each Board member has acknowledged and signed an excerpt providing that as a member of the Board he or she will promote the best interest of the School District as a whole and adhere to stated ethical standards and principles: recognizing that a Board member has no legal authority as an individual and that decisions can be made only by a majority vote at a public meeting of the Board; taking no private action that might compromise the Board or administration and respecting the confidentiality of privileged information; abiding by majority decisions of the Board while retaining the right to seek changes through ethical and constructive channels; and striving for a positive working relationship with the Superintendent, respecting the Superintendent's authority to advise the Board, implement Board policy, and administer the School District.

WHAT ABOUT VIOLATIONS — CENSURE. Citing Oxford Languages, censure is defined as the expressing of "formal disapproval." The quoted bylaw language provides that by a majority vote, the Board may censure an individual Board member or members for violating federal or Michigan law, these Bylaws or Board policy, or otherwise acting in a manner inconsistent with the office of a Board member.

DISCLAIMING ACTS OF INDIVIDUAL BOARD MEMBERS. Michigan law requires that a school board act only as a board, not as private individuals, and only the vote of a majority of a board's members creates action by the board. Under Section 1201 of the Revised School Code, trustees may only exercise power and perform their duties as trustees when doing so collectively and only at a regular or a properly called special meeting. When a trustee violates this law and fellow board members are concerned that the community may misconstrue the trustee's individual actions as representative of the board, they may disclaim the actions of that trustee; a disclaiming motion passed by the majority alerts the community that the actions of an individual trustee do not represent the will of the board.

ETHICS VIOLATIONS — TRUSTEE ELIZABETH HAMMOND. The deck states that the decision to publicly discuss the case for disclaiming and censure of Trustee Hammond did not come lightly, and that the violations of ethics and state law to be shared are not isolated instances over a short timeframe but a repeated pattern of behavior. It records that Trustee Hammond was informally advised on at least three different occasions to address behaviors violating the ethics of her role as trustee: the President's letter of October 2, 2019; the Board self evaluation of January 2020; and the special board meeting of September 29, 2020. Her response, the deck asserts, was to disregard this advice, leaving no recourse but to bring the discussion forward.

POST OF WEDNESDAY, SEPTEMBER 23, 2020. Quoted from the Troy Parent Group: "My position has always been that I support the parents' right to make a choice for their own families while we are in, what the governor defines as, Phase 4. That said, I do NOT believe that an in-person option should throw science out the window. A safely executed in-person option requires strict adherence to both required and recommended safety protocols. THE CURRENT PLAN DOES NOT DO THIS AND PUTS THE ENTIRE COMMUNITY AT RISK. Further, I believe the current scenario leaves those students who choose to remain at home, at both an educational and social disadvantage. It also makes highly effective teaching virtually impossible (no pun intended)." The response slide calls the post inaccurate, inflammatory and a creator of unnecessary fear and apprehension: the TSD Return to Learn plan does not throw science out the window nor put the entire community at risk; the plan was approved by the county and state and developed with epidemiologists, nurses and public health leaders at the Oakland County Health Division; and it meets all state-mandated safety measures while exceeding many recommended protocols, including requiring masks Pre K-12; cohorting students in elementary school and reduced class changes at secondary; seating charts in classrooms, lunchrooms and segregated playground areas by class; staggered passing time and enhanced safety procedures for building entry, recess and dismissal; plexiglass barriers between teachers and students; additional PPE such as face shields, gowns and gloves used in conjunction with masks; significantly limiting guests in buildings; mandatory health screening of all students, staff, vendors and contractors; attendance policy changes; enhanced cleaning protocols; walkthroughs in every building with OCHD nurses for guidance on sick rooms and other operational issues; dedicated nurses assigned to each building; and strict protocols for food distribution in cafeterias. The impact slide argues the post harms trust between the public, school community and district/board at a time when trust is critical, and insinuates the District is deliberately withholding information.

POST OF THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 2020 — MEETING TIME. A parent wrote of the September 29 special board meeting, "I feel they make it on 4pm on purpose because most of the parents are working at that time," to which Elizabeth Hammond replied, "I have the same concern.... unfortunately I couldn't control the time." The response states the post is inaccurate and does not reflect the need to manage around board members' schedules: special meetings are scheduled quickly and sometimes begin earlier than the normal 6 or 7 p.m. time to ensure board members can participate, with priority given to board members' availability based on responses to a timing poll; Trustee Hammond responded to the poll and did not request additional times be added. All meetings and workshops are streamed via Zoom, or when more than 1,000 people attend, streamed to Facebook and YouTube, and recordings are available. The impact slide argues the post insinuates the district is intentionally avoiding public participation and that her statement "I couldn't control the time" reflects a lack of ownership that erodes trust.

POST OF THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 2020 — FACE SHIELDS. A parent wrote, "I read today that due to the aerosol nature of the virus the face shields are actually ineffective at stopping the spread. No idea if this extends to plexiglass dividers." Elizabeth Hammond replied, "[PARENT NAME] right??? We are so screwed. Thank you for being so vocal." The response states the safety plan calls for multiple mitigation measures used together and does not rely on any single protocol; face shields are used in conjunction with masks with rare exceptions, such as a student with significant needs who cannot tolerate a cloth mask; and plexiglass shields are used in conjunction with physical distancing, signage, handwashing, other hygiene measures and strict policies for illness and health screening. The impact slide argues that Trustee Hammond had been present for hours of discussion on mitigation measures, that telling a community member "we are so screwed" rather than discussing facts and risks is intentionally inflammatory, and that "thanks for being so vocal" suggests she is creating fear to build support for her own personal choices as a parent, making a case for negligent behavior on the part of the board and district administration.

POST OF THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 2020 — LUNCH AND SPECIAL EDUCATION. Quoted: "From everything I read, it sounds like multiple classrooms will be in the cafeteria at the same time eating without masks! Also, for SE services, in most cases small groups would be pulled from multiple classes and spend a couple hours a week together. They would be with a SE teacher that would cover all classes in multiple grades — a potential SUPER SPREADER." The response notes she had been part of multiple discussions on lunch and support-service protocols. For lunch, additional locations such as art rooms, gyms and LGI rooms are used to keep classes isolated; in the cafeteria classes are distanced at least six feet from one another and individual classes are seated according to seating charts; photos posted on social media indicate that in most cases individual students are six feet or more apart when masks come off; and elementary schools have segregated areas of the playground, fields and blacktop with a rotating schedule so cohorts do not mix. For special education support services, protocols include mandatory hand washing before entering the interventionist's room and before returning to the general education classroom; assigned seats and physical distancing; classroom doors left open to ensure air flow; no more than three students in the room at one time; students wiping down their work area on arrival; masks for students and staff with additional PPE for teachers such as face shields, desktop and mobile plexiglass dividers, gloves and hand sanitizer; and mandatory daily health screenings with strong encouragement to stay home when sick. The impact slide states that referring to special education students and staff as "potential SUPER SPREADERS" is demeaning and unfair and potentially harms the integration of these students into general education classrooms.

TROY EDUCATION ASSOCIATION LETTER, SEPTEMBER 24, 2020. The excerpt reads: "The public communications on social media, the discussion of permissible bargaining issues, and the positional statements that run counter to the efforts of our collective teams, must stop. It is the position of the Association that any dialog with individual members of the Troy Education Association about decisions made by the Board and Central Administration on virtual learning or hybrid learning scenarios is an unfair labor practice. The Troy Education Association selects a bargaining team to represent the interests of all members. The Association contends that a board member discussing the specifics of the plan with individual members outside of the collective bargaining process is detrimental and a blatant attempt to undermine the rights afforded to the Association under the guidelines proscribed through PERA." The response notes that although individuals were not specifically named, Trustee Hammond is the only board member active on social media, and her social media behavior is being construed by the association as public negotiation and thus an unfair labor practice under the Public Employment Relations Act. The stated impact is that a PERA complaint could potentially lead to a lawsuit and financial damages to the district.

CASE FOR DISCLAIMING/CENSURE. The summary slide holds that Trustee Hammond committed to "take no private action that will compromise the board or administration" yet her social media posts presented inaccurate and inflammatory information harming trust between the District, its staff, students and community; insinuated that the District is intentionally avoiding public participation; potentially created bias regarding special education staff and students; and insinuated that the board and administration are negligent in their attention to student and staff safety. It further holds that she committed to "act in accordance with Michigan law" yet her posts are being construed as PERA violations by the Troy Education Association, and that she committed to "support decisions of the Board of Education after vote regardless of her individual position prior to vote" yet the letter of complaint from the Troy Education Association President and the dates of her social media posts show she continued to undermine board decisions made on Return to Learn plans on August 12.

MOTION TO DISCLAIM ACTS OF AN INDIVIDUAL BOARD MEMBER. The closing slides restate that Michigan law requires the board to act collectively and not let actions as private individuals compromise the board or District and its relationship with the community; that given the social media posts by Trustee Hammond, who is seen as a representative of the board, the community's interpretation of recent actions may be misconstrued to represent those of the board and District; and that a disclaiming motion is being made to alert the community that Trustee Hammond's actions do not represent, nor are authorized by, the Troy Board of Education. The motion as drafted reads: "I, Nancy Philippart move that the actions of Trustee Hammond are not the actions of the Troy Board of Education and that the community and its members be alerted that unless specifically authorized by motion of this board, Trustee Hammond opinions and actions are as an individual community member and should not be construed as representing the Troy Board of Education."

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of November 21, 2017 at the Services Building — the meeting after the sinking fund passed. The one-mill Building & Site Sinking Fund carried the November 7 election with about 68% of the vote, and the Board's sole recognition item thanks the CAPE steering committee that campaigned for it. It then spends the money: $5,299,830.00 of mechanical, electrical and door work at four elementaries under Bid Pack 21, $508,531.00 for the Troy High boiler replacement, $1,448,346.00 for fifteen replacement buses, and $350,778 to migrate the student information system to PowerSchool.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, November 21, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition — the sinking fund passed**
The single recognition item is the **CAPE (Citizens and Parents for Education) Steering Committee**. "Voters overwhelmingly came out in favor of the Troy School District one-mill Building & Site Sinking Fund in the November 7th Election. **The proposal passed with about 68% of the votes**, which is a testament to the support of our parents and the Troy Community." The Board thanks the volunteers whose work "both behind the scenes and in public forums—was integral to the success," singling out **CAPE chair Tracy Heikka**, who coordinated the effort — with the note that "Mrs. Heikka would say it took a team." Certificates go to the committee, among them Rebecca Anders, Nikey Bergy, Heather Blum and Scott & Renee Courtney.

The result exceeds the polling. Epic MRA's April survey had found 61% outright Yes plus 7% leaning Yes; the actual vote came in at about 68%.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the October 3 workshop, the October 17 special workshop and the October 17 meeting, the copy paper bid, and the September 2017 Treasurer's Report.

The copy paper bid (9847) tabulates seven vendors on 4,200 cases: **Paper Express, Inc. at $21.15 per case / $88,830.00** low, then Veritiv $21.90 / $91,980.00, W.B. Mason $21.87 / $91,854.00, Contract Paper Group $21.93 / $92,106.00, Costco Wholesale $21.99 / $92,358.00, Office Depot $22.94 / $96,366.57 and Quill Corporation $31.90 / $133,980.00 — a spread of more than $45,000 on the same commodity.

**Treasurer's Report — September 2017**
Total check disbursements are $8,837,893.61, the General Fund group $7,497,730.74 and the General Fund (101) itself $7,151,239.70. Adding $2,046,585.93 of wire transfers, $255,817.64 of P-Card purchases and $12,516.86 of ACH debits, less $3,995.45 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $11,148,818.59.

**Business — Bid Pack 21**
Mechanical and electrical upgrades at Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse, plus door replacement at those buildings and piping replacement at Barnard, Bemis and Wass. Reviewed by Rob Carson and the bond team of TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow. **$5,299,830.00** from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund:

| Category | Contractor | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanical (Costello, Leonard, Martell, Morse) | CSM Mechanical | $2,214,668.00 |
| Temperature controls | MCMI | $905,600.00 |
| Door and window replacement (Alts. A1, A2, A3) | Hewett Company | $685,900.00 |
| Electrical | Metro Electric Co. | $597,860.00 |
| Mechanical (Barnard, Bemis, Wass) | Ecker Mechanical | $414,000.00 |
| Contingency | — | $481,802.00 |

**Business — Troy High boiler, Bid Pack 22**
RFP 9846 issued October 15 covers boiler replacement with new boiler venting and circulation pumps, plus electrical service and building automation controls. **Work commences immediately upon award with completion January 2, 2018** — over the winter break. Award: Johnson & Wood mechanical $399,900.00, MCMI temperature controls $50,376.00, Great Lakes Power electrical $12,025.00 and $46,230.00 contingency, **$508,531.00** total from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

**Business — PowerSchool**
The district's student information system, eSchools, **was recently acquired by PowerSchool**. Beth Soggs' November 14 memo makes the scale argument: PowerSchool's SMS package represents **over 735,000 students across 455 districts** in Michigan — every district in Macomb County plus Birmingham, Lake Orion, Oxford and West Bloomfield in Oakland — against eSchools' **42,000 students across 11 districts**.

The five stated reasons for migrating: staff and parent concerns with eSchools; the ability to collaborate with neighboring districts on reports, training and integrations; online registration and forms; single sign-on for parents reaching Schoology, payments, attendance and report cards; and improved parent and teacher portals. Demonstrations were held for administrative staff and secondary scheduling staff with positive feedback. Award: **$350,778**, spread over 2017-18, 2018-19 and 2019-20, from the General Fund.

**Business — buses**
**Fifteen** of the district's buses have reached end-of-life — up from ten the previous January. Using the MSBO cooperative purchasing service, three proposals were reviewed with Transportation Liaison Dominick Asaro; low bidder **Hoekstra Transportation** is awarded **$1,448,346.00** from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund under the School Bus Replacement Program, 2016 Bond Series 2. The specification covers four types: 2 conventional 77-passenger, 5 special-needs 53-passenger with child integrated seating, 4 48-passenger with child integrated seating and 4 rear-engine 78-passenger.

**Other**
Trustee Gary Hauff is approved to attend the NSBA Advocacy Institute in Washington, D.C., February 4-6, 2018.

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, November 21, 2017, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. TSD Mission Moment: CAPE Committee; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the October 3, 2017 Board of Education Workshop, B. Minutes of the October 17, 2017 Special Board of Education Workshop, C. Minutes of the October 17, 2017 Board of Education Meeting, D. Copy Paper Bid, E. Treasurer's Report – September 2017; 6. Personnel — A. Consideration: Elementary and Secondary; 7. Curriculum; 8. Business — A. Consideration: Bid 9845 Mechanical & Electrical Upgrades and Door Replacements – Costello, Leonard, Martell, and Morse Elementary Schools, B. Consideration: Bid 9846 Boiler Replacement – Troy High School, C. Consideration: PowerSchool Contract, D. Consideration: Bus Purchase; 9. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 10. Other — A. Consideration: 2018 NSBA Advocacy Conference; 11. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition 2.A: the CAPE steering committee.** The item opens: "As you no doubt have heard, voters overwhelmingly came out in favor of the Troy School District one-mill Building & Site Sinking Fund in the November 7th Election. The proposal passed with about 68% of the votes, which is a testament to the support of our parents and the Troy Community. The results exemplified their faith in our schools and the value they see in the exemplary education we provide for the students of this District. We are very grateful for their confidence in the fiscal responsibility of our Board of Education and their trust in our stewardship of their investment."

It goes on: passage of the Sinking Fund could not have come without the tireless work of many people — parents, community volunteers, staff and administrators — and the Board wishes to personally thank the driving force behind it, the Steering Committee of CAPE, Citizens and Parents for Education, who volunteered countless hours to ensure the initiative passed. Their dedication and hard work, both behind the scenes and in public forums, was integral to the success of the proposal. The item especially acknowledges CAPE chair Tracy Heikka, who coordinated the group's efforts and worked tirelessly to ensure the measure passed, adding that "Mrs. Heikka would say it took a team." Names are read and certificates passed out, with Heikka invited up at the end to say a few words if she wishes. The committee members named include Rebecca Anders, Nikey Bergy, Heather Blum and Scott & Renee Courtney.

The outcome is worth setting against the packets that led to it. The Epic MRA survey delivered to the Board on June 13, 2017 tested a 1-mill proposal and found 61% Yes with a further 7% leaning Yes, warning across three separate slides that tax neutrality was what earned the community's endorsement and that raising the ask would collapse support. The Board placed exactly one mill on the ballot on July 18, over Mrs. Hammond's lone dissent, certifying the language by the August 15 deadline. The measure carried at about 68% — at or slightly above the survey's combined yes-and-leaning-yes, and comfortably above its outright yes.

**Consent agenda.** Minutes of the October 3, 2017 workshop; minutes of the October 17, 2017 special workshop; minutes of the October 17, 2017 board meeting; the copy paper bid; and the Treasurer's Report for September 2017.

**Consent item 5.D: copy paper bid.** Todd Hensley's November 7, 2017 memorandum covers BID 9847, copy paper for the 2017-18 school year. The bid tabulation, dated November 6, 2017, prices 4,200 cases from seven vendors: Contract Paper Group at $21.93 per case for $92,106.00; Costco Wholesale at $21.99 for $92,358.00; Office Depot, Inc. at $22.94 for $96,366.57; Paper Express, Inc. at $21.15 for $88,830.00; Quill Corporation at $31.90 for $133,980.00; Veritiv Operating Company at $21.90 for $91,980.00; and W.B. Mason Co., Inc. at $21.87 for $91,854.00.

Six of the seven cluster within about eighteen cents a case; Quill's bid is roughly ten dollars a case above the field, a difference of more than forty-five thousand dollars on the same commodity. Paper Express is low.

**Treasurer's Report, September 2017.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $7,151,239.70, with Total General Fund of $7,497,730.74 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $8,837,893.61. Adding ACH debits of $12,516.86, outgoing wire transfers of $2,046,585.93 and P-Card purchases of $255,817.64, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $3,995.45, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $11,148,818.59. The middle sections of the packet are the September check register run by fund.

**Business 8.A: mechanical and electrical upgrades and door replacements, Bid Pack 21.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on mechanical and electrical upgrades at Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse Elementary Schools. The bid also included door replacement work at those buildings along with piping replacement work at Barnard, Bemis and Wass Elementary Schools. Bid responses were reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations, and the bond team of TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow.

The resolution awards bid pack 21 in the amount of $5,299,830.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, allocated as: CSM Mechanical, mechanical work at Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse, $2,214,668.00; MCMI, temperature controls, $905,600.00; Hewett Company with alternates A1, A2 and A3, door and window replacement, $685,900.00; Metro Electric Co., electrical, $597,860.00; Ecker Mechanical, mechanical at Barnard, Bemis and Wass, $414,000.00; and a contingency budget of $481,802.00.

This is the largest single award in the 2017 packets and one of the largest in these records. Its scope maps directly onto the district's bond program sequencing: Barnard, Bemis and Wass had received mechanical and electrical upgrades under Bid Pack 18 in December 2016 and are here receiving hydronic piping replacement, while Costello, Leonard, Martell and Morse take their turn for the unit ventilators, HVAC and electrical work. The August 2018 bond and sinking fund update would list both as in-process 2018 projects.

**Business 8.B: Troy High School boiler replacement, Bid Pack 22.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on the Troy High boiler replacement, reviewed by Rob Carson and the same bond team. Carson's November 8, 2017 memorandum records that RFP Bid 9846 was issued on October 15, 2017; that the scope of work is to perform boiler replacement with new boiler venting and circulation pumps along with electrical service and building automation controls for the new boilers; and that the work will commence immediately upon award with a completion of January 2, 2018.

The RFP specified 3 bid categories. Carson recommends, on low bid per category: category 230000 mechanical, Johnson & Wood, $399,900.00; category 230900 temperature controls, MCMI, $50,376.00; and category 260000 electrical, Great Lakes Power, $12,025.00; plus a contingency budget of $46,230.00, for a total budget recommendation of $508,531.00. All proposals were reviewed and qualified by the bond team, with a separate purchase order to be issued for each bid category. The resolution awards bid pack 22 in the amount of $508,531.00 as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

The January 2 completion date is the point of the schedule: a high school's boilers can only be replaced in the window when the building is empty and still needs to be warm enough not to freeze, which in Michigan means the six weeks between award and the return from winter break.

**Business 8.C: PowerSchool contract.** The district currently uses eSchools as its student information management system, and eSchools was recently acquired by PowerSchool. PowerSchool has an SMS package widely used across Michigan, and there are many benefits to migrating.

Beth Soggs' November 14, 2017 memorandum to the Board makes the case in terms of market position. PowerSchool's SMS package represents over 735,000 students across 455 districts in Michigan; all districts in Macomb County use PowerSchool, as do four districts in Oakland County — Birmingham, Lake Orion, Oxford and West Bloomfield. In comparison, eSchools currently represents 42,000 students across 11 districts in Michigan.

The district plans to migrate for five stated reasons: staff and parent concerns with eSchools; the ability to collaborate with neighboring districts on reports, training, integrations and the like; online registration and forms; single sign-on for parents to access student information items such as Schoology, payments, attendance and report cards; and improved parent and teacher portals, HAC and TAC. Demonstrations were held for administrative staff and the staff responsible for secondary scheduling, and feedback from attendees was positive.

The resolution awards the student management system to PowerSchool in the amount of $350,778 as an expenditure of the General Fund, with the cost spread over the 2017-18, 2018-19 and 2019-20 school years.

The underlying situation is a vendor consolidation rather than a competitive procurement: the district's incumbent system was bought by a larger competitor, and the practical choice became whether to migrate to the acquirer's flagship product or remain on a platform serving a twentieth as many Michigan students. The collaboration argument — shared reports, training and integrations with neighboring districts — is a real benefit of that concentration, and the same logic that made eSchools acquirable.

**Business 8.D: bus purchase.** Fifteen of the district's school buses have reached end-of-life. The Michigan School Business Officials School Bus Purchasing Program was used to obtain competitive pricing, compared and reviewed by Mr. Dominick Asaro, Transportation Liaison.

Todd Hensley's November 9, 2017 memorandum, headed School Bus Replacement Program – 2016 Bond Series 2 – 2017-18 School Year, records that fifteen of the district's fleet have reached their end-of-life cycle; that MSBO offers a cooperative bus purchasing service to obtain competitive pricing from bidding dealers; that the service was used to obtain pricing for several models matching the district's needs; and that after analyzing three proposals and reviewing them with Asaro, they collaboratively recommend the low bidder, Hoekstra Transportation, at $1,448,346.00. The resolution awards the school bus purchase to Hoekstra Transportation in that amount as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

The bid tabulation specifies four bus types with quantities: 2 conventional 77-passenger; 5 53-passenger special needs with child integrated seating; 4 48-passenger with child integrated seating; and 4 rear-engine 78-passenger. Nine of the fifteen buses — the 53-passenger special needs and 48-passenger units, both with child integrated seating — are configured for students with disabilities.

This is the second bus purchase in these packets from the same vendor in the same calendar year: ten buses awarded in February 2017 under 2014 Bond Series 2, and fifteen here at $1,448,346.00 under 2016 Bond Series 2 — twenty-five buses replaced in ten months.

**Other 10.A: 2018 NSBA Advocacy Institute.** As required by Board Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board; Reimbursement of Expenses, any expenditure of district funds for members for out-of-state meetings must have prior approval by resolution. Board Trustee Gary Hauff has indicated his desire to attend the National School Boards Association Advocacy Institute Conference in Washington, D.C., February 4-6, 2018, and the resolution approves his attendance as a representative of the Troy Board of Education. Hauff would return to the same conference the following year, approved in October 2018 alongside Trustee Elizabeth Hammond for the January 27-29, 2019 institute.

Read as a whole, the November 2017 packet is the district turning a mandate into contracts. Two weeks after voters approved a one-mill sinking fund at about 68%, the Board thanks the volunteer committee that ran the campaign and then, in the same sitting, commits $5,299,830.00 to four elementary schools' mechanical and electrical systems, $508,531.00 to a boiler replacement scheduled around the winter break, $1,448,346.00 to fifteen buses of which nine are configured for students with disabilities, and $350,778 to move its student records onto the platform that had just acquired its vendor. The smallest item on the agenda — 4,200 cases of copy paper — is decided by a $45,000 spread between the cheapest and dearest bidder for an identical product.

**Meeting**
Agenda of Special Meeting, Troy Board of Education, June 16, 2015, 5:30 PM, Administration Building, 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, phone 248.823.4000. **Agenda order**
1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Public Communication; 3. Personnel (A. Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction; B. Director of ELD, Federal Grants & State Assessments; C. TESPA Contract Ratification); 4. Closed Session (A. Superintendent Evaluation); 5. Adjournment.

**3.A — Administrative Appointment: Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction**
Recommendation of Ms. Kristine Griffor. She comes to Troy from Warren Woods Public Schools, where she spent the past 8 years — first as an Intervention Specialist for 3 years, then 5 years as Director of Curriculum. Before Warren Woods she spent 4 years as an English Language Arts teacher for Richmond Community Schools. Oakland University degrees: Bachelor's in teaching (2003), Master's in Reading Instruction (2005), Educational Specialist in Educational Leadership (2007). **3.B — Administrative Appointment: Director of ELD, Federal Grants & State Assessments**
Recommendation of Ms. Christin Silagy. She joined the Troy School District in 2001 from Burbank Unified School District in Burbank, California, where she was a fourth grade teacher for 2 years. In 14 years with Troy she taught Science, Language Arts and English as a Second Language at Baker Middle School for 2 years, then moved to Bemis and Schroeder Elementary Schools as Program for Accelerated and Creative Education Resource Teacher for a year, and in 2004 moved to Morse Elementary School, where she currently serves as Elementary ELD Coordinator. Duties begin July 1, 2015.

**3.C — TESPA Contract Ratification**

Membership ratified on June 10, 2015. Term: one year, July 1, 2015 through June 30, 2016.

| Economic term | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Salary schedule | 1% across-the-Board increase, including longevity steps |
| Steps | Step movement for all eligible members |
| Off-schedule | 4% payment to tier 1 schedule members (hired prior to February 14, 2012) currently on step 5 or higher |
| Life insurance | Premium cost for an additional $20,000 in coverage for the 5 skilled trade employees |
| Work boots | $200 reimbursement for the 5 skilled trade employees |
| Stated net increase | Approximately $30,000 in new dollars over 2014/15; characterized as less than 1.5% |

A supporting memorandum dated Friday, June 12, 2015 from Larry Lobert, Interim Assistant Superintendent, Employee Services, and Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, to Dr. Rich Machesky and the Board notes that part of the increase is retained as off-schedule (non-compounding) payments, and that the agreement states such payments are for 2015/16 only and are not a basis or starting point for a successor contract — preserving flexibility if the district's financial condition requires modifications. Attachments: signed Tentative Agreement and Board Resolution. Remaining language changes are described as without significant monetary impact.

**4.A — Closed Session**

SUPPORTING MEMORANDUM ON THE TESPA TENTATIVE AGREEMENT. A memorandum dated Friday, June 12, 2015 is addressed to Dr. Rich Machesky, Superintendent, and the Board of Education, from Larry Lobert, Interim Assistant Superintendent, Employee Services, and Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, regarding the TESPA Tentative Agreement. Contact details shown on the memorandum are the Business Office, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, phone 248.823.4022 and fax 248.823.4013. The memorandum announces that a tentative agreement has been reached with TESPA and that it is recommended for Board action at the June 16, 2015 meeting since member ratification has occurred. It states the agreement allows for a net increase (new dollars over 2014/2015) of less than 1.5%, attributed to changes in the pay structure explained in the memorandum and outlined in the attached signed Tentative Agreement. The agreement is described as providing modest improvements to the salary structure while retaining portions of the increase as off-schedule (non-compounding) payments; a clear understanding is expressed in the agreement that such payments are for 2015/16 only and are not to be considered as a basis or starting point for a successor contract, which the memorandum says will help the district retain some flexibility if the district's financial condition requires modifications next year.

The memorandum states the total dollar net increase over 2014/15 is approximately $30,000, comprising the following economics: a 1% across-the-Board increase to the existing salary schedule, including longevity steps; step movement for all eligible members; a 4% off-schedule payment for employees on the tier 1 schedule (those hired prior to February 14, 2012) who are currently on step 5 or higher; premium costs for an additional $20,000 in life insurance coverage for the 5 skilled trade employees; and a $200 reimbursement for work boots for the 5 skilled trade employees. Readers are directed to contact either Larry Lobert or Rick West with questions, comments, or concerns. Attachments listed are the signed Tentative Agreement and the Board Resolution.

ITEM 4.A — CLOSED SESSION, SUPERINTENDENT EVALUATION. The packet notes the Board must pass a resolution to go into closed session to discuss the Superintendent Evaluation, and that following passage of the resolution the Board of Education will go into closed session, after which no additional business will take place other than to officially adjourn the meeting. The recommended action is adoption of a resolution stating that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), the Troy Board of Education shall go into closed session to discuss Superintendent Evaluation. A roll call vote is required, with named lines for Hauff, Miletti, Philippart, Schmidt, Underwood, Edmunds, and Fleming. The agenda concludes with item 5, Adjournment.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of December 18, 2018 at the Services Building — the year's closing meeting and Todd Miletti's last after 12 years. The Board formally names the new preschool building the Troy School District Preschool, awards $5,313,940.00 of Bid Pack 23 work across five buildings, and finally settles the Early Childhood Center casework at $662,570.00 after two failed bid rounds. The November 13 minutes carried here record the aftermath of the November 6 election, at which voters approved a replacement non-homestead operating millage of 21 mills with 18 the maximum allowable levy, and the Board's amended L-4029 setting the levy at 18 mills.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, December 18, 2018, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment recognizes the group developing "a world-class foundation for a comprehensive pre-kindergarten education experience for our youngest learners" — Kris Griffor and Erin Keyser share a video of the Early Childhood Center.

The second item is **Todd Miletti's 12 years of service**, this being his final meeting. The write-up notes that aside from being an elected position, serving on the Board is also a volunteer position requiring a great deal of time, effort and commitment, and that Miletti "has done a remarkable service to past and future generations of Troy students."

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the November 13 special meeting, closed session and workshop, the November 20 meeting, and the October 2018 Treasurer's Report.

**The millage, after the vote**
The November 13 special meeting existed to true up the tax levy. The 2018-19 Budget Appropriations Resolution adopted June 19, 2018 had authorized **17.6840 mills** on non-homestead property. At the November 6, 2018 election the district's electors approved a replacement non-homestead operating millage of **21 mills, with 18 mills being the maximum allowable levy**, effective for the 2018 calendar year. Resolution 18-085 amends the appropriations resolution to authorize a levy of **18 mills**, and authorizes the President and Secretary to sign an amended 2018 Tax Rate Request (Form L-4029) with **9.158 of the 18 mills levied on the December 1, 2018 levy date**, for submission to the Oakland County Clerk. It carried 5-0 with Miletti and Philippart absent.

**Also from November**
The November 13 workshop covered the Troy High sign, the Consumers and DTE easements at Boulan Park, the Boyd Street property sale and sidewalk, and board professional learning on **school start times**; Judge Kirsten Hartig and Dr. Nicole Wilson were in the audience.

The November 20 minutes record 18-087 through 18-092, all 6-0 with Miletti absent: the consent agenda, Cornelissen's appointment, the Signarama sign award at $21,739.30, the Boyd Street sale to Delmar Homes at $10,000.00, and — added to the agenda at Mr. Gottlieb's request — **resolution 18-091 directing Dr. Machesky and Human Resources to develop a succession plan** to maintain continuity and consistency of the district into the future and share it with the Board. The Troy College & Career High School Mission Moment described a Trunk or Treat event, a book drive that collected and delivered **more than 2,000 books** for students in Pontiac Schools, and a partnership with Oakmont Senior Living where students help with iPads, call bingo and perform skits for residents who often have no family nearby.

**Treasurer's Report — October 2018**
Total check disbursements are $9,173,492.59, the General Fund group $4,711,884.58 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,479,154.93. With $2,045,278.46 of wire transfers, $267,995.65 of P-Card purchases and $29,426.83 of ACH debits, less an unusually large $369,076.31 of prior period void disbursements, total disbursements in period are $11,147,117.22.

**Business 8.A — the casework, third time**
The Early Childhood Center casework and millwork had failed to draw acceptable bids in March and again in September. On this third attempt RFP 9864 produced 5 bidders in each category — but the bids came in over the construction budget. Rob Carson's November 29 memo records that collaborative efforts between the bond construction team and the low bidders identified **options which created cost savings while maintaining intent and function of the original design**. The award is Mica-Tec interior architectural millwork at $442,920.00 — reduced from a $515,000.00 base bid by three options totalling deductions of $24,180.00, $41,314.00 and $6,586.00 — and Architect Systems Group prefabricated casework at $219,650.00, for **$662,570.00** from the Early Childhood Center Fund. Mica-Tec's base bid was already well below the next bidders at $574,121.00, $576,400.00, $615,810.00 and $714,000.00.

**Business 8.B — Bid Pack 23**
The largest single award of the year after the preschool itself. The scope covers mechanical/electrical upgrades and window/door replacements at Schroeder, Troy Union and Smith; the Smith kitchen renovation; kitchen equipment for Barnard, Bemis and Hamilton; renovation of the Troy High auto and wood shop classrooms; conversion of the closed swimming pool area into classrooms at International Academy East; and bathroom renovation plus a new office suite for the TCT program at the International Academy building.

**Consent minutes: the November 13, 2018 special board meeting.** President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 5:33 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond and Hauff were present; Mr. Miletti and Dr. Philippart were absent.
