The single business item was resolution 18-085, the L-4029 amendment. Its recitals set out the sequence: the Board, pursuant to a 2018-19 Budget Appropriations Resolution adopted on June 19, 2018, approved the district's operating, debt and sinking fund millage rates for the 2018-19 school year, which included the authority to levy 17.6840 mills for general operating purposes on non-homestead property; at the November 6, 2018 election the district's electors approved a replacement non-homestead operating millage in the amount of 21 mills, with 18 mills being the maximum allowable levy, to be effective for the 2018 calendar year; and the Board desires to amend the approval in the 2018-19 Budget Appropriations Resolution to approve and authorize the district to levy 18 mills for general operating purposes on non-homestead property for the 2018-19 school year.

The resolution approves that amendment and further authorizes the President and Secretary to sign an amended 2018 Tax Rate Request, Form L-4029, with a non-homestead operating millage request for the levy of 18 mills for general operating purposes, and further with 9.158 mills of the 18 mills to be levied on the December 1, 2018 levy date, and the submission of the amended 2018 Tax Rate Request to the Oakland County Clerk. This is the completion of the work begun at the July 17 meeting, where the Board certified the ballot language for a replacement of the 18 mills approved by voters in 2015 and eroded by the Headlee Amendment. The 21-mill authorization with an 18-mill cap is the standard structure: the excess exists solely as headroom so that future Headlee rollbacks do not again cut the levy below the 18 mills the state's school finance formula assumes the district will collect. The levy actually restored — 18 mills against the 17.6840 the June appropriations resolution had authorized — is a difference of a fraction of a mill, which is what a rollback of that magnitude costs and what the election was called to fix.

The bids received exceeded the construction budget for these categories. Collaborative efforts from the bond construction team and the low bidders resulted in identifying options which created cost savings while maintaining the intent and function of the original design; the attached bid results summary identifies those options, cost savings and bid pricing. Carson recommends, on low bid for each category: 064023 interior architectural millwork, Mica-Tec, $442,920.00; and 123204 prefabricated casework, Architect Systems Group, $219,650.00 — total recommended awards $662,570.00, with a separate purchase order for each bid category and funding from the ECC Fund. The bid tabulation shows how the reduction was achieved. Mica-Tec's base bid was $515,000.00, against MOD Interiors at $574,121.00, Trend Millwork at $576,400.00, Wally Kosorski & Co at $615,810.00 and Division 6 at $714,000.00. Three options are applied to Mica-Tec's bid as deductions of $24,180.00, $41,314.00 and $6,586.00, bringing it to $442,920.00. The options are described in the tabulation headers as removing millwork at the classroom island, changing the reception desk work surface to plastic laminate in lieu of Corian, and installing carpet at the circle windows, with a note that Option 1 adds metal stud and drywall to replace millwork at $12,345.00 and Option 2 adds carpet at $8,340. **Business 8.C: wireless audio systems and installation.** Invitations were sent to eight potential bidders to provide closed sealed pricing for the required audio auditorium equipment at Athens and Troy High Schools, with three responses received. Todd Hensley, Purchasing Supervisor, reviewed the proposals with Gino Minchella, Theatre Manager, and recommends the low bidder to specification: Advanced Lighting & Sound, Inc. at $91,106.00, funded from the Facility Rental Fund. The resolution awards the wireless audio auditorium equipment for Athens and Troy High to Advanced Lighting & Sound, Inc. in the amount of $91,106.00 as an expenditure of the Facility Rental Fund — one of the few awards in the year drawn on that fund, which is fed by outside groups renting district facilities.

**Other 10.A: naming the Early Childhood Center.** In December 2017 the Board passed a resolution to proceed with the construction of an early childhood center facility, and while construction is ongoing it is appropriate to formally name the facility. The resolution recites that the district's mission is to ensure learning for all members of the school community; that the Board has adopted the district's strategic plan focusing its work on four characteristics of world class; that one of the four characteristics is to Invest in the Learning of Pre-Kindergarten Students through increasing access to a high quality, literacy-rich preschool experience; that to increase access for a rich preschool experience the Board approved the construction of a new Early Childhood Learning Center in December of 2017; and that the building is scheduled to open in the fall of 2019 and Board Policy 6000.09 states the selection of future school names will be left to the discretion of the Board. It resolves that the Board hereby names the new building the Troy School District Preschool.

The choice is notable for what it declines to do. Board Policy 6000.09 gives the Board complete discretion, and the district had spent the year selling land, borrowing $11 million without a public vote and awarding contracts on a building that had gone from resolution to nearly finished in twelve months; the name it settles on carries no person's name and no donor's, only the district's and the function's.

**Other 10.B: 2019 MASB Board of Directors nomination.** Seven seats on the MASB Board of Directors are up for election. The MASB Board of Directors is comprised of 19 members: 16 directors elected from the eight regions, two from each, and one director each from Groups V, VI and VII; directors are elected by active member school boards, with several seats up each year. As approved by the 2018 Delegate Assembly, beginning in 2019 and in each subsequent year the MASB President will nominate a member to serve as an at-large director subject to Board approval, and beginning in 2021 the Board of Directors will consist of 22 members including three at-large directors. Article VIII, Section 7 of the MASB Bylaws provides that a board's nomination of candidates must be forwarded to the MASB Executive Director by Wednesday, January 9, 2019. The resolution nominates Steve Gottlieb, who has agreed to be a candidate and meets the qualifications as approved by the 2018 Delegate Assembly, to run for a seat on the 2019 MASB Board of Directors, certified by Gary N. Hauff as adopted at the meeting of Tuesday, December 18, 2018.

Gottlieb's candidacy carries forward into the following February's packet, where the Troy Board casts its ballot in a Region 8 race in which he is one of seven candidates.

Read as a whole, the December 2018 packet closes a year that reshaped the district's physical plant and its balance sheet. The preschool it authorized in December 2017 has a name, a director, a completed construction award and — after three tries — its casework. Bid Pack 23 commits another $5,313,940.00 across five buildings. The operating millage the Headlee Amendment had eroded is restored at 18 mills by the voters and by an amended L-4029. And a twelve-year trustee leaves, one meeting after asking the superintendent to put a succession plan in writing.

**Business: budget public hearing.** Item 8.A recites that Michigan law requires every local unit of government, including a school district, to hold a public hearing on its proposed budget with notice at least six days before; that the notice must give the time and place and state where the proposed budget may be inspected; that it must carry, in 11-point bold faced type, "THE PROPERTY TAX MILLAGE RATE PROPOSED TO BE LEVIED TO SUPPORT THE PROPOSED BUDGET WILL BE A SUBJECT OF THIS HEARING"; and that the hearing must precede final adoption. It resolves that a public hearing be held on June 20, 2017 at a regular Board meeting beginning at 7:00 p.m. at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois Road, Troy 48098, and authorizes the Secretary to publish notice in substantially the form of Exhibit A. Exhibit A states that copies of the proposed budget will be available at the Administration Building, 4400 Livernois, from 8:00 a.m. until 5:00 p.m., Wednesday, June 14, 2017 through Tuesday, June 20, 2017, and is signed by Paula Fleming, Secretary.

**Other: bond projects update.** The presentation covers the 2013 bond issue, $125.7 M to be sold in three series. Series 1 is $59.2 M, Series 2 $37.2 M and Series 3 $29.2 M; construction including soft costs accounts for $45.8 M, $22.5 M and $14.1 M respectively, with $10 M, $8.5 M and $8.5 M going to furniture, technology and permits, fees and buses. Series 1 construction, at $45.8 M, is 98% complete. Construction is finished at Barnard, Bemis, Costello, Hamilton, Hill, Leonard, Martell, Morse, Schroeder, Troy Union, Wass, Wattles, Baker, Boulan, Larson, Smith, Troy High and IAE, with Athens High partially complete across 2016 and 2017. The 2017 building projects are Barnard, Bemis and Wass elementary schools, large group instruction space at Larson Middle School, the International Academy kitchen, and Athens High School. Sitework falls into four categories — traffic flow needs for bus and parent drop-off, paving reconstruction and replacement, concrete and sidewalk replacement, and site lighting upgrades. Roofing is either restoration (partial replacement, refurbishment or repair from the General Fund) or remove and replace. The 2016 roof condition table gives total square footage of 1,769,050, of which 543,799 is new including 2017 work, 234,031 is one to three years old, 456,975 is four to six years old and 534,245 is seven or more years old; the largest single roofs are Troy High at 250,250 square feet and Athens at 210,480, followed by Boulan and Larson at 105,000 each and Smith at 97,075. The summary states that including all 2017 projects the bond has made building improvements at every school, site improvements at 19 of 23 facilities, and replaced portions of roofs at 14 of 23 facilities.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, August 21, 2018, 7:00 PM, Administration Building, 4400 Livernois.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the July 17, 2018 meeting, the June 2018 Treasurer's Report, and the IA-East Schools of Choice resolution.

**What the July 17 minutes record**
A short meeting (7:05 to 8:00 p.m.) that did a great deal of contractual work, all 7-0 unless noted. Two-year probationary administrative contracts to Christine Foren as Supervisor, Special Education and Jessica Carrier as Director, Special Education, both effective July 1, 2018. **The Superintendent's contract extended July 1, 2018 through June 30, 2021.** The four assistant and deputy superintendents — Mark Dziatczak, Rick West, Kris Griffor and Jordan Harris — extended through June 30, 2020. Twenty-nine other administrators' contracts extended through June 30, 2020; **Mr. Gottlieb excused himself from voting on this item for reasons of a personal nature** — the list includes Jennifer Gottlieb, Director of Student Growth, Equity & Accountability — so it carried 6-0 with one abstention.

Troy High also joined Athens, Avondale and Berkley in a cooperative boys' and girls' skiing team for 2018-19 and 2019-20. And the Board certified ballot language for a **replacement operating millage** — restoring and replacing the authority to levy 18 mills on non-homestead property, approved by voters in 2015 and since rolled back by the Headlee Amendment, with headroom against future rollbacks — for the November 6, 2018 general school election, the wording due to the Oakland County Clerk no later than August 14, 2018.

**Treasurer's Report — June 2018**
June is the fiscal year's closing month and the numbers show it. Total check disbursements are **$17,527,051.55**, of which the General Fund group is $12,632,198.69 and the General Fund (101) itself $11,582,952.38. Adding $2,373,385.53 of wire transfers, $209,641.78 of P-Card purchases and $31,230.57 of ACH debits, less $35,280.06 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are **$20,106,029.37**. Two lines show the capital program running at full speed: Building & Site Funds $3,271,337.13 and the Early Childhood Center Fund $724,608.21.

**Curriculum — 85 seats at IA East**
The Board adopts a Section 105c resolution accepting applications for **85 non-resident 9th grade students** who reside outside Oakland County, where that ISD is contiguous with Oakland ISD's boundaries, for the purpose of attending the International Academy East program located in the Troy School District. Unlike the elementary and middle school Schools of Choice resolutions adopted each February, this one is 105c only — IA East draws from beyond the county by design.

**Personnel — the August hiring class**
Probationary contracts for roughly sixty teachers for 2018-2019, heavily weighted toward the elementary grades and to special services. Hamilton alone takes six (Takouhy Kinzer and David Anderson in 3rd grade, Shalyn Fortuna in 1st, Ewa Dabrowski in 2nd, Christina Connolly in the resource room, Gabriella Mancini in the kindergarten resource room, plus Rebecca McNally in 3rd); Wattles takes five; Bemis four. The list includes six speech and language pathologists, three school social workers, a school psychologist, four resource room teachers and several early childhood program teachers at the Niles Center.

**Business — the custodial contract**
The Board authorizes administration to finalize an addendum to the Custodial, Grounds and Warehouse Services Contract with D.M. Burr Facilities Management, Inc. "to reflect the increased wages necessary to compete in the current labor market" — raising the aggregate contract price to reflect a **minimum wage of $12.00 per hour for custodians**, with the base contract increase not to exceed **$364,000** from the General Fund.

**Other — bond and sinking fund update**
Completed 2017 projects include Athens mechanical upgrades phase 2, mechanical and electrical upgrades at Barnard, Bemis and Wass, Administration Building mechanical upgrades, Athens and Troy High door replacements, the IA East kitchen renovation on MDE funds, the Troy High chiller replacement and roof replacements at six buildings. In process for 2018: mechanical and electrical upgrades at Costello, Leonard, Morse and Martell; hydronic piping replacements at Barnard, Bemis and Wass; an Athens vestibule for a special education entrance; an ADA-accessible ramp for the Troy Union stage; Bemis offices converted to a classroom; the Boulan old office renovation; and roofs at six more buildings.

The four-year Building Site and Sinking Fund projection is where the constraint shows. Against **$3,900,000 of projected revenue each year**, planned spending is $1,365,000 in 2018, **$6,160,000 in 2019**, $3,470,000 in 2020 and $3,345,000 in 2021 — the 2019 spike funded by carrying $2,535,000 forward from 2018 and drawing the balance down to $275,000, recovering to $705,000 and $1,260,000 thereafter. The 2019 bulge is mostly three items in the TSD approved projects line: **IAE at $2,000,000**, the Troy High pool at $250,000 and high school woods and autos at $250,000, plus a $150,000 board office.

A tennis court decision is put to the Board for Larson, Smith and International Academy/Baker: remove and replace four regulation courts at $55-$60K per court, $220-$240k per site, **$660-$720K total**, expected to last 7-8 years before requiring maintenance — or remove and restore with seed rather than sod at $30-$35K per site, **$90-$105K total**.

President Schmidt moved public communication for non-agenda items up on the agenda since one community member had asked to address the Board: Kristina Gerami, a Leonard parent, spoke regarding her concerns about specific information in her son's school records.

Resolution 18-062 approved the consent agenda 7-0: minutes of the June 5, 2018 meeting, the June 12, 2018 special meeting and closed session, the June 12, 2018 workshop and the June 19, 2018 meeting, plus the Michigan High School Athletic Association membership resolution for 2018/2019.

Resolution 18-063 issued a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Ms. Christine Foren as Supervisor, Special Education, effective July 1, 2018, carried 7-0. Resolution 18-064 issued the same form of contract to Ms. Jessica Carrier as Director, Special Education, effective July 1, 2018, carried 7-0.

Resolution 18-065 extended the contract of the Superintendent of Schools, in effect from July 1, 2018 through June 30, 2021, without tenure in the administrative position and subject to the provisions of the written agreement, carried 7-0.

Resolution 18-069 certified the ballot language for an operating millage proposal. It recites that the Board has determined it is necessary for the continuing operation of the School District to restore and replace the authority to levy 18 mills for operating purposes on non-homestead property, which was previously approved by the voters in 2015 and has been rolled back by application of the Headlee Amendment to the Michigan Constitution, and to increase the prior authority in the event of future rollbacks, as described in the Replacement Operating Millage Proposal attached as Exhibit A; that it is necessary and desirable to submit the proposal to the district's electors at the general school election to be held on November 6, 2018; and that in order to do so the Board must certify the ballot wording to the Clerk of the County of Oakland, the School District Election Coordinator, as required by Act 116, Public Acts of Michigan, 1954, as amended, not later than August 14, 2018. **Consent item 5.C: Schools of Choice, Section 105c, 9th grade for 2019-2020.** In accordance with Michigan state law, school districts shall pass a resolution each school year if they intend to participate in a Schools of Choice program. The totals are $1,165,000 in 2018, $5,960,000 in 2019, $3,270,000 in 2020 and $3,145,000 in 2021, plus $200,000 of soft costs each year, for $1,365,000, $6,160,000, $3,470,000 and $3,345,000. Projected revenue is $3,900,000 in each of the four years. Carry-over runs from nil in 2018 to $2,535,000 available in 2019, $275,000 in 2020 and $705,000 in 2021, with the closing balances $2,535,000, $275,000, $705,000 and $1,260,000. In other words, the fund underspends in 2018 to bank the money for a 2019 program that runs well over a single year's revenue, and the IAE line alone consumes more than half of that year's excess.

A final decision is put to the Board on tennis courts at Larson Middle School, Smith Middle School and International Academy/Baker. Remove and replace four regulation courts would cost $55-$60K per court, or $220-$240k per site, for a $660-$720K total, with an expectation of 7-8 years before the courts require maintenance. Remove and restore, seeding rather than sodding, would cost $30-$35K per site, or $90-$105K total. The presentation ends there, on a question rather than a recommendation.

Read as a whole, the August 2018 packet is the district's start-of-year meeting: roughly sixty new teachers hired at once, 85 out-of-county seats opened at IA East for the following year, a labor-market wage increase pushed through the custodial contract at up to $364,000, and a capital plan that has banked $2,535,000 to spend a year's revenue and a half in 2019. Behind all of it sits the millage the Board had put on the November 6 ballot the month before — a replacement of the same 18 non-homestead mills the district had been levying since 2015, eroded by Headlee.

AGENDA ITEM 6.B - ADMINISTRATIVE APPOINTMENT. Mr. John Pagel is recommended as Principal of Martell Elementary School on a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position, effective August 17, 2016. He has a 25-year career in education, beginning as a fourth and fifth grade teacher in the Algonac School District, then middle school Assistant Principal in the Avondale School District, and most recently 16 years as principal at Deerfield Elementary in Avondale. AGENDA ITEM 7.A - SCHOOLS OF CHOICE, SECTION 105c. Michigan law requires a resolution each school year for districts intending to participate in a Schools of Choice program. Under Section 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979, as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, the Board would accept applications for the 2017-2018 school year for 90 non-resident 9th grade students attending a school district in another county, provided that intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries, to attend the International Academy East program located in the Troy School District. IA East enrollment totals run 116, 240, 342, 441, 451, 475, 504, 533 and 564 for the years 2008-2009 through 2016-2017, with 2016-2017 grade counts of 158, 155, 135 and 116 and a four-year percent decrease of 18%. Lottery information for the class of 2020 lists 80 Troy School District seats against 167 applicants, reaching #151 on the wait list, and 90 out-of-county school-of-choice seats against 172 applicants with 78 seats filled. The recommendation is no change to the lottery process for the class of 2021. If classes of 155 to 170 continue, approximately 0.8 to 1.0 additional FTE will be needed for 2017-2018 to support the increase of seniors from the current 116 to 135.

**Items 10.B and 10.C – policy first readings.** B-0102, Board Members' Term of Office, sets a term of six (6) years commencing with the general school election in November of 2016 and on the November general election date in even years thereafter (adopted January 15, 2008). B-1202, Place of Meeting, locates meetings at the District Administrative Centers unless otherwise announced at least twenty-four hours in advance with notice posted per law (adopted April 8, 1975; revised March 15, 1977, January 16, 1979, April 15, 2003). B-1204, Quorum, provides that four members of the Board constitute a quorum, permits remote participation with the presiding chair's permission but without voting, and yields to the Open Meetings Act, MCL 15.261 et seq. (adopted January 16, 1979; revised July 10, 2012). B-1211, Public Participation in Board of Education Meetings, replaces 30 minutes of agenda-item comment at the beginning and 30 minutes of non-agenda comment at the end with public participation limited to 60 minutes per Board meeting, opening comment generally reserved for items posted as "Consideration." **Item 5.D, Oakland ISD budget.** Under Section 624 of the Revised School Code, as amended, the intermediate school board must submit its proposed budget no later than May 1 each year, and each constituent board must, not later than June 1, adopt a resolution expressing support or disapproval and submit objections and proposed changes. The Troy Board resolved that it had reviewed the proposed Oakland ISD budget and expressed its support, adding that "it is the responsibility of the Intermediate School District to be responsible for its own operations, including adoption of its budget" and that its support "is for the sole purpose of complying with Section 624 of the Revised School Code." The secretary or designee was directed to forward the resolution to the intermediate school board or its superintendent no later than June 1, 2016, and conflicting resolutions were rescinded; certification cites a regular meeting held May 17, 2016 noticed under the Open Meetings Act, 1976 PA 267, as amended. No ISD dollar amounts appear.

**Items 6.A and 6.B, personnel.** A tentative agreement with the Troy Educational Support Personnel Association/MEA/NEA (TESPA), comprised of paraprofessionals and skilled-trades employees, was reached April 26, 2016 and ratified by the membership (the ratification day is left as a placeholder). A tentative agreement with the Troy Educational Secretaries Association/MEA/NEA (TESA) was reached April 27, 2016 and ratified May 11, 2016. Both contracts run three (3) years, July 1, 2016 through June 30, 2019, with red-lined versions in the Board packet; no wage percentages or dollar figures are stated.

**Item 8, copier lease.** After a Technology and Business Services review of existing copiers and installations, the Board was asked to authorize the Superintendent or designee to execute a Master Equipment Lease Agreement with Great America Financial Services for a fleet of copiers for a period no greater than four (4) years at an annual cost not to exceed $73,374.72 per year, and a Cost per Copy Maintenance Agreement with Applied Imaging not to exceed $.0032 per impression for Canon Monochrome Equipment and $.0049 black and .059 color per impression for Canon Color Equipment, also not to exceed four (4) years, both as General Fund expenditures.

**Item 10.A, Oakland Schools Board election.** Under Public Act 419 of 2004 the Board must designate a representative to the 2016 electoral body and identify supported candidates by resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days before the election and considered at not less than one public meeting. The resolution names Barbara DeMarco and Connie R. Williams for two (2) positions on the Oakland Schools ISD Board of Education, each for a six (6) year term ending June 30, 2022, with the designated representative directed to vote for them at least on the first ballot at the June 6 election. A supporting email from Kathy Boike, Executive Assistant in the Oakland Schools Office of the Superintendent and Board of Education, sent Monday, May 09, 2016 4:25:09 PM to the OCSA ListServ, notes that both filers are unopposed incumbents so no "Meet the Candidates" forum will be scheduled; that ballots must be cast in person from 5:30 to 7:30 PM Monday, June 6, 2016 in Conference Room B at Oakland Schools, 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford, MI 48328, absentee ballots being prohibited; that resolutions may be adopted no earlier than May 16, 2016 and must be faxed to 248.209.2206 by end of business Friday, June 3, 2016; and that questions go to Sherry McMillan at 248.209.2062. Attachments included mcl-380-614 Revised School Code.pdf, 2016 Sample Local Board Resolution.pdf and OS BOE 2016 Election Timeline Revised.2.pdf.

FOOD SERVICE EQUIPMENT UPDATE. Troy began investigating a temperature monitoring system in November 2012 and installed a Smart Temps pilot unit at Larson in May 2014; as of February 2015 the system has been very dependable. It would monitor walk-ins, reach-ins and hot holding units and document food temperatures during preparation and serving, mandatory under HACCP and currently done manually. Listed Smart Temps clients include University of Michigan (most recent), Central Michigan, Ball State University, Notre Dame, Stanford, Saline Schools, Walled Lake Schools, West Bloomfield Schools, Jefferson County, Kentucky (largest district), and Michigan City Schools, Indiana; districts installed in 2008 were still operating strong in 2014, life expectancy could be 10 years or more, and technology changes about every 5 years. Annual monitoring provides unlimited Command Center logins, phone support, onsite training, loading of food and serving menus, automatic updates, monthly data logs, data archiving for 7 years, and alerts by SMS, e-mail and phone. Alternate vendor Great Lakes Hotel gave no response on monitoring costs; its reference School City of Hammond, Indiana (Dr. Julie Boettger) uses E-Control for walk-in coolers/freezers and dish machines only across 22 schools and is piloting Smart Temps, while Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools, North Carolina (Cindy Hobbs) and Charlotte County Public Schools (Don Buck) had not responded as of 2/4/15.

POLICY REVIEW. The packet includes a page of the August 2013 Troy School District Board Policy table of contents (B-1206 Rules of Order through B-4001 Cable-casting of Board Meetings, plus Chapter C items C-1001 through C-1103) and full policy texts. B-1703 Suspension permits temporary suspension by a vote of four members (adopted April 8, 1975; revised January 16, 1979). B-1704 Notification requires first and second readings (adopted April 8, 1975; revised January 16, 1979 and July 10, 2007). B-1801 Policy Drafting reserves drafting to the Board and requires legal counsel review. B-1901 gives the superintendent power to act absent policy. B-2001 requires prior approval by resolution for out-of-state meetings (adopted June 21, 1976; revised March 17, 1998). B-2002 sets board member compensation at $100 per annum (adopted January 16, 1979; revised March 17, 1998 and April 15, 2003). B-2101 bars member conflicts of interest and hiring of immediate family during a member's term (adopted June 21, 1976). B-3001 provides that the first applicant receiving four votes is appointed and vacancies filled within thirty (30) days (adopted March 17, 1998; revised September 2003). B-4001 requires unedited cablecast except where comments violate Regulation 9130, the Open Meetings Act or FERPA (adopted March 17, 1998).

Tentative agreement with the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA was reached March 27, 2020 and ratified by TEA membership April 2, 2020, covering February 1, 2020 through January 31, 2021. **Economic terms (Article 11.1)**
As of May 1st, eligible teachers on Steps 2 through 13 receive a lump sum equal to half their current step increment and move a half step. As of May 15th, teachers who began 2019-2020 on Longevity 1, 2 or 3 receive $500.00 and all teachers receive a $200.00 ratification bonus. As of July 1, 2020 eligible teachers move one step and each cell of Schedule A (Steps 1 through 14) increases by $500.00, with a $500.00 off-schedule payment in the first pay period of 2020-2021.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 41,800 | 45,500 | 48,700 | 52,000 |

BA-lane longevity increments are 2,682, 4,564 and 6,445, for service beyond 15, 20 and 25 years. Schedules B and C pay a percentage of $64,000 (raised from $60,467) — varsity football and basketball 11.60% ($7,424.00). Schedule D pays $30.00 per hour for curriculum development.

**Minimum Fund Balance**
A minimum fund balance of 12% is defined as the audited General Fund Equity balance of at least 12% of the 2017-2018 and 2018-2019 fiscal year total expenditures per each June 30 audit. Any shortfall measured at November 30, 2018 and/or November 30, 2019 is the "Deficiency"; multiplied by 55.6% it becomes the "Contribution," an equal-percentage off-schedule reduction of base salaries. A balance above 17% yields a "Surplus"; multiplied by 55.6% it becomes the "Bonus," paid in the second payroll in March 2019 and/or March 2020. Capital asset sale proceeds over $2 million are excluded.

**COVID-19 policy (item 4.A)**
Adopted in accordance with Executive Order 2020-35, with the first reading waived under policy 1000.03. Employees testing positive or showing principal symptoms (fever, atypical cough, atypical shortness of breath) may not enter district property until three days after symptoms resolve and seven days after they first appear or since swabbing, or upon a negative test; close contact within approximately six feet requires 14 days. Executive Order 2020-36 bars retaliation. FFCRA emergency paid sick leave provides up to 80 hours capped at $511 per day and $5,110 in the aggregate for an employee's own quarantine, and $200 per day and $2,000 in the aggregate for care of others. Emergency FMLA expansion gives up to 12 weeks for care of a child under 18, capped at $200 per day and $10,000 in the aggregate. The policy expires December 31, 2020.

Zoom access was Meeting ID 248 952 1600, with dial-in at 253-215-8782 or 301-715-8592. Public participation is limited to one-half hour each for agenda and non-agenda items, three minutes per speaker. The agenda reads: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Public Communication; 3. Personnel — A. Consideration: Troy Education Association Contract Ratification (page 3); 4. Other — A. Consideration: Adoption of COVID-19 Board Policy (page 326); 5. Adjournment. Roll-call lines name Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson and Anne.

ITEM 3.A — TEA CONTRACT RATIFICATION (dated 04.14.20). Board representatives and the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA reached a tentative agreement March 27, 2020; TEA membership ratified it April 2, 2020. The contract period is February 1, 2020 through January 31, 2021. The attached agreement is between the Troy Education Association, a local affiliate of MEA/NEA (17500 West 11 Mile, Ste. 200, Lathrup Village, MI 48076) and the Troy School District Board of Education, executed "this 14th day of April 2020," with signature blocks for the Board President and Superintendent and the TEA President and Secretary. The redlined Table of Contents places Article 37 Ancillary Teachers at page 62, Article 38 Minimum Fund Balance at page 78 and Article 39 Duration of Agreement at page 80, which directs both teams to meet on or before October 15, 2020 to discuss negotiations.

SALARY SETTLEMENT (Article 11.1). As of May 1st, eligible teachers on Steps 2 through 13, and those who moved to Step 13.5 during 2019-2020, receive a lump sum equal to half their current step increment and move a half step. As of May 15th, eligible teachers who began 2019-2020 on Longevity 1, 2 or 3 receive $500.00, added to the 2020-2021 Schedule A longevity steps, and all teachers receive a $200.00 ratification bonus. As of July 1, 2020 all eligible teachers move one salary step and each cell of Schedule A (Steps 1 through 14) increases by $500.00; a $500.00 off-schedule payment is made in the first pay period of 2020-2021. Teachers elect 21 or 26 equal payments. Six paid holidays are observed: Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, New Year's Day, Good Friday and Memorial Day.

SCHEDULE A, 2020-2021. Eleven lanes are printed — BA, BA20, MA, MA30/EDS/ESL Endorsement, PHD/EDD, and grandfathered BA25, MA5, MA10, MA15, MA20 and MA25. Step 1 pays 41,800 (BA), 45,500 (MA), 48,700 (MA30/EDS) and 52,000 (PHD/EDD); Step 14 pays 73,500, 85,000, 93,400 and 96,700, topping out at 91,750 in MA25. Longevity increments run 2,682 / 4,564 / 6,445 in the BA lane and 3,269 / 5,734 / 8,204 in PHD/EDD, paid for service beyond 15, 20 and 25 years in Troy Schools. Teachers were barred from BA+15, BA+25, MA+5, MA+15 and MA+25 after 1996-97 and from MA+10 and MA+20 after 2009-10; only teachers hired on or before December 14, 1971 may advance to BA+30.

EXTRA-DUTY SCHEDULES. Schedules B and C pay a percentage of $64,000, raised from $60,467. Varsity football and basketball pay 11.60% ($7,424.00); assistant varsity and junior varsity 7.50% ($4,800.00); varsity gymnastics, wrestling, swimming and competitive cheer 9.00% ($5,760.00); varsity baseball, track, soccer, volleyball, lacrosse and hockey 8.00% ($5,120.00); varsity tennis, golf and cross country 6.00% ($3,840.00). Schedule C spans 7.50% ($4,800) for K-12 arts coordinators and the high school band director down to 1.00% ($640) club sponsorships. Schedule D pays $30.00 per hour for curriculum development, teaching in place of a substitute and TEAM/SAT meetings, $35.00 per hour plus a $60.00 annual prep fee for instructional trainers, and $20.00 per hour for web design, with mileage at the prevailing IRS maximum rate.

CLASS SIZE, STIPENDS AND SEVERANCE. Elementary maximums are 26 in kindergarten (27), 28 in first and second grade (30) and 29 in third through fifth (30), with $80 per marking period per student over the cap paid to the TEA Education Fund. Secondary base maximum is 30, with Advanced Placement at 25 (30), Progressive Learning Support at 21 (23), physical education at 33 in middle school and 36 in high school, and counselor caseload at 400 with $500 per semester if caseload exceeds 25 after count day; exceeding a maximum by one pupil in an emergency costs $1,000.00 per occurrence. Other stipends include $500 per year for secondary teachers traveling between schools, $350 per semester for early/late building assignments and $500 per mentee. Severance pays tenure teachers with ten or more years half the per diem rate for unused sick days to a maximum of 60 days plus 30 days at the substitute rate, and those with less than ten years the substitute rate to a maximum of 90 days; payments of $5,000.00 or more go into a District 403(b). Retirement severance pays $1,000.00 at 10-14 years, $1,500.00 at 15-19 years and $100.00 per year at 20 or more.

INSURANCE AND EARLY CHILDHOOD EDUCATORS. Article 26 maintains compliance with the Publicly Funded Health Insurance Contribution Act (PA 152 of 2011), the Board paying the annual maximum allowable and teachers the difference over 21 pays. MESSA PAK A bundles medical, Delta Dental, VSP III vision, life and long-term disability; life is two times salary, except $50,000 AD/D for teachers hired on or after June 4, 1991. Long-term disability begins after 60 calendar days and pays up to two-thirds of salary to age 70. Plan B pays $1,000 annually, or $2,500 if 45 or more teachers decline district medical coverage. New Article 36 covers early childhood educators in the Board's tuition-based preschool program under Michigan's Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA), with a salary schedule of $28,008, $29,564, $31,120, $32,676 and $34,232 for Steps 1 through 5, a $1,000 annual master's stipend, a $3,000 cafeteria plan in lieu of medical coverage, a $50,000 term life policy and disability capped at $3,000 per month. Appendix 5 lists BCBSM plans CB 2, CB 3, CB 4 and Simply Blue effective 1/1/2020 with in-network deductibles of $100, $250, $500 and $1,400, and dental under Group #9941.

MINIMUM FUND BALANCE. The article sets a minimum fund balance of 12%, defined as the audited General Fund Equity balance of at least 12% of the 2017-2018 and 2018-2019 school/fiscal year total expenditures determined by each June 30 audit. If that balance falls below 12%, the amount needed to restore it is calculated as of November 30, 2018 and/or November 30, 2019 as the "Deficiency"; the Deficiency multiplied by 55.6% is the "Contribution," achieved by reducing base salaries of all actively employed bargaining unit members by an equal percentage through an off-schedule reduction beginning with the first payroll period in January 2018, accounting for retirement and FICA, unless another method is agreed before December 31, 2018 and/or December 31, 2019. Where the balance exceeds 17%, the excess measured on the same dates is the "Surplus"; the Surplus multiplied by 55.6% is the "Bonus," paid as an equal-percentage off-schedule lump sum in the second payroll in March 2019 and/or March 2020. Costs of new programs in excess of $2 million should not increase total year-over-year budgetary expenditures unless federally or state mandated, and one-time revenues from capital asset sales in excess of $2 million are excluded. Article 25.2 entitles the TEA to monthly financial reports.

CALENDARS AND APPENDICES. The 2020/2021 calendar totals 186 teacher days and 181 student days, with 6-12 marking periods ending November 5, January 21, March 25 and June 16. The payroll schedule runs from 8/21/2020 through 8/20/2021. A Letter of Agreement on Schoology grading amends Sections 14.14 and 14.15 of the 2017-2020 agreement through June 16, 2020. Appendix 1 is the grievance report form (rev/10-96), Appendix 2 the mentoring log, Appendix 3 board policies 4000.03 and 4000.04, and Appendix 4 the Child Care Supervisor Evaluation.

ITEM 4.A — COVID-19 BOARD POLICY. The Board considered a policy on COVID-19 Mitigation, Self-Reporting, Leave of Absence, noting that policy 1000.03 Adoption or Amendment of Bylaws and Policies permits waiver of a first reading. Adopted in accordance with Executive Order 2020-35, it bars employees and contractors who test positive or display principal symptoms from entering district property until three days have passed since symptoms resolved and seven days since symptoms first appeared or since swabbing, or until a negative test; close contact requires 14 days. Principal symptoms are fever, atypical cough or atypical shortness of breath; close contact is being within approximately six feet of an individual for a prolonged period. Executive Order 2020-36 prohibits retaliation for staying home. Employees must maintain at least six feet of distance and follow Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance; health information is protected under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 and the Family Education Rights and Privacy Act of 1974, with exposure reporting under Board Policy 5502. Under the FFCRA Emergency Paid Sick Leave Act, full-time employees receive up to 80 hours and part-time employees hours equal to their 2-week average, capped at $511 per day and $5,110 in the aggregate for the employee's own quarantine or symptoms, and $200 per day and $2,000 in the aggregate for caring for others. The Emergency Family and Medical Leave Expansion Act provides up to 12 weeks to care for a child under 18 whose school or child care is closed, for employees with at least 30 calendar days of service, the first 10 days unpaid and later days at not less than two-thirds of pay, capped at $200 per day and $10,000 in the aggregate. Legal references are PL 116-127 § 5101 et seq. and § 3101 et seq., 134 Stat. 177, and Executive Orders 2020-35 and 2020-36. The policy expires December 31, 2020 unless state or federal law extends the date.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, June 20, 2017, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The agenda opens with business rather than recognition, because item 2.A is a **public hearing on the preliminary 2017-2018 budget**.

**Recognition**
Dr. Machesky introduces the "2016-2017 School Year in Review" video. The Mission Moment features Athens' **AP Capstone program**: AP Seminar teachers Brenda Rice and Sue Syme and AP Research teacher Rachel Webb present, followed by a question-and-answer session in which the students themselves field Board questions about the program — chosen, the item says, "based on their success in the program and their ability to express themselves well."

**Consent agenda**
Treasurer's Report for April and May 2017.

**Personnel — the teacher contract**
A tentative agreement between the Board and the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA was reached **June 9, 2017**, signed by TEA president Tony Lucchi and Assistant Superintendent Jordan Harris, and **ratified by the TEA membership June 16**. The contract runs **July 1, 2017 through January 31, 2020**. The bargaining team the Board appointed in February — Harris as chief spokesperson with West, Dziatczak, Griffor, Trotter and Pass — closed it eleven days before the old agreement expired.

**David Recker** is appointed Assistant Principal, Larson Middle School, effective July 1, 2017, on a two-year probationary contract. He began teaching language arts and journalism at Dayton Early College Academy in 2012, moved to Troy in 2014 to teach language arts at Troy High, implemented ISTE standards, led the Continuous Improvement Committee and coordinated several clubs; he holds a bachelor's from the University of Dayton and an M.A. in K-12 education administration from Michigan State.

**Curriculum — two adoptions**
Secondary world language materials for grades 6-12 covering **Chinese, French, German, Japanese and Spanish**, presented by Mark Dziatczak and Jennifer Gottlieb, at **$419,606.82**. ELD materials for grades 6-12, presented by Dziatczak and Christin Silagy, at **$171,735.32**. Board members reviewed the textbooks and discussed both at the June 13 workshop.

**Business — the budget**
The 2016-17 budget amendment sets the General Fund at **$146,020,168**, Capital Projects at $16,288,758, Food Service at $4,032,399, Troy Career Center at $2,215,068 and Capital Maintenance at $1,885,000.

The 2017-18 appropriations resolution then sets the year ahead:

| Fund | Appropriation |
| --- | --- |
| General Fund | $147,430,144 |
| 2014 Capital Projects Funds | $21,615,000 |
| Debt Service Funds | $18,778,792 |
| Special Revenue Funds | $9,516,614 |
| Capital Maintenance Fund | $1,270,000 |

General Fund revenue is budgeted at $147,458,385 — local $37,990,138, state $97,760,866, federal $3,506,988, incoming transfers and other $8,200,393 — against an estimated July 1, 2017 fund balance of $22,335,432, for $169,793,817 available to appropriate. Instruction takes $101,335,630 (basic programs $83,230,516, added needs $17,245,604, adult and continuing education $859,510). Millage rates: **non-homestead general operating 18.0000, commercial personal property 11.6320, homestead 5.6320, and all properties debt retirement 4.7000.**

**Business — selling Section 11**
The RFP for 18 +/- acres north of Long Lake, east of Rochester Road and west of Allison Street (Sidwell 20-11-328-003 and 20-11-401-001) drew **twelve proposals**, examined with Clark Hill and Great Northern. The recommendation is **Mondrian Properties, L.L.C. at $4,225,000.00** — the same firm that had bid on Section 23 in January and would go on to buy Section 16 and the Section 1 frontage. As with the Section 23 item, the resolution authorizes Dr. Machesky to negotiate and execute a final Offer To Purchase on terms acceptable to him after consulting counsel, rather than approving a completed agreement.

**Business — four service contracts**
Rick West's June 8 memo explains that three contracts expire June 30, 2017.

- **First Student** (buses), initial three-year term from July 1, 2014, extended two years. The reasoning is candid: Troy's per-route cost is very competitive, but "the starting wage for bus drivers is low relative to neighboring districts. This is causing difficulty in staffing" — so the recommendation is a renewal **increasing per-route cost by 5%–8% in the first year and 3%–5% in the second**, citing the nationwide bus driver shortage.
- **Safe-Ed** (security at Athens, Troy High and Troy Career and College High School), a partner since 2011, renewed three years: base contract **$305,000, $310,000 and $315,000** against a current $300,500.
- **Clean-Ed**, six facility maintenance technicians supplementing skilled trades staff, renewed three years at **no additional cost** — Clean-Ed charges a flat fee per employee to handle the HR functions.
- **Sodexo Management, Inc.** food service, renewed for 2017/2018, already approved by the Michigan Department of Education.

**Business — workers' compensation**
The district is self-insured through the State of Michigan with York Risk Management as third-party administrator and Midwest Casualty on excess claims. Claims history has been excellent, which keeps cost low, "however, we do continually have **$400,000 exposure per employee injury**." The Board accepts MASB-SEG's full-coverage proposal effective July 1, 2017 at **not to exceed $98,968.00** — buying a predictable budget number and eliminating that exposure.

**Other — the sinking fund survey**
Epic MRA, the Lansing firm that ran the 2013 bond survey, polled **400 Troy residents** April 20-24, 2017 — registered voters who at least "seldom" vote in local school elections, 20% cell-only, 80% cooperation rate, ±5% at 95% confidence. To keep costs down, a Board member with market research expertise drafted and analyzed it.

The background is stated plainly: the 2013 bond was structured to be tax-neutral, which "also meant it wouldn't cover everything the District knew it needed," and the Board's hope that state funding would recover "hasn't happened." Recent legislative changes broadened permitted sinking fund uses to maintenance, facility improvements and construction, safety and security, and technology. Because the district recently retired debt, a **1-mill sinking fund could be structured with no property tax increase**, yielding **$3.6 million per year for ten years**.

The finding: **61% Yes, 7% leaning Yes, 4% leaning No, 16% No, 12% not sure.** Reasons for Yes run maintenance and upkeep (21%), pro-education or always vote yes (18%), more funding needed (16%), no tax increase (15%), educational quality (5%) and property values (4%). The report's blunt conclusion, repeated across three slides: no tax increase is what earns the endorsement — **"raising it collapses support."** That matters because, as the background notes, a district can pursue only one sinking fund every ten years.

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, June 20, 2017, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Business — A. Public Hearing: 2017/2018 Proposed Budget; 3. Recognition — A. 2016-2017 School Year in Review, B. Mission Moment: Athens AP Capstone & Seminar Students; 4. Additions & Deletions; 5. Public Communication (agenda items); 6. General – Consent Agenda — A. Treasurer's Report – April & May 2017; 7. Personnel — A. Consideration: Troy Education Association Contract Ratification, B. Consideration: Administrative Appointment – Assistant Principal, Larson Middle School; 8. Curriculum — A. Report: World Language Materials, B. Consideration: World Language Materials Adoption, C. Report: ELD Materials, D. Consideration: ELD Materials Adoption; 9. Business — A. Consideration: 2016/2017 Budget Amendment, B. Consideration: 2017/2018 Budget Appropriations Resolution, C. Consideration: Section 11 Purchase Agreement, D. Consideration: First Student Contract Renewal, E. Consideration: Safe-Ed Contract Renewal, F. Consideration: Clean-Ed Contract Renewal, G. Consideration: Worker's Compensation Insurance, H. Consideration: Food Service Contract Renewal for 2017-2018; 10. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 11. Other — A. Report: Survey Results; 12. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

The agenda's ordering is itself notable: business comes before recognition, because item 2.A is the statutory public hearing on the proposed budget, which must precede adoption later in the same meeting.

**Business 2.A: public hearing on the preliminary 2017-2018 budget.** The item attaches a PowerPoint presentation and a draft of the 2017-18 budget book, to be finalized following board adoption of the budget.

**Recognition 3.A: 2016-2017 School Year in Review.** Dr. Rich Machesky, Superintendent of Schools, introduces the video.

**Recognition 3.B: Athens AP Capstone and Seminar students.** Athens AP Seminar teachers Brenda Rice and Sue Syme, along with AP Research teacher Rachel Webb, present a brief overview of the AP Capstone Program. The overview is followed by a question and answer session in which Board members put questions to the students themselves, who answer about their experiences and the unique learning opportunity the program provides. The item records that the students were chosen for the event based on their success in the program and their ability to express themselves well. Athens Principal Lara Dixon introduces the teachers, who in turn introduce their students; the AP Seminar students named include Rija Awan, Nathan Babcock, Saihaj Deol and Rishita Gudeti. Gudeti would appear again eighteen months later among the district's 54 National Merit Scholarship semifinalists.

**Consent agenda 6.A.** The Treasurer's Report for April and May 2017 — two months presented together, as the June meeting is the last of the fiscal year.

**Personnel 7.A: TEA contract ratification.** A tentative agreement between representatives of the Troy Board of Education and the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA was reached on June 9, 2017. The TEA membership voted to ratify the agreement on June 16, 2017. The tentative agreement is a contract for the period of July 1, 2017 through January 31, 2020, and its specifics are attached, signed by Mr. Tony Lucchi, President of the TEA, and Mr. Jordan Harris, Assistant Superintendent, Employee Services, on June 9, 2017. The resolution ratifies and adopts that agreement.

The timing is tight and deliberate. The Board appointed its negotiating team on February 28, 2017 — Jordan Harris as chief spokesperson with Rick West, Mark Dziatczak, Kris Griffor, Stephanie Trotter and Dave Pass — against a contract expiring June 30. The tentative agreement came on June 9, membership ratification on June 16, and Board ratification on June 20, ten days before expiry. The term chosen is unusual: rather than a clean three-year deal ending June 30, 2020, the contract runs to January 31, 2020, placing the next expiration mid-school-year.

**Personnel 7.B: Assistant Principal, Larson Middle School.** The recommendation is Mr. David Recker. He started his career in education following graduation from college in 2012, teaching language arts and journalism at the Dayton Early College Academy in Dayton, Ohio. He moved to the Troy area in 2014 and accepted a language arts teaching position at Troy High School. During his time in Dayton and at Troy High he fulfilled many additional responsibilities including implementing the International Society for Technology in Education's standards, leading the Continuous Improvement Committee to increase use of best practices, and serving as coordinator for several extracurricular clubs and committees. He holds a bachelor's degree in adolescent to young adult education from the University of Dayton and a Master of Arts in K-12 education administration from Michigan State University. The resolution issues a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position, effective July 1, 2017. The packet attaches his Oakland Human Resources Consortium online application, submitted May 10, 2017.

**Curriculum 8.A and 8.B: secondary world language materials adoption.** Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent, and Jennifer Gottlieb, Director of Student Growth, Equity and Accountability, report that Board members reviewed and discussed the recommended world language materials for grades 6-12 for the upcoming school year. The consideration item records that Dziatczak and Gottlieb, along with members of the Teaching and Learning team, provided information on the recommended Chinese, French, German, Japanese and Spanish world language materials for grades 6-12, and that Board members had an opportunity to review textbooks, ask questions and discuss the recommendation at the June 13 Board Workshop. The total cost of these materials is $419,606.82, and the resolution approves them for the 2017-2018 school year in that amount.

**Curriculum 8.C and 8.D: ELD materials adoption.** Mark Dziatczak and Christin Silagy, Director of ELD, Federal Grants and State Assessments, report that Board members reviewed and discussed the recommended ELD materials for grades 6-12. The consideration item records the same June 13 workshop review, gives the total cost of the materials as $171,735.32, and the resolution approves them on the same terms.

The two adoptions together commit close to six hundred thousand dollars of instructional materials in a single meeting, both for grades 6-12, and both reviewed by the Board in person the week before — the packet is careful to record that trustees handled the textbooks themselves.

**Business 9.A: 2016-17 budget amendment resolution.** The amendment covers the General Fund, Debt Service Funds, Food Service Fund, Troy Career Center Fund, Adult Education and Community Service Fund, Facility Rentals Fund, Capital Projects Funds and the Capital Maintenance Fund. The item notes the resolution need not be read in its entirety but must be made part of the official minutes. The amended fund totals include General Fund $146,020,168; Food Service Fund $4,032,399; Troy Career Center Fund $2,215,068; Capital Projects Fund $16,288,758; and Capital Maintenance Fund $1,885,000. This is the year's final true-up, following the Budget Amendment #2 adopted in March.

**Business 9.B: 2017-2018 Budget Appropriations Resolution.** The appropriations resolution covers the General Fund, Special Revenue Funds, Debt Service Funds, Capital Projects Funds and the Capital Maintenance Fund as required by the Department of Education. The resolution approves the general appropriations and budget and millage rates for fiscal year 2017-18 as attached and made part of the official minutes of the June 20, 2017 regular meeting: General Fund $147,430,144; Special Revenue Funds $9,516,614; Debt Service Funds $18,778,792; 2014 Capital Projects Funds $21,615,000; and Capital Maintenance Fund $1,270,000.

The millage rates approved are, by tax base and purpose: non-homestead general operating, 18.0000 mills; commercial personal property general operating, 11.6320 mills; homestead general operating, 5.6320 mills; and all properties debt retirement, 4.7000 mills.

On the revenue side, the General Fund is budgeted at local $37,990,138, state $97,760,866, federal $3,506,988 and incoming transfers and other $8,200,393, for total revenues and incoming transfers of $147,458,385. The estimated fund balance at July 1, 2017 is $22,335,432, all of it available to appropriate, giving total available to appropriate of $169,793,817. Of that, $147,430,144 is appropriated: instruction takes $101,335,630, comprising basic programs $83,230,516, added needs $17,245,604 and adult and continuing education $859,510; support services begin with pupil services at $10,678,738.

The 18 non-homestead mills approved here are the same levy that would be eroded by Headlee and restored by the November 2018 replacement election.

**Business 9.C: Section 11 purchase agreement.** The School District issued a Request For Proposals To Purchase Real Property to obtain proposals to purchase certain surplus vacant real property located in Section 11, and received twelve proposals, examined in conjunction with legal counsel Clark Hill and consultant Great Northern. The recommendation is that the Board authorize the sale of the property to Mondrian Properties, L.L.C. in the amount of $4,225,000.00.

The resolution describes the property as 18 +/- acres of vacant land located north of Long Lake, east of Rochester Road and west of Allison Street in Troy, Michigan, Sidwell Numbers 20-11-328-003 and 20-11-401-001. It recites the proposal from Mondrian Properties, L.L.C. to purchase the property for a purchase price of Four Million Two Hundred Twenty Five Thousand and 00/100 ($4,225,000.00) Dollars; that the district is desirous of authorizing the sale on the terms generally described and substantially similar to those contained in the Purchaser's response and clarifications to the RFP; and that it wishes to authorize Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky, or his designee, to negotiate the terms and conditions of a final Offer To Purchase on terms acceptable to him after consultation with legal counsel, and to execute the negotiated Offer To Purchase and any documents necessary and incidental to the sale.

This is the sale the March 2017 district-owned property resolution authorized marketing, and it is the largest of the district's land transactions in these packets. The structure is the same one used for Section 23 in January — the Board authorizes a negotiation rather than approving a signed agreement — but unlike the January item, this resolution names the buyer and states the price. Mondrian Properties had first appeared in these packets as one of two bidders discussed at the January 10, 2017 workshop on Section 23; it takes Section 11 here, and would go on to buy Section 16 and the Section 1 front parcel in 2018. Twelve proposals for this parcel is the largest field the district drew for any of its properties.

**Business 9.D through 9.F: service contract renewals.** Rick West's June 8, 2017 memorandum to the Board, copied to Dr. Machesky, explains that the initial terms for three service contracts expire on June 30, 2017 and that the district has been negotiating renewal terms for each.

First Student provides bus transportation services. The initial term was the three-year period commencing July 1, 2014 and ending June 30, 2017, with an option to extend for up to two additional years. West writes that the district currently has a very competitive contract based on per-route pricing and believes it can negotiate a better deal for a two-year renewal than by rebidding the services. His recommendation is candid about the pressure: "Given our competitive per route cost, the starting wage for bus drivers is low relative to neighboring districts. This is causing difficulty in staffing; therefore, we will be recommending a renewal contract that will increase the per route cost by 5% - 8% for the first year and 3% - 5% for the second year." He cites comparative per-route data from other county districts and the nationwide bus driver shortage, and notes the increase will be reflected in the 2017-18 proposed budget. The resolution authorizes administration to finalize the renewal for the 2017/2018 and 2018/2019 school years.

Safe Ed provides professional security consultation solutions at Troy Athens, Troy High School and Troy Career and College High School, under an initial three-year term commencing July 1, 2014. West records that Safe Ed has been a quality partner in providing security services since 2011 and recommends a successor agreement for three years commencing July 1, 2017 and ending June 30, 2020. The current base contract cost is $300,500, and the recommended base contract for the three years is $305,000, $310,000 and $315,000 respectively. The resolution authorizes finalizing the renewal for 2017/2018, 2018/2019 and 2019/2020.

Clean Ed employs six facility maintenance technicians responsible for providing supplemental support to the district's skilled trades staff. The initial term was one year commencing July 1, 2016. West recommends a successor agreement for three years commencing July 1, 2017 and ending June 30, 2020, noting there will be no additional cost for these services as Clean Ed charges a flat fee per employee to handle the human resource functions of employment for these positions.

**Business 9.G: worker's compensation insurance.** The district solicited a worker's compensation insurance proposal from MASB-SEG. It is currently self-insured through the State of Michigan with York Risk Management serving as third-party administrator and Midwest Casualty handling excess insurance claims.

West's June 8, 2017 memorandum explains the trade: "Our claims history has been excellent over the past few years which keeps the cost of our workers compensation low; however, we do continually have $400,000 exposure per employee injury." SET SEG, the district's current property casualty insurance carrier, provides full coverage workers compensation insurance, and given the claims history the district has an opportunity to switch to very affordable full coverage. He recommends making the change, which "will provide us a more predictable budget number for workers compensation and eliminates the $400,000 exposure per employee injury," and notes it would be discussed at the June 13 workshop with the SET SEG proposal attached for review.

The resolution authorizes administration to accept the proposal from MASB-SEG for full coverage worker's compensation insurance effective July 1, 2017 for an amount not to exceed $98,968.00. The item is a clean illustration of what a district buys with insurance: not a lower expected cost — self-insurance with good claims experience is cheap — but the removal of a tail risk and a number the budget can rely on.

**Business 9.H: renewal of food services contract.** On June 21, 2016 the Board approved a resolution allowing administration to enter into a contract with Sodexo Management, Inc. to continue providing the food service operation for the district. The renewal must be approved by the Michigan Department of Education and the Troy Board of Education annually, and the item records that MDE has approved this renewal. The resolution authorizes administration to approve the contract renewal with Sodexo for the 2017/2018 school year.

**Other 11.A: 2017 Sinking Fund Community Input Survey.** The final report, commissioned by the Troy Board of Education and dated June 13, 2017, is organized as introduction, perceptions of district performance, projected sinking fund voting patterns and prevalent public attitudes.

The background section states the problem without hedging. Because of persistent funding gaps from the State, the district continues to seek other ways to fund quality education. In 2013 voters overwhelmingly supported a $125 million bond to help cover many expenses over the bond's 10-year lifespan; the district structured that bond so as not to raise property tax rates, but keeping the bond tax-neutral "also meant it wouldn't cover everything the District knew it needed." The Board hoped state funding would increase sufficiently when the economy improved, "but that hasn't happened." As a result the district continues to struggle to pay for things like preventative maintenance on its buildings. Recent legislative adjustments to appropriate uses for a sinking fund have made it a potential avenue for covering significant district costs such as maintenance, facility improvements and construction, safety and security measures, and technology.

Consequently the Board is considering whether to place a sinking fund proposal on the November ballot. Because the district recently retired some debt, it could structure a new 1-mill sinking fund so that the total school millage rate in Troy would stay where it is, with no property tax increase from what homeowners pay today. That 1 mill would provide the district with $3.6 million per year for the next ten years, to be used to fill current holes in preventative maintenance, update classrooms and technology in a timelier manner, and cover debt payments on new or existing buildings. The report notes the strategic tension: given ongoing needs it would be appropriate to ask for more than 1 mill, "especially because a school district can only pursue one sinking fund every ten years."

Methodology: a phone survey fielded by Epic MRA, a Lansing-based market research company and the firm that completed the 2013 TSD bond survey, averaging 18 minutes in length and fielded April 20 to 24, 2017. To keep district costs as low as possible, a Board member with market research expertise drafted and analyzed the survey following standard research industry practices. The sample was 400 Troy residents living within the Troy School District area, registered voters who indicate they are at least "seldom" voters in local school related elections, with age distribution consistent with voting patterns from the 2011 and 2013 Troy elections. Twenty percent of interviews were completed with cell-only households, and the cooperation rate was extremely high — 80% of those who answered and qualified completed the survey. Full sample results are accurate to within +/- 5% at the 95 percent confidence level. The sample profile is 53% women and 47% men, with an age distribution of 5% aged 18 to 29, 7% aged 30 to 39, 17% aged 40 to 49, 35% aged 50 to 64, 34% aged 65 or older, and 2% declining to say.

The headline finding: the 1-mill sinking fund proposal enjoyed wide support, driven most by a sense of necessity and general educational commitment. On the vote question, 61% said Yes, 7% leaning Yes, 4% leaning No, 16% No and 12% not sure. Reasons given for Yes were maintenance and upkeep important (21%), pro-education or always vote yes (18%), more funding needed (16%), no tax increase (15%), educational quality (5%) and property values (4%).

The report's conclusion is stated three separate times across its slides, in identical words: no tax increase is what earns the endorsement from the community — and raising it collapses support. On the segment analysis, "maybe" voters are characterized as more pragmatic than supporters and less pessimistic than non-supporters, with a conversation around new technology and investment protection identified as the productive line of argument for them.

Read against the strategic tension the background sets out — that a district gets one sinking fund per decade and therefore has reason to ask for more than a mill — the survey's answer is unambiguous: the support is real but it is contingent entirely on tax neutrality, and the district's own polling told it not to reach.

Read as a whole, the June 2017 packet closes the fiscal year and sets up the next several. It ratifies a teacher contract running into 2020, adopts a $147,430,144 General Fund at 18 non-homestead mills, sells eighteen acres for $4,225,000.00 to the developer who would buy two more parcels from the district, locks in four service contracts through 2020, trades a $400,000 per-injury exposure for a $98,968.00 premium, buys nearly six hundred thousand dollars of secondary language materials, and receives the polling that would shape the November ballot question.

Item 4.A.1 provides the nomination form for president — one member nominating another to serve as president of the Troy Board of Education until December 31, 2019 — followed by the close of nominations and a suggested resolution, with the same structure repeated for vice president and secretary. Item 4.B appoints the treasurer. Item 4.C establishes fund depositories and the investment resolution for both 2018/19 and 2019/20. Item 4.D designates board and district legal counsel; 4.E designates the superintendent to be deputy secretary of the Board; 4.F designates a person responsible for posting notices of meetings; and 4.G adopts the meeting schedule for the 2019 calendar year.

**Consent agenda.** A. Minutes of the December 4, 2018 Board of Education Workshop; B. Minutes of the December 18, 2018 Board of Education Meeting; C. Treasurer's Report for November 2018; D. Budget Adjustment #1. **Business 11.C: Troy High School pool renovation.** The resolution awards the pool renovation as set out in the attached schedule, as an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund and the Sinking Fund: B & B Pools for pool upgrades at $209,090.00, Shoreview Electric for electrical work at $123,400.00, Paint Plus for painting at $149,300.00, and a contingency of $48,179.00, for a total of $529,969.00.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of February 26, 2019 at the Services Building. It sets the district's enrollment posture for 2019-2020 — closing Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, Boulan Park and both high schools to open enrollment except for up to 25 incoming ninth graders transferring to Athens, while opening a limited Schools of Choice program for 50 kindergarten, one first grade and 20 middle school seats — and awards the two largest remaining pieces of the new preschool: $702,576.00 of playground construction to Rolar, Inc. and $482,495.76 of furnishings. It also carries the December 2018 Treasurer's Report with total disbursements in period of $8,420,287.20.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Meeting**
Regular meeting, February 26, 2019, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
Three items: the Fall 2018 All-State Athletes; a Mission Moment on elementary student artwork created for the new TSD Preschool; and Principal Appreciation Month.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the January 8 workshop and the January 15 organizational and regular meeting, the December 2018 Treasurer's Report, and second reading and adoption of new and revised board policies reviewed by the Board Policy Committee for compliance with the Revised School Code.

**Treasurer's Report — December 2018**
General Fund check disbursements total $4,103,654.39 and total disbursements in period are $8,420,287.20. At December 31, 2018 the General Fund balance stands at $18,641,192, consolidated Debt Service at $8,096,255 and consolidated Special Revenue at $2,454,680.

**Curriculum — who may enroll in 2019-2020**
Dr. Machesky presents enrollment projections for 2019-2020 and beyond, built on an analysis of the district's enrollment history prepared by Dr. Fred Ignatovich of Stanfred Consultants.

On the strength of those projections, administration recommends closing several buildings to open enrollment. Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park are closed on total enrollment and physical space constraints. Athens and Troy High have been closed for several years as the district works to maximize each building's enrollment, and both are closed again — with one exception: **not more than 25 incoming ninth grade students who live in the Troy High attendance area but wish to attend Athens**, with applications accepted during a two-week window at the beginning of March. Students with siblings already at Athens or Troy High in grades 9 through 11 may open enroll to remain for the year.

Separately, and in the opposite direction, the Board adopts the annual Schools of Choice resolution required by state law. Under Section 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, the district will accept applications for a limited program for 2019-2020 covering **50 kindergarten, 1 first grade and 20 total 6th-8th grade nonresident students** at Baker, Larson and Smith middle schools, open to students from districts within or outside Oakland County where that intermediate school district is contiguous with Oakland ISD boundaries.

**Business — finishing the preschool**
RFP 9873, Bid Pack 5 of the Early Childcare Center project, sought competitive bids for playground area construction — site construction, playground equipment and site amenities for the new building. Five bidders responded, and Rob Carson and Barton Malow recommend Rolar, Inc. on low bid for its category, including four alternates, at $702,576.00 from the Early Childcare Center Fund.

Furnishings for the preschool were sourced and priced through cooperative bid contracts and reviewed by Rob Carson, Kris Griffor, Erin Keyser and TMP Architecture, awarded at $482,495.76 from the Early Childhood Center Fund with the resolution made part of the official minutes.

**Other**
The Board casts its ballot in the 2019 MASB Board of Directors' election for Region 8, a three-year term with one seat. The candidates are Joshua Denzler (Lake Shore Public Schools, Macomb County), **Steve Gottlieb (Troy School District, Oakland County)**, Birgit McQuiston (Lake Orion Community Schools), Darlene Pomponio, Ph.D. (Southgate Community Schools, Wayne County), Angie Smith (Farmington Public Schools), Michael Swiecki (Wyandotte Public Schools, Wayne County) and Regina Williams (Harper Woods School District, Wayne County).
