Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, February 26, 2019, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. All-State Athletes Fall 2018, B. Mission Moment: Elementary Student Artwork for TSD Preschool, C. Principal Appreciation Month; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the January 8, 2019 workshop, B. Minutes of the January 15, 2019 organizational and regular meeting, C. Treasurer's Report – December 2018, D. Second Reading and Adoption of New/Revised Board Policies; 6. Personnel; 7. Curriculum — A. Report: Enrollment Projections, B. Consideration: Schools Closed to Open Enrollment, C. Report: Schools of Choice 105 & 105C, D. Consideration: Schools of Choice 105 & 105C; 8. Business — A. TSD Preschool Playground, B. TSD Preschool Furniture; 9. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 10. Other — A. 2019 MASB Board of Directors' Election; 11. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition.** The evening opens with recognition of the All-State Athletes for Fall 2018, a Mission Moment featuring elementary student artwork created for the new Troy School District Preschool, and Principal Appreciation Month.

**Consent agenda.** Minutes of the January 8, 2019 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the January 15, 2019 Board of Education Organizational and Regular Meeting; the Treasurer's Report for December 2018; and second reading and adoption of new and revised board policies. The policy item records that members of the Board Policy Committee reviewed the listed policies against the Revised School Code and that the first reading of the revised and additional policies was conducted at the prior meeting.

**Treasurer's Report, December 2018.** General Fund check disbursements total $4,103,654.39, and total disbursements in period — check disbursements together with ACH debits, outgoing wire transfers, P-Card purchases and prior period void disbursements — come to $8,420,287.20. The summary revenue and expense budget reports for the period ending December 31, 2018 give a General Fund balance of $18,641,192, a consolidated Debt Service Funds balance of $8,096,255 and a consolidated Special Revenue Funds balance of $2,454,680. The middle sections of the packet carry the December check register run by fund.

**Curriculum 7.A: enrollment projections.** Dr. Machesky presents to the Board on enrollment projections for the 2019-2020 school year and beyond. The analysis of the district's enrollment history and projections was provided by Dr. Fred Ignatovich of Stanfred Consultants.

**Curriculum 7.B: schools closed to open enrollment for 2019-2020.** Administration reports having reviewed enrollment for the elementary, middle and high school attendance areas. Because of the elementary and middle school buildings' total student enrollment and physical space constraints, it recommends that Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park schools be closed to open enrollment. It notes that the district's goal for Athens and Troy High has been to maximize each building's enrollment, which has resulted in both being closed to open enrollment for the past several years, and that based on current projections for 2019-2020 both should be closed again — with the exception of not more than twenty-five incoming ninth grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School. Applications for those twenty-five spots at Athens will be accepted during a two-week window at the beginning of March.

The resolution closes Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park schools as well as Athens and Troy High Schools to open enrollment for the 2019-2020 school year, with that twenty-five-student exception, and provides that students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High who are currently enrolled in grades 9 through 11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain for the 2019-2020 school year.

**Curriculum 7.C and 7.D: Schools of Choice under Sections 105 and 105c.** A report precedes the resolution. In accordance with Michigan state law, school districts must pass a resolution each school year if they intend to participate in a Schools of Choice program. The item anticipates that a limited number of seats will be available for 2019-2020 for kindergarten, first grade, and grades six through eight at Baker, Larson and Smith Middle Schools, and proposes a resolution for fifty kindergarten, one first grade, and twenty total sixth through eighth grade nonresident students who attend a school district within or outside of Oakland County, provided that intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries.

The resolution accordingly provides that the Board of Education, exercising the option permitted by Section 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, will accept applications for a Limited Schools of Choice program for the 2019-2020 school year for fifty kindergarten, one first grade and twenty total sixth through eighth grade nonresident students on those terms. Read alongside item 7.B, the two resolutions set the district's enrollment posture from both directions in a single meeting: closing the buildings under space pressure while opening a bounded number of seats where capacity exists.

**Business 8.A: preschool playground.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on playground area construction as part of the Troy School District Preschool project, with responses reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations, and Barton Malow Company. Rob Carson's February 21, 2019 memorandum to Rick West, covering RFP 9873, Bid Pack 5 of the ECC Building Project, records that the RFP produced five bidders and that the scope of work is site construction, playground equipment and site amenities for the new Early Childcare Center building, with an attached bid summary detailing four alternates he recommends as part of the RFP. He recommends, on low bid for the category, category 116000 Playground Equipment to Rolar, Inc. including alternates A1, A2, A3 and A4 at $702,576.00. The resolution awards the playground area construction to Rolar, Inc. in the amount of $702,576.00 as an expenditure of the Early Childcare Center Fund.

**Business 8.B: preschool furnishings.** Quotations were received for competitive pricing on furnishings for the Troy School District Preschool. The recommended items were sourced and priced through cooperative bid contracts and reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations; Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent for Elementary Instruction; Erin Keyser, Director of Early Childhood Programs; and TMP Architecture. The resolution awards the furnishings as attached in the amount of $482,495.76 as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund, with the resolution made a part of the official minutes of the February 26, 2019 regular meeting; the attached award schedule assigns vendors by category on low bid.

**Other 10.A: 2019 MASB Board of Directors' election.** Biographical data for the candidates is attached for the Board's review. The Region 8 seat is a three-year term with one seat, and the candidates are Joshua Denzler of Lake Shore Public Schools in Macomb County; Steve Gottlieb of the Troy School District, Oakland County; Birgit McQuiston of Lake Orion Community Schools, Oakland County; Darlene Pomponio, Ph.D. of Southgate Community Schools, Wayne County; Angie Smith of Farmington Public Schools, Oakland County; Michael Swiecki of Wyandotte Public Schools, Wayne County; and Regina Williams of Harper Woods School District, Wayne County. The resolution casts the Troy Board of Education's ballot for one candidate to serve on the 2019 Michigan Association of School Boards' Board of Directors for the Region 8 three-year term — an election in which one of the district's own trustees, Steve Gottlieb, is a candidate.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, October 16, 2018, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois — ending in closed session on attorney-client privilege.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment invites Athens parents and district teachers Dawn and Mark Hayes to tell the story of how their special-needs daughter Allie was asked to be this year's Grand Marshall of the Athens Homecoming Parade.

The Board then commends **54 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists**. More than a million students from some 22,000 high schools entered the program nationwide and only 16,000 seniors are selected; semifinalists score in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT and earn comparable SAT scores. The packet prints the roster with phonetic pronunciation guides beside most names, for reading aloud. Copies of the resolution go to the students at an October 30 reception.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the September 4 workshop and the September 18 meeting, the August 2018 Treasurer's Report, the Sex Education Advisory Board membership, the revised Code of Conduct and the Oakland Schools PAC representative.

The Sex Education Advisory Board is co-chaired by Kristy Pierce and Nicole Jenkins; by statute at least half its members must be parents and one parent must co-chair. Janet Grieme and Toina Wilson serve as Troy's parent representatives to the Oakland Schools special education Parent Advisory Committee, which participates in developing and reviewing the county plan for delivery of special education programs and services.

**What the September 18 minutes record**
Hammond and Miletti were absent, so everything carried 5-0. Twelve spring all-state athletes were recognized, all in girls' sports. The Mission Moment honored Troy Center for Transition students who spent the summer at the Technology Resource Center: TRC collected every district-owned iPad and **replaced 5,000 at the elementary level, handling almost 15,000 iPads in all**, and the TCT students uncased, cleaned, de-stickered and re-cased them at a rate the TRC team struggled to keep up with. The district also received ASBO International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for the CAFR for fiscal year ended June 30, 2017, and three MASB awards: Karl Schmidt's Master Board Member Award (a minimum of 368 education credits), Elizabeth Hammond's Level One Certification, and Gary Hauff's 20 Years of Service.

Mark Dziatczak's enrollment update as of September 12, 2018: **elementary down 61, middle school up 91, high school down 26 — the district up 4 students overall** against the same point the prior year.

And resolution 18-075 sold the Section 1 front parcel: 5.95 +/- acres plus up to an additional 1.74 +/- acres for a detention pond, to **Mondrian Properties for $1,974,000.00 plus an additional $40,000.00 for each unit over 24 approved by the City of Troy**, with a $25,000.00 earnest money deposit — the same buyer that took the Section 16 land in March, and the second half of the Section 1 plan adopted 4-2 that same month. The remaining land, including 11.28 +/- acres at Sidwell 20-01-451-001, is designated the Conservation Property.

**Treasurer's Report — August 2018**
Total check disbursements are $9,488,186.13, the General Fund group $4,846,208.08 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,614,275.55. With $1,612,398.21 of wire transfers, $205,054.03 of P-Card purchases and $16,089.81 of ACH debits, less $10,486.00 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $11,311,242.18.

**Curriculum — the gap analysis**
Mark Dziatczak and Kris Griffor report on 3rd grade reading and gap analysis. On combined grades 3-8 M-STEP for 2017-18, Troy is at **73% ELA, 48% math, 55% science and 44% social studies**, against Oakland's 28 LEAs at 51%, 36%, 33% and 27% and Michigan at 44%, 33%, 24% and 27% respectively. By grade, Troy's ELA runs 73%, 73%, 77%, 73%, 73% and 68% across grades 3 through 8. On the 2017-18 PSAT and SAT, Troy posts 84% on PSAT ELA grade 9, 80% on grade 10 and 79% on SAT ELA 11, against Oakland's 28 LEAs at 70%, 69% and 67%. Ranked across the 28 Oakland LEAs, Troy sits at or within two places of the top on every measure shown.

**Business — the audit**
David Youngstrom, audit partner at Yeo & Yeo, reports an **unmodified opinion**, the highest level of assurance, on the June 30, 2018 financial statements, with no material weaknesses, no significant deficiencies and no material noncompliance — and unmodified opinions on both federal major programs, the Child Nutrition Cluster and the Special Education Cluster.

General Fund revenue for the year: state $101,977,419 (67%), local $38,844,065 (26%), interdistrict sources $7,537,593 (5%) and federal $3,333,254 (2%). Expenditures: salaries $73,741,957 (49%), employee benefits $48,780,644 (32%), purchased services $19,695,836 (13%), supplies and materials $6,053,649 (4%) and other $1,980,625 (1%) — or by function, instruction $104,214,738 (69%) and supporting services $46,452,918 (31%), holding at 69% instructional for the third straight year against an Oakland County average of 64%.

Per-pupil General Fund revenue has risen from $10,641 in 2013 to $11,596 in 2018, with expenses at $11,516 — revenue exceeding expense in each of the last several years by a narrowing margin. The unassigned General Fund balance is between 14.74% and 16.52% of expenditures across 2014-2018. Enrollment over ten years runs 12,177 (2009) down to 12,032 and back up to **13,089 in 2018**.

Management comments carry federal procedures forward from the prior year as in progress, note time and effort record keeping as corrected, and raise federal procedures and athletic receipt procedures for the current year. Future challenges named: the state economic and political condition, rising fringe benefit costs, the retirement rate increase, **a post-employment benefit obligation of nearly $77M and a net pension liability of over $225.2M**.

Also present were Superintendent Machesky, administrators Carrier, Gottlieb, Fulcher, Griffor, Dziatczak, Harris, Soggs and West, and approximately 60 additional members of the audience. Every vote carried 5-0 with two absences.

Mr. Fulcher and the Board recognized the 2018 spring all-state athletes: Angela Anderanin (girls tennis), Paige Anderson (girls track), Tahra Brodbine (girls soccer), Jenna Doyle (girls track), Lauren Fulcher (girls track), Grace Johnson (girls track), Morgan MacDonald (girls lacrosse), Lauren Miller (girls soccer), Hanna Palomino (girls track), Sahaja Pinnu (girls tennis), Hailey Stewart (girls soccer) and Megan Worrel (girls track).

The Mission Moment recognized Troy Center for Transition students for their summer work at the Technology Resource Center. TRC collected all district-owned iPads over the summer and replaced 5,000 iPads at the elementary level, a project that required TRC staff to handle almost 15,000 iPads. Beth Soggs described how students from the Troy Center for Transition played an enormous part in the successful completion of the project, volunteering for weeks on end to help with uncasing iPads, cleaning the devices, removing stickers, putting new cases on, sorting charging bricks and cables, and "providing us daily with great company and an abundant supply of smiles." The minutes record that the students displayed amazing work ethic, showed up each day ready to work, and plowed through iPads at a rate that was difficult for the TRC team to keep up with a steady supply for them to case; the TRC team felt extremely fortunate to have established the relationship and looked forward to partnering again. Recognized were Emily Bernacki, Charley Mapes, Erin O'Donovan, Jared Weinberg, Phil Chu, Johnathan Kim, Alec Watson and Megan Daley.

**Curriculum 7.A: 3rd grade reading and gap analysis.** Deputy Superintendent Mark Dziatczak and Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, report on the gap analysis and third grade reading presentation first shared at the October 2 Board Workshop. The presentation opens on the OneTroy mission statement — "The purpose of the Troy School District is to ensure learning for all members of the school community" — the core value "ALL!", the vision of World Class by 2020, and a quotation from Fullan, Quinn and McEachen 2018: "It is an 'old notion' that struggling students must wait until they have mastered foundational skills before engaging in authentic and engaging tasks."

On combined M-STEP results for grades 3 through 8, percent proficient or advanced, the four-year series 2014-15 through 2017-18 runs: English language arts, Troy 81, 75, 73, 73 against Oakland's 28 LEAs at 58, 58, 56, 55 and Michigan at 48, 47, 46, 44; mathematics, Troy 73, 70, 69, 68 against the 28 LEAs at 50, 51, 51, 55 (with Troy's 48 for 17-18 shown separately in the grade-level chart) and Michigan at 37, 37, 38, 44; science, Troy 27, 38, 35, 48 against the 28 LEAs at 25, 26, 25, 36 and Michigan at 18, 19, 19, 26; and social studies, Troy 43, 48, 45, 44 against the 28 LEAs at 33, 36, 33 and Michigan at 27, 27, 24. In every subject and every year Troy runs well above both the county average and the state.

By subject and grade for 2017-18, Troy's ELA percentages are 73 (3rd), 73 (4th), 77 (5th), 73 (6th), 73 (7th) and 68 (8th); mathematics 73, 69, 66, 67, 70 and 66; science 43 (4th) and 47 (7th); social studies 55 (5th) and 56 (8th) — against Oakland 28 LEA and Michigan comparison lines running roughly 54, 54, 49, 48, 49, 44 and 45, 47, 41, 43, 43, 34, 35, 36 across the same categories.

On the PSAT and SAT, percent proficient or advanced across 2015-16 to 2017-18: PSAT ELA grade 9, Troy 82, 87, 84; PSAT ELA grade 10, Troy 80, 84, 85; SAT ELA grade 11, Troy 83, 80, 79; PSAT math grade 9, Troy 72, 77, 75; PSAT math grade 10, Troy 64, 68, 72; SAT math grade 11, Troy 70, 68 — against the 28 LEAs at 70, 69, 70, 69, 70, 69, 67, 68, 54, 52, 47, 47, 49, 47, 48 and Michigan at 61, 61, 61, 61, 63, 61, 60, 59, 58, 41, 42, 43, 36, 38, 38, 37, 36 across the corresponding series.

The presentation then ranks all 28 Oakland LEAs plus Michigan on 2017-18 percent met, separately for ELA grades 3-8 combined, mathematics grades 3-8 combined, PSAT ELA grade 9 and PSAT ELA grade 10 career or college ready. On the ELA ranking Troy stands at the top of the list; on mathematics Troy is third from the top behind Novi and Birmingham with Bloomfield Hills adjacent; on the PSAT grade 9 ranking Troy is second behind Birmingham; and on the grade 10 ranking Troy again sits at the top end. Oak Park, Pontiac and Hazel Park anchor the bottom of each ranking, with Michigan's statewide figure falling roughly a third of the way up the county list — a reminder that the county's spread is wider than the gap between the county and the state.

**Business 8.A and 8.B: the 2017-2018 audit.** David R. Youngstrom, CPA, audit partner from Yeo & Yeo, presents to the Board; a draft copy of the audit report had been presented at the October 2, 2018 workshop, and item 8.B asks the Board to accept and approve the audited 2018 financial statements as presented.

The financial statements receive an unmodified opinion — described in the presentation as the highest level of assurance, meaning the school's financial records and statements are fairly and appropriately presented in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America, including the design, implementation and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation and fair presentation of financial statements free from material misstatement whether due to fraud or error.

General Fund revenue for the year ended June 30, 2018, including other sources: state $101,977,419, or 67%; local $38,844,065, or 26%; interdistrict sources $7,537,593, or 5%; and federal $3,333,254, or 2%. General Fund expenditures by object: salaries $73,741,957, or 49%; employee benefits $48,780,644, or 32%; purchased services $19,695,836, or 13%; supplies and materials $6,053,649, or 4%; and other $1,980,625, or 1%. By function: instruction $104,214,738, or 69%, and supporting services $46,452,918, or 31%. The presentation notes that instruction consists of basic programs — elementary, middle and junior high, high school, pre-kindergarten and summer school — plus added needs covering special education, compensatory education, career and technical education and adult and continuing education, while supporting services covers pupil, instructional staff, general administration, school administration, business, operations and maintenance, pupil transportation, central and athletic activities.

The instructional expenditures comparison shows Troy at 68% for 2014-15 and 69% for each of 2015-16, 2016-17 and 2017-18, against an average of all Oakland County schools of 64% for 2016-17.

The per-pupil analysis of General Fund revenues and expenditures runs from 2013 to 2018: revenues $10,641, $10,812, $10,924, $11,094, $11,353 and $11,596, against expenses $10,585, $10,526, $10,560, $11,028, $11,145 and $11,516 — with revenue exceeding expense in each year but the gap tightening at the end of the series.

The ten-year enrollment trend runs 12,177 in 2009 down through 12,076 and 12,032, then back up through 12,312, 12,438, 12,563, 12,591, 12,717, 12,881 and 13,089 in 2018 — the audit's own confirmation of the growth the enrollment projections had been tracking.

The General Fund unassigned balance is charted with its percentage of expenditures for 2014 through 2018: 16.44%, 16.52%, 15.76%, 15.00% and 14.74%, drifting down across the five years even as the dollar balance holds.

On internal controls and compliance, the financial statements show no material weaknesses identified, no significant deficiencies identified and no material noncompliance. On federal awards, both major programs — the Child Nutrition Cluster and the Special Education Cluster — receive unmodified opinions with no material weaknesses, no significant deficiencies and no material noncompliance. Management comments carry forward from the prior year federal procedures, noted as in progress, and time and effort record keeping, noted as corrected; current year comments are federal procedures and athletic receipt procedures.

Under future challenges the auditor lists the state economic and political condition, rising fringe benefit costs, the retirement rate increase, a post-employment benefit obligation of nearly $77M, and a net pension liability of over $225.2M. Those last two are the largest figures in the packet, and they sit outside the year's operating numbers entirely.

**Business 8.C: Early Childhood Center Bid Pack 2.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on joint sealants, roller shades and access and security controls for the Early Childhood Center, reviewed by Rob Carson and the bond team of TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow. Christa Amalio of Barton Malow writes to Rick West on September 25, 2018 that bid proposals were received for four bid categories on September 18, 2018 for Bid Package 2 — the rebid categories being roller shades, joint sealants, casework and access control — and that due to low bidder turnout for the casework category the casework bids were not opened and that category will be rebid in October 2018. The proposals and qualifications of the apparent low bidders were reviewed during post-bid interviews over the preceding week, and the categories in the award recommendation are within the construction budget currently set for the project.

The awards are: 07000 joint sealants, D.C. Byers, $28,978.00; 12200 roller shades, The Sheer Shop, $30,163.00, with the bid tabulation noting that the first and second low bidders were disqualified; and 23000 access control, Mechanical Controls & Maintenance Inc. (MCMI), $86,225.00 — a total award of $145,366.00, approved as an expenditure of the Early Childhood Center Fund under bid 9862. The project location is given as 205 Square Lake Road, Troy, MI 48083. The unopened casework category included alternates for TMI Systems prefabricated casework — 416 cubbies, 48 inches high by 13 inches deep with 12-inch-wide cubbies modified to include sloped tops, located outside classrooms — and four casework units in each of 26 classrooms.

That casework has now failed to attract acceptable bids twice: it was one of the three categories held back from the March 2018 award of bid 9855, and it is held back again here.

**Business 8.D: International Academy paving improvements.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on site improvement work at International Academy East and Baker Middle School, reviewed by Rob Carson and Barton Malow. Carson's September 27, 2018 memorandum on RFP 9863, Bid Pack 2, BSSF, IAE site work, records that the scope is to reconstruct the Boyd entrance drive so that it can safely handle two-way traffic along with a pedestrian walk, that the RFP produced 4 bid responses and competitive pricing, and that he recommends the low qualified bidder: category 320000 sitework, Best Asphalt, Inc., at $57,750.00, plus a contingency of $5,775.00. The resolution awards the site improvement work to Best Asphalt, Inc. in the amount of $63,525.00 as an expenditure of the Building Site and Sinking Project Fund — one of the projects named in the August BSSF four-year projection.

**Business 8.E: purchase agreement, Wattles Road property.** The resolution recites that the School District has marketed and desires to sell a parcel described as part of the southeast quarter of Section 14, Town 2 North, Range 11 East, City of Troy, Oakland County, beginning at a point on the north right-of-way line of E. Wattles Road distant North 88 degrees 40 minutes 52 seconds West 1550.47 feet along the south line of Section 14 and North 00 degrees 26 minutes 24 seconds East 60.01 feet from the southeast corner of Section 14; thence North 88 degrees 40 minutes 52 seconds West 237.09 feet along the north right-of-way line of E. Wattles Road; thence South 00 degrees 26 minutes 24 seconds West 60.01 feet to a point on the south line of Section 14; thence North 88 degrees 40 minutes 52 seconds West 60.00 feet along that south line; thence North 00 degrees 26 minutes 24 seconds East 203.96 feet; thence North 89 degrees 52 minutes 26 seconds East 295.10 feet; thence South 00 degrees 18 minutes 09 seconds East 151.43 feet to the point of beginning — containing 47,324.04 square feet, or 1.086 acres of land.

The district has received an Offer To Purchase from Madhu Babu Jampala at a purchase price of Two Hundred Seventy Five Thousand and 00/100 ($275,000.00) Dollars with an earnest money deposit of Ten Thousand and 00/100 ($10,000.00) Dollars, and the resolution authorizes the sale on terms substantially similar to the Offer, with the Superintendent or designee authorized to execute it. This is the smallest of the year's land transactions and the only one sold to an individual rather than a development company.

**Other 10.A: NSBA Advocacy Institute.** As required by Board Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board; Reimbursement of Expenses, any expenditure of district funds for members for out-of-state meetings must have prior approval by resolution. Board Secretary Gary Hauff and Board Trustee Elizabeth Hammond have indicated their desire to attend the National School Boards Association Advocacy Institute Conference in Washington, D.C., January 27-29, 2019, and the resolution approves their attendance as representatives of the Troy Board of Education.

**Closed session 11.A.** The Board must pass a resolution to go into closed session to discuss an attorney-client privilege, and no additional business will take place after that other than officially adjourning. The resolution provides that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), the Troy Board of Education shall go into closed session to discuss an attorney-client privilege, on a roll call vote of Schmidt, Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Miletti and Philippart.

Read as a whole, the October 2018 packet is the district's annual reckoning meeting. The audit confirms a system operating well by every conventional measure — an unmodified opinion, no findings, 69% of spending on instruction against a county average of 64%, per-pupil revenue exceeding per-pupil expense, enrollment at a ten-year high of 13,089 — and the gap analysis confirms the same on the academic side, with Troy at or near the top of all 28 Oakland LEAs on every test reported. The two figures that do not fit that picture are in the auditor's closing slide: a post-employment benefit obligation of nearly $77M and a net pension liability of over $225.2M, neither of them visible anywhere in the operating statements the Board is asked to accept.

Closed Session, consisting of A. Consideration: Attorney-Client Privilege; and 5. Adjournment.

Business item 3.A., tabbed 03.17.16 in the packet, carries the heading Consideration: Policies Services Provider. It recommends that the School District engage Lusk Albertson to assist in reviewing, preparing, and maintaining Board bylaws, policies, and administrative regulations as stated in the resolution that follows, and the recommended action is to accept that resolution. The suggested resolution, printed with blank lines for "Moved by," "Supported by," and for Yes and No tallies, reads that the Troy Board of Education engage the services of Lusk Albertson to assist in review, preparation and maintenance of Board bylaws, policies, and administrative regulations consistent with their submitted proposal dated March 8, 2016, in the amount not to exceed $15,000; and $4,000 annually for updates; and that these amounts be approved as an expenditure of the General Fund.

The supporting exhibit is an engagement letter dated March 8, 2016 from Kevin T. Sutton of Lusk Albertson, PLC, marked "Via Email Only," showing the email address KSutton@LuskAlbertson.com and Direct Dial No. (248) 988-5695, addressed to Mr. Rick West, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098, under the subject line "Re: Lusk Albertson Policy Service - Updated." The letter opens by stating that the firm is pleased the Troy School District is considering retaining Lusk Albertson School Policy Services (referred to throughout as LA) to help prepare its Board bylaws, policies, and administrative regulations, and recalls that it was Sutton's pleasure to meet with the Board of Education on February 2, 2016 to discuss the service. If the district wishes to move forward, it is asked to counter-sign where indicated and forward a copy to Sutton's attention to confirm the terms of LA's engagement for the project.

Under the heading "LA Bylaws, Policies, and Administrative Regulations," the letter provides that LA will supply the district with a standard set of bylaws, policies, and administrative regulations. As discussed with the Board, LA's standard documents are described as much more concise than the district's current version and, among other things, do not attempt to re-state the law, since the district is obligated to follow the law regardless of its policies and administrative regulations. LA can deliver the standard bylaws and policies upon engagement; the standard administrative regulations were still in the process of being completed and were anticipated to be finished by the end of that month. LA will also obtain and incorporate input from the Board of Education and Administration as necessary to finalize the district's documents.

Under "Copyrighting and Branding," the district understands and acknowledges the efforts undertaken by LA to create model bylaws, policies, and administrative regulations, as well as LA's intellectual property rights in those products, and in recognition agrees that all bylaws, policies, and administrative regulations prepared by LA will be copyrighted and will be and remain the property of LA even if the model policies are modified consistent with district input, with the district holding LA's license to use them. It is expressly understood and agreed that the district will continue to have license to use documents created under the agreement even if the district decides at some future point to discontinue its relationship with LA's School Policy Service, and that if the district invokes the opt-out provision, it shall continue to have license to maintain and use the bylaws, policies, and administrative regulations created with LA's assistance. The district agrees that it will not facilitate the unauthorized use or sale of LA's bylaws, policies, or administrative regulations, and understands and agrees that the final documents will include a visible and easily identifiable text reference reflecting LA's ownership rights; LA agrees that it will consult with the district regarding the manner in which that text reference is presented to the public.

Under "Cost," the letter sets the cost of the initial set of bylaws and policies at $5,000.00, payable upon delivery, and the cost of the initial set of administrative regulations at $10,000.00, payable upon delivery. These flat fees include whatever time it takes LA attorneys to obtain the necessary input from the Board of Education and Administration to create the final complete sets of bylaws, policies and administrative regulations. The cost of updates to bylaws and policies is stated as $1,500.00 annually, and the cost of updates to administrative regulations as $2,500.00 annually. The district will be billed for annual updates on or about December 1st of every year and will receive advance notice of any price increases. Under "Opt-Out," the district may elect to opt out of the LA Policy Service by providing LA with notice, in writing, at least 30 days before December 1st of any year. The letter closes over the signature of Kevin T. Sutton for Lusk Albertson, PLC, followed by a countersignature block for Troy School District with blanks for "By," "Its," and "Dated."

Item 4.A., also tabbed 03.17.16, is the closed session. The packet explains that the Board must pass a resolution to go into closed session to discuss an attorney-client privilege, that following passage of the resolution the Board of Education will go into closed session, and that no additional business will take place after that time other than to officially adjourn the meeting. The recommended action is to adopt the resolution, which is printed with blanks for "Moved by" and "Supported by" and provides that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8 (c), the Troy Board of Education shall go into closed session to discuss an attorney-client privilege. A roll call vote is specified, and the roll is printed as Miletti, Philippart, Schmidt, Underwood, Edmunds, Fleming, Hauff, with no votes recorded, consistent with the packet being a pre-meeting agenda rather than approved minutes. The agenda ends with item 5, Adjournment. Aside from the Lusk Albertson engagement and the closed session, no other business, personnel action, purchase, or financial report appears in the packet.

An attached confidential October 1, 2016 letter from Dennis R. Pollard of Secrest Wardle, 2600 Troy Center Drive, P.O. Box 5025, Troy, MI 48007-5025, 248-851-9500, reports that the Court of Appeals dismissed the appeal in its entirety on September 20, 2016 and that the Liaison Committee authorized seeking leave to appeal to the Michigan Supreme Court on a single issue: the Legislature's practice of adopting a categorical appropriation while concurrently reducing other appropriations to the same local units. The letter recounts the 1997 decision holding special education services mandated under the Headlee Amendment, the resulting dollar-for-dollar deduction and "three bucket funding scheme," and the 2010 decision on the Center for Educational Performance and Information (CEPI), after which the Legislature adopted School Aid Act Section 152a in 2011 with an equal offsetting reduction in each district's general operating revenues. It quotes Article 9, Section 25, cites Section 29, and sets a deadline of November 1, 2016 to submit the application for leave.

**Meeting**
Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting, Tuesday, June 5, 2018, 7:00 P.M., Athens High School, 4333 John R, Troy, MI 48085. Agenda: Pledge of Allegiance; Recognition (items A through GGG, followed by a five-minute recess); Additions & Deletions; Public Communication (agenda items); General Consent Agenda; Personnel; Curriculum; Business; Public Communication (non-agenda items); Other; Adjournment. Public participation is limited to one-half hour for agenda items and one-half hour for non-agenda items, three minutes per speaker, with the President able to shorten the limit to accommodate everyone. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) Mondays and Wednesdays at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. and posted at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition**
Mike Jolly reads the three athletics items; the remaining scripts are assigned to board members by first name (Karl, Steve, Gary, Paula, Elizabeth, Todd, Nancy). Items 2.A through 2.C name the Synchronized Swim State Champions by grade and school, the All-State Athletes for Winter 2017, and the Senior Scholar Athletes for 2017-2018 who carried a 3.5 grade point average. Items 2.D through 2.GGG recognize competition results, among them: AMC8 first and second in the nation (Boulan Park); a 2nd in Nation at the Intermediate Level in the 13th Annual Chinese Bridge Speech Contest at the University of Massachusetts; "Best in Show" at the 50th Michigan Student Film Festival at the DIA's Detroit Film Theatre for a Larson documentary on the Bosnian War, with Athens taking Best of Show for "Don't Turn Your Windshield Into A Screen," "Saving Lake St. Clair" and "Athens Fringe Fest"; an IA-East FIRST Robotics team placing 30th in the Curie Division at the World Championships, with a student named to the First Deans List, one of ten students in the world; MATHCOUNTS 1st in State and 7th and 12th in Nation; a 2nd place internationally at the Intel Science and Engineering Fair for "Context-Aware Medical Image Super-Resolution using Convolutional Neural Networks"; a Michigan History Day national finalist website, "The Internment of Japanese Americans"; 1st place in the U.S. in the National High School Biology Scholarship; and 1st in Nation at the Washington University Chemistry Tournament against 54 other teams.

**Consent agenda (item 5)**
A. Minutes of the May 1, 2018 Board Workshop. B. Minutes of the May 15, 2018 Board Meeting. C. Resolution to hold a public hearing on the proposed 2018/2019 school year budget.

**May 15, 2018 minutes, as attached**
The May meeting recognized the Facilities Study Attendance Area Review Team — City Attorney Lori Bluhm, Emily Cremers, Pupil Accounting Coordinator Laura Duzey, Jeff Frederick, Victoria King, Veronica Pala, Delia Rodi-Barczys, Lori Sisk and Courtney Spangler, with Mark Dziatczak and Kris Griffor as administrative liaisons — and named Tina Houser, Health Care Aide at Morse Elementary, the Outstanding Support Staff Employee of the Year from seventeen nominees. The retiree list runs to twenty-eight names, described by the superintendent as 688 years of collective service.

Nine administrative appointments passed, each a two-year probationary contract without tenure: Kandice Moynihan as Finance Director (June 6, 2018), John Pagel as Director of Employee Services, Tim Fulcher as Director of Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment, Sarah Young as Special Education Supervisor, Erin Keyser as Director of Early Childhood Programs, Shari Pawlus as Principal of Hill Elementary, Jonathan Cross as Principal of Baker Middle School, Anthony Morse as Principal of Boulan Park Middle School and Christian Mueller as Principal of Smith Middle School, the last eight effective July 1, 2018. Business actions awarded flooring replacement to Conventional Carpet at $650,000.00 and asbestos abatement to Abatement & Demolition Services at $37,645.00, both from the Building Site and Sinking Project Fund. Under Public Act 419 of 2004 the Board designated Mr. Steve Gottlieb as its representative to the 2018 Oakland Schools electoral body and directed him to vote for Dr. Theresa Rich and Mr. Marc Katz for six-year terms ending June 30, 2024. Every vote recorded 6 yes, 0 no, with Philippart absent.

**5.C. Budget public hearing**
Michigan law requires a public hearing on a proposed budget with notice at least six days ahead, stating the time and place, where the proposed budget may be inspected, and — in 11-point bold faced type — that the property tax millage rate proposed to be levied will be a subject of the hearing. The resolution sets the hearing for June 19, 2018 at 7:00 p.m. at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois Road, and makes copies available at the Administration Building from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., June 13 through June 19, 2018. Exhibit A carries the notice text for publication.

Resolution to hold a public hearing on the proposed 2018-2019 school year budget.** The resolution recites that Michigan law requires every local unit of government, including a school district, to hold a public hearing on its proposed budget with notice at least six days before; that the notice must include the time and place of the hearing and where a copy of the proposed budget is available for public inspection; that the notice must include, in 11-point bold faced type, the statement "THE PROPERTY TAX MILLAGE RATE PROPOSED TO BE LEVIED TO SUPPORT THE PROPOSED BUDGET WILL BE A SUBJECT OF THIS HEARING"; and that the hearing must precede final adoption. It resolves that a public hearing be held on June 19, 2018 at a regular Board meeting beginning at 7:00 p.m. at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois Road, Troy 48098, to receive testimony and discuss the proposed 2018-2019 budget, and authorizes the Secretary to publish notice in substantially the form of Exhibit A in a newspaper of general circulation at least six days before the hearing. Exhibit A states that copies of the proposed budget will be available for public inspection at the Administration Building, 4400 Livernois, from 8:00 a.m. until 5:00 p.m., Wednesday, June 13, 2018 through Tuesday, June 19, 2018, and is signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education.

**8.A — Building and site sinking fund on the November ballot**
The Board resolves to ask voters for a building and site sinking fund tax of one mill annually for ten years, from July 1, 2018 through June 30, 2028, at a special school election on November 7, 2017, and authorizes the Superintendent or designee to certify the ballot language to the Election Coordinator no later than 4:00 p.m. on August 15, 2017. The ballot text explains that proceeds must be audited and cannot be used for teacher, administrator or employee salaries, maintenance or other operating expenses, and may go to purchasing real estate for sites, constructing or repairing school buildings, school security improvements, and acquiring or upgrading technology. One mill is $1.00 per $1,000 of taxable valuation, estimated to provide approximately $3,745,257 during the 2018 calendar year.

A draft campaign timeline accompanies it, running from April vendor outreach through an August 1 petition filing, the August 15 ballot certification, a September 8 School Life kickoff issue, a September 15 informational mailer, an October 10 registration deadline, an October 15 podcast and an October 16 mailer to district homes, to the November 7 election.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, August 15, 2017, 7:00 PM, **Administration Building**, 4400 Livernois — not the usual Services Building. No recognition items.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the July 18 special workshop and July 18 meeting, and the June 2017 Treasurer's Report.

**What the July 18 minutes record**
The special workshop (6:15–7:40 p.m.) covered a teaching and learning report and a business update on the **Building and Site Sinking Fund Tax Proposal**. The regular meeting followed at 7:46.

Administrator contracts were extended — the roster names Ryan Brinks at IA-East, Lara Dixon at Athens, Remo Roncone at Troy High, Joe Duda at Larson, **Timothy Fulcher at Smith**, **Audra Melton at Baker**, Joyce Brasington, **Janice Brzezinski at Hill**, Brian Canfield, Mike Cottone, Tammy DiPonio, Sarah Glasser, Matt Jansen, Melanie Morey, **John Pagel at Martell**, Jeremey Whan, and assistant principals Melissa Curth, Robert Dowd, Dan House, Dan Mills, William Turner, Brian Zawislak, Amy Buchanan, **Jonathan Cross at Baker** and **Anthony Morse at Boulan Park**. Nearly all of these names recur in the May 2018 reshuffle: Fulcher to athletics, Pagel to employee services, Cross and Morse to principalships, Brzezinski and Melton to the retiree list.

Added to the agenda that night was a Leonard principal appointment: **Dr. Erin Detmer**, approved 7-0 — the Hill literacy specialist whose Teachers College coaching work the Board had recognized in May.

**Resolution 17-072 — the sinking fund goes to the ballot.** The recitals state that the district is a Michigan general powers school district whose elections are governed by the Michigan Election Law, Public Act 116 of 1954; that **in order to improve and repair its facilities it is necessary to ask the voters to approve a building and site sinking fund tax levy of one (1) mill annually for a period of ten (10) years from July 1, 2018 through June 30, 2028**; and that the district wishes to submit the proposal at a **Special School Election on November 7, 2017**. Ballot language must be certified to the Election Coordinator by 4:00 p.m. on **August 15, 2017** — the day of this very meeting.

The vote was **6 yes, 1 no — Mrs. Hammond**. This is the proposal the Epic MRA survey had tested in April, which found 61% outright Yes at one mill and warned repeatedly that raising the ask would collapse support; the Board asked for exactly one mill.

**Treasurer's Report — June 2017**
The fiscal year's closing month. Total check disbursements are **$12,522,371.11**, the General Fund group $9,310,856.14 and the General Fund (101) itself $8,670,831.46. Adding $3,352,991.59 of wire transfers, $165,585.20 of P-Card purchases and $24,980.62 of ACH debits, less $671.00 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are **$16,065,257.52**.

**Curriculum — 90 seats at IA East**
The Board adopts a Section 105c resolution accepting applications for **90 non-resident 9th grade students** who reside outside Oakland County, where that ISD is contiguous with Oakland ISD's boundaries, for the purpose of attending the International Academy East program. Like the August 2018 version, this is a 105c-only resolution adopted more than a year ahead of the school year it governs; the seat count would drop to 85 the following August.

**Business — the surveillance upgrade**
The district shares its video surveillance system with the City of Troy, and the City is moving to Pelco's latest **VideoXpert** platform. Beth Soggs' July 26 memo — her first business item as the Director of Technology appointed in May — explains that the current Pelco software used by both is **discontinued, with an end-of-support announcement expected**, and that the City wants to stay on a supported platform.

At the time of the City's upgrade the district's system converts to a **standalone Pelco VideoXpert Enterprise system**, with the City repurposing some of its existing hardware to supply what the district needs. Afterward the district manages its own system, the City retaining view access to district cameras. The practical gain is access: today footage can be reached only from a few specific computers and is slow because of the connection speed between City and District; the new configuration lets the Pelco client run on any computer on the district network, giving Safe-Ed and building administration far better access and search.

The award is **Tyco SimplexGrinnell, $44,682.00**, from the General Fund.

Detmer is the Hill literacy specialist whose work with the Teachers College coaching model the Board had recognized two months earlier, moving from literacy specialist to building principal.

Resolution 17-071 addressed the six secondary schools for 2016/2017.

**Resolution 17-072: the Building and Site Sinking Fund Tax Proposal for a Special School Election on November 7, 2017.** Moved by Mr. Miletti and supported by Mr. Hauff, the resolution recites that the School District is a Michigan general powers school district operating under the Revised School Code, and as such its elections are governed by the Michigan Election Law, Public Act 116 of 1954, as amended; that the School District has determined that in order to improve and repair its facilities it is necessary to ask the voters to approve a building and site sinking fund tax levy of one mill annually for a period of ten years from July 1, 2018 through June 30, 2028; that the district desires to submit the proposal to the voters at a Special School Election to be held on November 7, 2017; that the Michigan Election Law requires the district to certify ballot language for any proposals to the district's Election Coordinator not later than 4:00 p.m. local time on the twelfth Tuesday before the election date; and that the district desires to approve the proposal and authorize the Superintendent or his designee to certify the ballot language.

It resolves that the Building and Site Sinking Fund Tax Proposal attached as Exhibit A is approved; that the Superintendent or his designee is authorized to certify the Proposal to the district's Election Coordinator not later than 4:00 p.m. local time on August 15, 2017; and further authorizes the Superintendent or designee to take related steps.

The vote was 6 yes, 1 no — Mrs. Hammond. It is the only recorded dissent in the July meeting and one of the few in these 2017 packets, where nearly every resolution carries unanimously.

Two details are worth drawing out. First, the certification deadline in the resolution is 4:00 p.m. on August 15, 2017 — the date of the very meeting whose packet carries these minutes, meaning the ballot language had to be filed the same day the Board next convened. Second, the ask is exactly one mill. The Epic MRA community survey delivered to the Board on June 13 had tested precisely that figure, found 61% outright Yes with 7% leaning yes, and stated in identical words across three separate slides that tax neutrality is what earns the community's endorsement and that raising the ask collapses support. The survey background had also noted the countervailing pressure — that a district can pursue only one sinking fund every ten years, so there is reason to ask for more. The Board asked for one mill, over a single dissent.

**Treasurer's Report, June 2017.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $8,670,831.46, with Total General Fund of $9,310,856.14 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $12,522,371.11. Adding ACH debits of $24,980.62, outgoing wire transfers of $3,352,991.59 and P-Card purchases of $165,585.20, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $671.00, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $16,065,257.52 — the largest month of the fiscal year, as June closes out contracts, capital work and the year's payroll obligations. The middle sections of the packet are the June check register run by fund.

**Personnel 6.A: elementary and secondary.** The item covers the personnel recommendations for the incoming school year.

**Curriculum 7.A: Schools of Choice, Section 105c, 9th grade for 2018-2019.** In accordance with Michigan state law, school districts shall pass a resolution each school year if they intend to participate in a Schools of Choice program. It is anticipated that seats will be available for the 2018-2019 school year for grade 9 at the International Academy East, and the item proposes a Section 105c resolution for 90 non-resident 9th grade students who reside outside of Oakland County, if that intermediate school district is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries.

The resolution provides that the Board of Education of the Troy School District, exercising the option permitted by Section 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, will accept applications for a Schools of Choice program for the 2018-2019 school year for 90 non-resident 9th grade students who reside outside Oakland County, if that Intermediate School District is contiguous with the Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries, for the purposes of attending the International Academy East program located in the Troy School District.

As with the equivalent resolution adopted in August 2018, this is a 105c-only measure — the International Academy is a consortium program drawing from beyond the county by design, so there is no companion Section 105 resolution as there is for the district's elementary and middle school seats. It is also adopted more than a year ahead of the school year it governs. The seat count would be reduced from 90 to 85 in the following year's resolution.

**Business 8.A: video surveillance software system upgrade.** The Troy School District collaborates with the City of Troy for its video surveillance system. The City needs to update its system, which also requires the district to update its software.

Beth Soggs' July 26, 2017 memorandum to the Board explains the situation — her first business item in the packets as the Director of Technology appointed in May. The City needs to update its system to Pelco's latest VideoXpert software platform, and as a result the district also needs to update its software. The current Pelco software utilized by both the City and the district has been discontinued by Pelco, and an end of support announcement is expected in the future; the City wants to ensure it remains on a supported platform and desires several of the features available in the new software.

At the time of the City upgrade, the district's system will be converted to a standalone Pelco VideoXpert Enterprise system. The City will repurpose some of its existing hardware to provide the district the hardware necessary for this configuration and software update. After the update, the district will manage its own system on the updated platform, with the City retaining access to view district cameras.

Soggs sets out the benefits, which are about access rather than image quality. With the current configuration, footage can only be accessed from a few specific computers in the district, and access is slow due to the connection speed between City and district. The updated software and configuration allows the Pelco client to be installed on computers anywhere on the district network, providing greater access to Safe-Ed and building administration, and better search capabilities.

The resolution awards the video surveillance software upgrade to Tyco SimplexGrinnell in the amount of $44,682.00 as an expenditure of the General Fund. The packet attaches system documentation for both the City of Troy Police Department and the Troy School District video surveillance systems.

The arrangement is a small but revealing piece of municipal infrastructure: the school district's camera system is not its own but a shared platform with the city police department, and a vendor's end-of-life announcement on the City side obliges the district to spend $44,682.00 and take on management of a standalone system it had not previously run. The upgrade's chief benefit — that Safe-Ed and building administrators can reach footage from any district computer rather than a handful — connects directly to the Safe-Ed security contract the Board had renewed for three years the month before.

Read as a whole, the August 2017 packet is thin on its own business and heavy in what it carries forward. Its two actions are 90 out-of-county seats at IA East and a $44,682.00 software upgrade the City's vendor forced. ## Item 5.F - Oakland Intermediate School District 2020-2021 budget

Section 624 of the Revised School Code requires the ISD to submit its proposed budget by May 1 and each constituent board to adopt a resolution of support or disapproval by June 1. Troy expresses support while stating that its support is for the sole purpose of complying with Section 624 and that the Intermediate School District is responsible for its own operations, including adoption of its budget. The transmittal letter of March 24, 2020 from Superintendent Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson projects growth in Oakland Schools property tax revenues of 3.25%, tempered by a possible Headlee rollback of the operating millage measured against the Consumer Price Index. Literacy Essentials Oakland, prompted by declining 3rd grade M-STEP reading levels, is a four-year, $5 million pre-K through 3rd grade initiative with all 28 constituent districts. The CTE allocation to LEAs was increased by more than 25% in 2019-20 and continues in 2020-21. Shared services cover technology for thirteen (13) districts and business office services for five (5); Illuminate Education has served all twenty-eight (28) districts and two (2) public school academies since Fall of 2016 with a 50% subsidy again in 2020-21. Personnel costs carry step increases plus a 1.0% across-the-board increase; the Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy retirement rate rises from 27.5% to 28.21% on October 1, 2020, with a blended rate projected at 28.0%. Health care hard caps are $18,596.96 family, $14,260.37 individual plus one and $6,818.87 single after 1/1/20, projected at $19,154.87, $14,688.18 and $7,023.44 after 1/1/21 assuming medical price index growth of 3.0%. PA-18 base special education distribution is budgeted to increase approximately $10.0 million, or 7.9%, with $3.5 million more for group homes, startup, extraordinary expenditures and capital, following $3.39 million above base in FY 2019-20.

## Item 10.A - Oakland Schools biennial election

Under Public Act 419 of 2004 and MCL 380.614, intermediate board members are elected biennially on the first Monday in June by an electoral body of one designee per constituent district, on a resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days before the election. Troy supports Mr. George Ehlert for the one (1) position, a term of six (6) years ending June 30, 2026, directing its representative to vote for him at least on the first ballot. Filing closed May 1, 2020 and resolutions were due May 29, 2020; balloting is in person 5:30-7:30 PM June 1, 2020 at the Oakland Schools Conference Center, 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford, with no absentee ballots and oath of office July 7, 2020. The March 25, 2020 cover letter is from Barb DeMarco, Secretary, Oakland Schools Board of Education, and a May 4, 2020 email from Nicole Christian notes Mr. Ehlert is the only filed candidate; the statute sets a nonrefundable $100.00 filing fee in lieu of petitions.

**Item 8.A — Resolution to submit replacement operating millage proposal.** The Board determined it necessary for continuing operation to restore and replace the authority to levy 18 mills for operating purposes on non-homestead property, previously approved by voters in 2015 and rolled back by application of the Headlee Amendment to the Michigan Constitution, and to increase the prior authority in the event of future rollbacks. The proposal is to be submitted at the General School Election of November 6, 2018, and the ballot wording must be certified to the Clerk of the County of Oakland, State of Michigan — the School District Election Coordinator — not later than August 14, 2018, as required by Act 116, Public Acts of Michigan, 1954, as amended. The resolution directs the Election Coordinator to post and publish notice of the last day of registration and notice of election and to have ballots prepared and printed in the form of Exhibit A, and rescinds conflicting resolutions. It is signed by Gary Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education, with a certification that the resolution was adopted at a regular meeting held July 17, 2018 in compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976. Exhibit A, the Replacement Operating Millage Proposal for the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, explains that the proposal would restore and replace the authority to levy the statutory limit of 18 mills on non-homestead property (principally industrial and commercial real property and residential rental property), which currently expires with the district's 2025 tax levy, and allow continued levy of the statutory limit of 18 mills in the event of future Headlee rollbacks of up to 3 mills, allowing the district to continue receiving revenues at the full per pupil foundation allowance permitted by the State. Owner occupied homes and qualified agricultural property are exempt. The ballot question asks whether the limitation on total taxes assessed against all property except principal residences and other property exempted by law within the Troy School District be increased in the amount of 21 mills, with 18 mills being the maximum allowable levy ($18.00 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation), for a period of eight (8) years, 2018 to 2025 inclusive, with 17.684 mills of the 21 mills being a replacement of authorized millage that would otherwise expire on December 31, 2025 and 0.316 mills being a restoration of millage lost as a result of the reduction required by the Michigan Constitution. The proposal states that the operating millage, if approved and levied, would provide estimated revenues to the School District of $22,644,260 during the 2018 calendar year, to be used for general operating purposes.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of November 20, 2018 at the Services Building — a short meeting after a heavy October. The Board appoints Kimberly Cornelissen assistant principal at Smith Middle School, chosen from 148 applications, awards $21,739.30 to Signarama of Troy for refurbishing the Troy High messaging sign, sells a six-foot strip of Boyd Street frontage to Delmar Homes for $10,000.00, and grants Consumers Energy a permanent pipeline easement across the Boulan Park Middle School property. The September 2018 Treasurer's Report carries total disbursements in period of $10,004,593.88.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, November 20, 2018, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**Recognition**
The Mission Moment features Troy High's "Counseling Colts Care" initiative — a program the Troy High counselors started this year working with all 9th grade students to help them feel welcome and at home at the school. Jesse Allgeier, Anne Young and Tommy Keegan present and receive certificates. A second Mission Moment on the Troy College & Career High School Community Connection brings Deb MacDonald-Linford and Jason Garza to the podium.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the October 2 workshop, the October 16 meeting and the October 16 closed session, the September 2018 Treasurer's Report, and the Consumers Energy easement at Boulan Park.

**What the October 16 minutes record**
Miletti was absent, so everything carried 6-0. The "Protect the Vulnerable" Mission Moment is described more fully here than in the October packet: Allie Hayes, a student at the Troy Center for Transition, was chosen by Athens students as Grand Marshall of their Homecoming Parade, "an opportunity to live out the district's mission of 'All means All.'" Faculty and students from Athens and Troy High, para educators and colleagues from every building, multiple media outlets and Dr. Machesky all took part; the community stood beside Allie in yellow shirts, cheering and calling her name. Her family "witnessed a restored positive self-image armed with courage to continue to fight to protect all vulnerable adults." Allie handed out yellow tee-shirts and cookies to Board members.

Also recorded: the 54 National Merit semifinalists; the audit accepted; ECC Bid Pack 2 at $145,366.00; IA East site work to Best Asphalt; the Wattles Road sale approved 6-0 by name (Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt); and NSBA Advocacy Institute attendance approved. In public communication, Troy resident **Robert Shingles addressed the Board on the district's anti-bullying policy** and said he would like to offer suggestions to add to the current language. The Board went into closed session at 8:52 p.m. on attorney-client privilege and adjourned at 9:40.

The October 2 workshop had run to 9:37 p.m. with Taylor Diener of Yeo & Yeo present, covering the audit report, bids 9862 and 9863, third grade reading and the gap analysis, the Code of Conduct, board professional learning on athletics and student participation and on diversity and inclusion, OCSBA proposed bylaws changes and the NSBA Advocacy Institute.

**Treasurer's Report — September 2018**
Total check disbursements are $7,791,368.76 — matching the register's own TOTAL REPORT line — of which the General Fund group is $4,888,631.83 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,687,037.44. With $2,039,260.79 of wire transfers, $163,415.24 of P-Card purchases and $12,339.09 of ACH debits, less $1,790.00 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $10,004,593.88.

**The Consumers Energy easement**
Consumers Energy has requested a permanent easement on the Boulan Park Middle School property to construct, operate, maintain, inspect, survey, replace, reconstruct, improve, remove, relocate, change the size of, enlarge and protect a pipeline or pipelines in, on, under, over, across and through a portion of the parcel. The resolution authorizes Superintendent Richard M. Machesky to execute the agreement. The attached document is captioned "Easement for Pipelines — Coolidge & Golf View Scada Pressure Monitor," SAP# 32537548, Master Tract# TRN000916037635, Agreement# MI00000038782.

**Personnel — 148 applications for one job**
Kimberly Cornelissen is appointed Assistant Principal, Smith Middle School, on a two-year probationary administrative contract effective December 3, 2018. She began her career as a fourth grade teacher at Wass Elementary, served as a Summer Success Academy teacher from June 2014 through July 2016, sat on the Wass leadership and continuous school improvement teams, and attended the Aspiring Principals' Leadership Academy at Oakland Schools as a Troy representative; she holds a B.A. in special education and an M.A. in K-12 educational administration, both from Michigan State.

The packet publishes the whole funnel: **148 applications submitted, 17 granted first round interviews, 2 to the final round** — Cornelissen and Laura Schlitt — with Cornelissen the final selection. Several of the seventeen are the district's own recent hires and teachers, among them Jessica Blumer and Zack MacIntosh.

**Business**
RFP 9866 sought bids to replace the electronic message center, school logos and aluminum skirting on the Troy High school sign at the Long Lake entrance. Five bids were opened October 30 and **Signarama of Troy** was the low qualified bidder: base bid $19,763.00 plus 10% contingency of $1,976.30, for a total project cost of **$21,739.30** from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund.

The Boyd Street item sells **the easterly 6.00 feet of Lot 27, "Beaver Run Subdivision"** in the southwest quarter of Section 23 to **Delmar Homes for $10,000.00** — the district's fourth land transaction of 2018 and by far its smallest, a six-foot strip rather than a development parcel. (The certification block and Exhibit A cover sheet carry over text from the October Wattles Road item, reciting an October 16 meeting date and naming Madhu Babu Jampala; the resolution itself is the November Delmar Homes sale.)
